The Doctrine of Pervasion (Vyāptivāda) // 1 //

Now, the definition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) according to our own system. Next, regarding the auxiliary means of knowledge (*anupramāṇa*), [it was stated]: "That [pervasion] is primarily [the basis] of cognition and verbal testimony. *Commentary titled Nyāyadīpa:* [The text continues: ...in the context of the auxiliary means of knowledge... (Note: The provided fragment appears to be the opening of a commentary on a section concerning the definition of *vyāpti* within the framework of *anupramāṇa*, specifically referencing the relationship between cognition and verbal testimony.)
The Doctrine of Pervasion // 1 //
Now, the definition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) according to our own system:

I pay homage to that Lord of Kamalā, who is endowed with perfect and auspicious qualities, whom the Vedas— accompanied by sound reasoning (*sattarka*)— proclaim, and who is to be propitiated through dharma and worshipped by the deities.
Showing the connection with what precedes, he states the purpose of what follows: "Now," etc.

Following the determination of the nature of the means of valid cognition known as verbal testimony (*śabda*) along with its auxiliary factors, the means of valid cognition known as inference (*anumāna*), together with its auxiliaries, is discussed in this chapter.
In the *Tarkatāṇḍava* accompanied by the *Puṇyāyadīpa*, the third chapter:
Since it has been stated that verbal testimony (*śabda*) in the form of the Veda is the primary means of knowledge, inference (*anumāna*), which supports it, is now being discussed.
Establishment by logical proof (*upapatti*) is inference (*anumāna*).
Proof is that which is pervaded (*vyāpya*).
What is the reason?
That which supports it is "pregnant with a reason" (*hetugarbha*);
the meaning is that it is so called because it supports verbal authority (*śabdapramāṇa*) and inference (*anumāna*). Immediately after that, [the question is] "from what? (*kutaḥ*).

The meaning is that since it has been stated that "sound in the form of the Veda is a means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa), the mention of that which supports [the means of cognition] occurs immediately after the mention of the primary [means]. Alternatively, one might ask why the mention of that which supports the Veda is made without first mentioning that which supports other means of cognition; the answer is that sound in the form of the Veda has been declared to be the primary [means].

In the *Anuvyākhyāna* on the *Yuktipāda*, it is stated: “Veridicality alone is the primary validity (*prāmāṇya*) of both cognition and words. And in the *Brahmatarka*: “Veridicality alone is the primary [validity] of both cognition and words.

The intended meaning (*tātparya*) of this—that veridicality is the primary, that is, the principal factor, in cognition as a mere means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and in the Veda as a means of knowledge—is because it has been so declared.

And as for its being a supporter of the Vedas: it is the stabilization of the authority [of the Vedas] by the total removal of all those causes of non-authority attributed to the Veda— such as untruthfulness, contradiction, tautology, the teaching of impossible matters, the teaching of difficult means, and the lack of means for understanding the meaning— and likewise,
it is the stabilization of the nature of the Dharma, the Devas, and Brahman as understood through the Veda, by removing doubts regarding their being otherwise than they are as presented therein.
Regarding the general definition of inference, they state exactly what was taught by the venerable Bhagavatpāda in his *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa*: "That which is faultless... and so forth.
Inference (*anumāna*) is said to be that which follows after what has been inferred (*anumeti*).
That which is free from defects (*nirdoṣa*) because it has emerged (*niṣkrāntā*) from defects, and which is also a logical justification (*upapatti*), is "faultless justification" (*nirdoṣopapatti*).
The faults of justification are made clear in the discussion on the statement of faults in inference within our own system.

If [the term] *upapatti* here were intended to mean "reasoning devoid of fallacious reasons" (*hetvābhāsa*), as in the case of expressions such as "the basis for the origination" (*atropapattipadam*) or "the justification through explanatory statements" (*arthavādopapatti*), then the qualification "faultless" (*nirdoṣa*) would be redundant; therefore, he says:
"The *upapatti* is the pervaded" (*upapattir vyāpyam*).
[The definition of pervasion: Pervasion (vyāpti).
[Page 3] By qualifying [the probans] with "being faultless," there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) to cases such as the unestablished (asiddha).
For it is stated in the *Paddhati*: “*Upapatti*, *yukti*, and *liṅga-vyāpya* are synonyms.

Although the point would have been complete by stating merely that “*upapatti*” here is the *vyāpya*, the inclusion of the terms *yukti* and *liṅga* by the venerable Bhagavatpāda is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that there might be a contradiction with his own statements that “inference is precisely what is called *yukti*” and that “*liṅga* is the logical reason (*hetu*).”

In the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇaṭīkā*, however, it is stated that "the mark (*liṅga*) is that which makes an object known through concomitance. This refers merely to concomitance by omitting the restrictive element from the pervasion (*vyāpti*), which consists of the necessity of such concomitance; this is intended on the grounds that over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to common [marks] and the like is avoided simply by including the requirement of being "faultless" (*nirdoṣa*).
Now, one might object: In the *Lakṣaṇaṭīkā*, it was stated that "the mark is the logical justification (*upapatti*)."
Regarding this, it is said: "It is pervaded.
To the question "How so?", he says "For it has been stated," with the intention that there is no fault because [the terms] are synonyms.
He states the purpose of the mention of the four words with the word "here" (atra).
"In the fulfillment."

The meaning is that this is because the definition [of a valid means of knowledge] is possible through that alone, as it possesses faultless and purposeful significance; for it has been stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna* on the "Chapter on Reasoning" (*Yuktipāda*) that "it is indeed reasoning (*anumā-yukti*)," and in the refutation of the inference of falsity (*mithyātva-anumāna-khaṇḍana*) that "the mark (*liṅga*) is the reason (*hetu*)."
Now, it might be argued: "The pervaded (vyāpya) is indeed the object of pervasion (vyāpti), and pervasion is defined as the rule of concomitance (sāhacarya-niyama).
But if this were so, there would be a direct contradiction with the *Lakṣaṇa-ṭīkā*.

Having stated that "the mark (liṅga) is the arising therein," since it was said that a mark indicates an object through concomitance (sāhacarya), the restrictive element (niyamāṃśa) is indeed intended;

however, because its result is obtainable from another qualification, it is not explicitly mentioned. With this intention, he removes the contradiction by saying, "But in the commentary on the definition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇalakṣaṇaṭīkā)... and so forth.
It is common.
The meaning is: [it occurs] in the case of the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) known as the "inconclusive due to being common" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) and so forth.
[End of] *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava*, Third Chapter.
Inseparable relation is pervasion.

Now, is "inseparable connection" (avinābhāva) the non-existence of the probans (sādhana) without the probandum (sādhya), or is it the existence of the probans together with the probandum? It cannot be the first.

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because there is no pervasion (*avyāpti*) due to the non-establishment of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) in the case of a purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) inference;
furthermore, according to your own view, this would lack the status of being a constituent of inference (*anumānānaṅgatva*) because it consists of negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*).
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable.
Because the coexistence with the probandum (*sādhyasāhitya*) exists even in cases of deviation (*vyabhicārin*).

If it is intended that there be a rule of coexistence with the probandum, then since a rule consists of the very nature of pervasion (*vyāpti*) as it is being defined, this would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Now, [an objection]: "The object of pervasion is the pervaded (*vyāpya*); thus, the nature of the pervaded is known dependent upon the knowledge of pervasion. Therefore, what is pervasion? In response to this inquiry, he states the definition given in the *Paddhati*: "Inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*).

In order to refine that [work], he raises an objection against the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerning the theory of pervasion (*vyāpti*), following the direction of the arguments in the *Maṇi* and other texts—beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*).
The first alternative assumes a connection by transposing the negative particle (*nañ*);
the second assumes the connection exactly as it is heard in the text.
He states the meaning of the commentary: "by means of association with the thing to be accomplished" (sādhyasāhityena).
It is called "purely positive" (kevalānvayin).
The meaning is: in a reason where the probandum is purely positive (anvayi-sādhya), such as "sound is denotable because it is knowable" or "because it is a quality," and so forth.
"Regarding 'the probandum and so forth'..."
The meaning is the absence of both the probandum and the probans.

In the view of the Siddhāntin, since everything is a negative concomitant (vyatirekin), there is no non-establishment of absence; because of a lack of enthusiasm for this [position], he says: "of this" (asya).

The meaning is that "absence without the probandum" signifies "the absence of the probans where there is the absence of the probandum," and thus this constitutes negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*);

furthermore, according to the final position (*siddhānta*), it is not a constituent of inference, following the direction that will be stated in the section on the theory of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavāda*). "In your view" refers to the view of the proponent of the final position.

He says, "accompanied by the probandum," because of the statement in the *Paddhati*: "Inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) is pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is to say, the rule of concomitance (*sāhacarya-niyama*)."
Because it would reside in itself— that is to say, in cognition—
this is the intended meaning.
[This concludes] the section on the nature of self-dependence (*svatve-tyāni-rūṇam*).
[Now begins] the discourse on pervasion (*vyāptivādaḥ*), page 5.
Furthermore, because it is impossible for there to be a coexistence (*sāhitya*)—either spatially or temporally—between the flooding of a river in a lower region and the rain in an upper region.

By this, the following definitions of pervasion (*vyāpti*) are refuted: that it is a rule of concomitance (*sāhacarya-niyama*), or a relation not based on an external condition (*upādhi*), or an intrinsic relation (*svābhāvika-sambandha*), or the non-occurrence in that which possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavad-avṛttitva*).
This is because there is no concomitance or relation—whether spatial or temporal—between two things located in different substrates (*vyadhikaraṇa*), such as a river-flood and rain;
furthermore, the river-flood occurs in a lower region where the probandum, namely rain, is absent.

It is said: when there is an impossibility for something connected to a particular place and time to occur without another thing connected to a particular place and time, that is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the former by the latter—as in the case of a river flood at a lower location [implying] rain at a higher location.
The meaning is that even for those two, the relationship of indicator (liṅga) and indicated (liṅgin) is observed because they exist in different locations and at different times.
By this [it is meant]:...

The meaning is: by virtue of being pervaded and non-pervaded respectively, as found in the case of rain at a location and the preceding [clouds], which have entered into a relationship of pervader and pervaded across different places and times.
The rule of concomitance.

Having previously accepted that "inseparable relation" (*avinābhāva*) was intended [by the author], the restriction of concomitance (*sāhityaniyama*) was refuted; however, here, having accepted that it is explicitly stated as being characterized by separate pervasion (*pṛthagvyāpti*), it is presented again—thus there is no fault of tautology.
He clarifies what was stated by the words "by this" with the phrase "of two [terms] having different loci."
He defines pervasion as a pervasion that resides in all things—whether they share the same place and time or have different places and times—and which extends to the limit [of those objects].
"That by which he teaches" means that by which he disciplines.
The intention is that the under-extension (*avyāpti*) in the case of a purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) inference will be rescued later;
furthermore, he himself will demonstrate that this [under-extension] is common to all [types of inference].
And he himself will explain the nature of the impossibility (*anupapatti*) through the passage beginning with "impossibility is non-occurrence" (*anupapattiścāsaṃbhavaḥ*).

1. *Kaḥ sa-ka*. 2. *Vāsaṃ-ka*; *Cāsaṃbha-ga. ṭa. rā*. 3. *Pptala-ṭha*. 4. *Dduṣṭatvamabhipretyapu-ṭha*. *Pu-6. Nyāyadīpāvatāratarkatāṇḍavam* (Third Chapter). Furthermore, the status of "inexplicability" (*anupapatti*) as a pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established because, in the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it was stated that there is no distinction between presumption (*arthāpatti*) and inference (*anumāna*), since both are said to be indicative through necessary inexplicability—just as presumption is, so too is inference. This is also true for comparison (*upamāna*), for by the statement, "Indeed, something unseen has never been seen to resemble its own counterpart," it is shown that the resemblance of the cow residing in the gavaya is inexplicable without the resemblance of the gavaya residing in the cow. Moreover, in the *Paddhati*, the word "inexplicability" (*upapatti*) found in the definition of the means of valid cognition—as in "inference is an inexplicable [conclusion] free from defects"—is not merely a synonym for another term.
However, since "presumption" (*upapatti*) is explained as "that which is possible only when the probandum exists, but not otherwise," it is understood as the pervaded (*vyāpya*);

for this is stated in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa-ṭīkā*: "Presumption is the cognition of an object that is otherwise impossible, given a pervaded property such as 'not being in the house' while [the person] is alive"; furthermore, because of the inclusion of the term "otherwise impossible" (*anupapadyamāna*), and because methods such as elimination (*pariśeṣa*) are not accepted as forms of inference, it was said that even smoke, if it were to indicate [fire] through "impossibility" alone, would not be inference.
And because [the reason] is not established, there is no pervasion (vyāpti).
The syntactical connection [of the sentence] is that it is precisely what the author of the Bhāṣya and others intended.
He states the meaning of the word "without distinction" according to the method explained in the Ṭīkā: "like presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)," and so forth.
"Even in the case of a simile," it says.
The meaning is: even in the context of stating that the comparison based on a Śabara is included within another form of inference (anumāna).

In the *Paddhati*, the words "reasoning" (*upapatti*), "logical argument" (*yukti*), and "that which is pervaded by the mark" (*liṅgavyāptam*) are stated to be synonyms; by this statement, the absence of contradiction with other texts is established, as they are said to convey a single intended meaning (*abhiprāya*).
Furthermore, he states another intended meaning for the sake of relevance to the present subject: "And in the *Paddhati*... (6).
The demonstration that there is no fault in this treatise titled *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa* proceeds by accepting this very point:

[...]* By this, the meaning is [as follows]—*ga.ṭa.rā.*; 2. something seen—*ga.ka.rā.ṭa.*; 3. situated—*ga.*; *sdhaṃ*—*u-*; *rā.*; 4. with the intention that it is not so—*ga.rā.*; 5. thus it was said—*ga.rā.ṭa.*; 6. by that alone—*ṭha.ḍa.*; (*svate-vyāni-rūṇam*). *Note: The text provided contains fragments of commentary or marginal notes (indicated by superscripts such as *ga.*, *ṭa.*, *rā.*, etc. attached to the main Sanskrit text, which has been integrated into the translation where appropriate.*

And in the *Sudhā*, it is stated: “Because the word ‘reasoning’ (*yukti*) found in the *Anuvyākhyāna*— in the passage ‘only the reasoning of inference has been stated’— is explained as ‘it is indeed joined (*yujyate*), therefore it is reasoning (*yukti*)’.”
This is precisely what the author of the Bhāṣya and others intended.

As for the attempt in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa-ṭīkā* to establish the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the reason and the probandum by stating—"The cow under dispute is similar to a gavaya, because it is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the similarity residing in the gavaya"—that was done by relying on the view of another school.
For this very reason, it was stated in that same work that such a formal argument (*prayoga*) is possible.

Consequently, in the *Paddhati*, the argument was formulated with a lack of co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) as follows: "That cow is similar to this gavaya, because this gavaya is similar to that cow."

For this very reason, in the *Sudhā* [commentary], regarding the statement in the *Anuvyākhyāna*: “The rising of Rohiṇī is near; Kṛttikā has already risen,” it is said that since this is a construction with different grammatical loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*), one might suspect a single locus by taking time and so forth as the subject; therefore, it is stated that such a transformation of the formulation is not a valid means of proof.

— Having set this forth in the *Paddhati*, it was stated [by the author] that "it belongs to the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa-stha*)," because of the explanation that "it is the pervaded" (*vyāpyam*).
And this is for the purpose of making known that this is the opinion of the original author (Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya).

Now, one might object: if this is so, then in the context of the inclusion [of analogy] within the other means of valid cognition as stated by Śabara—namely, "A cow is similar to a gavaya, because a gavaya is similar to a cow"—[how is this to be accounted for?]
Having raised the objection regarding the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) in the formulation, he states the formulation in terms of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
To the question of how, by that [coreferentiality], there is no understanding of that which is non-coreferential, he says: "As for that which... (*yattu*).
Thus [it is stated] in the Anuvyākhyāna, verse 7.

Because of the statement in the *Bhaktapādīyānuvyākhyāna*: 8. [Notes: 1. *vahipa*—Ga, Rā; 2. *syaita*—Ga, Rā; 3. *vacasu*—Ka, Rā; 4. *mepra*—Ga, Ṭa, Rā; 5. The word *upapatti* following *tatrastha* is added—Ṭha; 6. *śābaropamānāntarbhā*—Ṭha;
7. *nokta*—Ṭa, Ṭha; 8. *kte*—Ṭha, Ḍa.
*Pu*—8. *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam* (Third Chapter):
"Inconsistency" (*anupapatti*) means non-connection, that is to say, contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For it has been stated in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇaṭīkā*: "Inconsistency is impossibility."

As for the objection raised by the author of the *Ṭīkā* against one who questions the distinction between inference (*anumāna*)—which makes its object known through universal concomitance (*vyāpti*)—and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—which makes its object known through "inexplicability" (*anupapatti*)—stating that "the inexplicability of one thing without another does not hold without their being a concomitance," this statement regarding the difference between inexplicability and concomitance intends either (1) relations such as the vertical priority of the regulator and the regulated, or cause and effect;

or (2) the type of concomitance favored by the opponent, which consists of a restricted co-location (*niyata-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or a relation free from limiting conditions (*anaupādhika-sambandha*). Thus, there is no contradiction with the *Ṭīkā*.

And this very pervasion (vyāpti) is called "inseparable connection" (avinābhāva) and "the rule of concomitance" (sāhacaryaniyama), with the underlying sense that it is the non-occurrence of the probans (sādhana) without the probandum (sādhya), which is to say its impossibility (anupapatti).
Having thus stated the accepted view that the impossibility [of the probans] constitutes pervasion, he now describes its essential nature: "And the impossibility... and so forth.

The meaning is this: when the existence of one thing is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the absence of another, that [absence] constitutes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the latter by the former.

He refutes the contradiction with the statement in the *Ṭīkā* on the definition of the means of knowledge—that logical consistency (*upapatti*) must in every respect be admitted as depending upon pervasion—by saying "as for that which... (*yā tv iti*).
"Desired by others."
The meaning is that [the definition] does not intend to refer to pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the form of impossibility (*anupapatti*).

Now, one might object: "In that case, there is a contradiction with the statement in the *Paddhati* that 'pervasion is inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), which is to say, the necessity of concomitance (*sāhacarya-niyama*),' because this [definition of yours] is different. To this, he replies: "This very [is it]."

Now, if pervasion (*vyāpti*) is defined as "logical impossibility" (*anupapatti*), then what would be the status of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*)? To this, he says: "Of which... (*yasyeti*).
(An Examination of Pervasion by Its Own Nature)

The Theory of Pervasion (Vyāptivāda): That whose non-occurrence [in the absence of another] is impossible is the pervaded (vyāpya). That without which [the other] cannot occur is the pervader (vyāpaka).

And this pervasion (vyāpti) is present everywhere— in well-known inferences such as those from smoke [to fire], in inferences such as those from the absence of light [to the presence of darkness] which take the form of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), in the reasonings (tarka) that serve as the basis for self-dependence (ātmāśraya), mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya), circularity (cakraka), infinite regress (anavasthā), and contradiction (vyāghāta), and in both purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) and purely positive (kevalānvayin) inferences; otherwise, there would result the fallacy of the reason being non-conclusive (aprayojakatva).
For it is suspected that there might be no pervasion (avyāpti) due to the possibility that "the reason may exist while the probandum does not.
Nor can [faults such as] self-dependence (ātmāśraya) and the like be established, because they have never been known to occur in a state of co-occurrence (samānādhikaraṇatva) with the probans;
for if that were the case, it would be impossible for them to be undesirable.
And it has been stated by the commentators:

"For nowhere is self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) or the like established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To the question, "What is the distinction in adopting this [definition] while abandoning pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the form of a relation that is not based on limiting adjuncts (*anopādhika*)? he says: "And this... (*iyaṃ ca*).
The phrase "and in the case of purely positive (kevalānvayi) [reasons]" is stated according to the view of others;

for in our own system (siddhānta), every reason possesses negative concomitance (vyatireka). Alternatively, this statement is made with reference to reasons that establish a purely positive probandum (sādhya) consisting of space or time.
This statement is intended to mean that the cause is a property belonging to a related object that possesses a single similarity;
and he clarifies that this [meaning] is necessary by saying "otherwise."
The lack of a probative force.
The phrase "of that which is intended as the pervaded" (*vyāpyatvena-abhimatasya*) is to be supplied [to the definition].
He also establishes that this alone is the correct pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), stating: "the reason" (*hetu*).

One might object: "In cases such as self-dependence (ātmāśraya), let there simply be the pervasion (vyāpti) consisting of co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) as stated by [Kṛṣṇa]bhaṭṭa in the *Maṇi*; what is the use of this [present definition]? To this, he says: "Or not" (*na vā*).
And it has been said:

In the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇaṭīkā*, at the point of explaining the passage beginning with "self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*)," "mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*)," and so forth: [The text continues: ...in order that [the fault] might not arise, by means of a tarka (reductio) that brings about such a consequence... [and so on]. (Note: The numbers 1–7 refer to variant readings found in the manuscript traditions cited in the footnotes.)
Pu — 10. *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (Third Chapter):
Now, an objection: Is the impossibility of smoke [due to its absence] in the absence of fire in general, or in the absence of the fire on the mountain?
It cannot be the first.
Because, by that [reason], fire on the mountain is not established.
Nor is the latter [alternative] possible; for as long as fire on the mountain is not established, it is difficult to ascertain the "inexplicability" (anupapatti) of the reason without it.
Furthermore, since that very [cognition] is the result in the form of an inference, it is impossible for it to be its own cause.

For it is said in the *Khaṇḍana*: "Because otherness [is required], and because that [otherness] is not established prior to the establishment of that [inference]. If this is argued, [we reply that] the objection applies equally whether one considers the co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of smoke with fire-in-general or with the fire on the mountain. This is because the refutations of both alternatives are identical.
Now, if it is argued that the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the cognition of the co-inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of smoke-in-general with fire-in-general,
while the result (*phala*) is the cognition of the fire on the mountain as being fire by its nature according to the actual state of things,

and that the establishment of the fire’s location on the mountain arises from the force of the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), then this is equally untenable even in the case of [the opponent's] own position.
He raises an objection regarding this pervasion (vyāpti) with the words "But surely" (nanu).
"In non-establishment" means when there is ignorance;
likewise, it is also the case with "in establishment."
Because that [reason] is established prior to that [thesis], whereas it is not established after it.
Because the fire on the mountain is not established prior to the establishment of that [specific] fire;

nor is its establishment achieved through the establishment of the universal, since there is a difference between the universal and the particular—this is the meaning. To state the resolution by means of that [distinction], he offers a response by way of a counter-objection: "Of smoke... and so forth.

Regarding the objection that—since this [reason] is a negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*), it is not a constituent of inference according to your own position—he anticipates that and refutes it: [The text continues: "By its own nature...

(*svata-evyāni-rūṇam*). (Note: *iti* is omitted in Ṭa and Rā; *tīti cet* is read as *tīti ce* in Ga and Rā; *cenna* is read as *cenna* in Ka, Ga, and Rā; *-tatpha-* is read as *-tatpha-* in Ga, Ṭa, and Rā; the passage beginning with *na ca* is absent in Ṭa and Ḍa.)
The Theory of Pervasion (Vyāptivāda), Part 11:
Nor is this a negative pervasion (vyatirekavyāpti),
because even in the case of a purely positive inference (kevalānvayin), there exists the fact that the probandum cannot be established without [the probans].

Furthermore, although there is no negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*)—since the absence of the probans in the form of a flood does not exist in the lower region where the absence of the probandum in the form of rain exists—the fact that a flood is "otherwise inexplicable" (*anupapatti*) without rain is observed. Moreover, the "inexplicability" (*anupapatti*) resides in the smoke, whereas the "negative concomitance" (*vyatirekavyāpti*) resides in the absence of fire; how then could these two be identical?
The pervasion of the absence of fire by the absence of smoke is likewise nothing other than the non-occurrence [of the absence of fire] without the absence of smoke.

And that [pervasion], when the absence of smoke is to be proven by means of the absence of fire, serves as a factor precisely as a positive pervasion (*anvaya-vyāpti*) because it resides in the pervaded (*vyāpya*).
However, when fire is to be proven by means of smoke, it does not serve as a direct factor because it does not reside in the smoke.
And this is not so.
To the proponent who claims that this negative concomitance (vyatirekavyāpti) will be one that contains a common substratum (sāmānādhikaraṇyagarbhā), he says: "Furthermore... (kiṃ ca).

Now, one might object: "In all positive concomitant (anvayi) inferences—such as the case of inferring the absence of smoke from the absence of fire—a different kind of pervasion (vyāpti) must be stated; therefore, this [pervasion] does not apply to them. To this, he says: "Of the absence of fire... and so forth.
If it is asked why positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*) alone is not a constituent factor even in the inference from smoke, he says: "By means of smoke... (dhūmena).
Not directly.
However, the intention is that [the definition] is a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) precisely by way of excluding deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

He states the following to dispel the previously mentioned objection—that there is no pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of a purely positive inference (*kevalānvayin*) because the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is unestablished: "And not in the case of a purely positive [inference]," etc.
Nor is there non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of a purely positive inference (*kevalānvayin*).

For in that case, since the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) exists, there is indeed the presence of the impossibility—which consists in the non-existence of the logical reason (*sādhana*)—given that the probandum is absent. Thus, the required condition is satisfied.
In my view, even that which lacks epistemic warrant can be the counter-positive of a negation.
And likewise: [the inference of] taste without its color, which shares the same location and time;

the color produced by baking (*pākaja-rūpa*) and so forth without the baking process, which shares the same location but occurs at a different time; and the rising of Kṛttikā without the rising of Rohiṇī, which occurs at the same time but at a different location.
Since the overflow of a river in a lower region at a particular time is impossible without rain in a higher region,
such a form of pervasion (vyāpti) is logical even in the case of heterogeneity (vaiyadhikaraṇya), just as it is in the case of homogeneity (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
On the contrary, in the case of a river's overflow and so forth, such a form of pervasion is illogical if restricted to homogeneity alone.

For a river flood located in an upper region is not impossible without rain occurring in an upper region; rather, it [requires] even more upstream rain. — "Even for that which lacks authoritative proof" means:
And how this is so has been established in the first chapter of the *Nyāyāmṛta*.
He clarifies what was previously stated—that [the definition] "pervades all" (sarvatrānugatā)—by means of its application to specific examples, beginning with the words "And thus," and so forth.
As if there were grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).

The meaning is: just as in the Nyāya system pervasion (vyāpti) is established by somehow achieving co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), so too here it is done without such difficulty, even though there is a lack of co-referentiality between the mark (liṅga) and the marked (liṅgin) as they actually exist.

Now, one might object: "In your view as well, let it be said that pervasion (vyāpti) is stated by taking recourse to co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in that case. To this, he says: "On the contrary" (pratyuta), verse 7.

Anticipating the objection that there is a sublation [of the pervasion] because the probans (*liṅga*) and the probandum (*liṅgin*), which reside in different loci, stand in a relationship of pervaded and pervader as they actually exist, he provides an answer by way of a counter-objection (*pratibandī*) with the words beginning "But surely" (*nanu*).

[Note: The variants provided indicate that in some versions the reading is *sattvādeḥ* (because of existence), while others have *tasyāsattvāt* (because of its non-existence); furthermore, the particle *ca* is absent in some versions. 3. *yasya samānakā-* [The text appears to be incomplete here.]
-ga.ṭa.rā. 4. yāro-ga.rā. 5. kālayo-ga.ṭa.rā. 6. svade-ga.ṭa.rā. 7. Then there is only "avyadhikaraṇa" and so forth—ṭa.ḍa. (svate-vyāni-rūṇam) Vyāptivādaḥ, page 13.

If it is asked: "How can there be a pervasion (vyāpti) of the flood in the river—which is related to the absence of the probandum—with the rain, which is the probandum? [we reply: How then can there be a pervasion of substanceness (dravyatva), which is invariably related to the absence of the probandum, with conjunction (saṃyoga), which is the probandum?

If, however, in that case, the pervasion is established by the force of the result through the inclusion of the qualification "not co-located with the counter-positive" (pratiyogyasamānādhikaraṇa) in the definition of pervasion.
In that case, here too, the establishment of that [pervasion] is equal [to the other], because another definition of pervasion has been stated by the very force of the result.

If it is asked, "How can there be a restriction of the locus of the probandum (*sādhya*) when there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*)?", [the answer is that] this is the case even in the presence of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*): for instance, by means of smoke, fire is restricted to only its lower portion;
and by the rising of one scale of a balance, the sinking is restricted to the other portion.
Since substance-ness, which is pervasively present, establishes conjunction— which is non-pervasively present— and since conjunction, which is non-pervasively present,
establishes substance-ness, which is pervasively present, how can there be a restriction to a specific location within the subject itself?
"By the absence of the probandum," and so forth.

According to the opponent's view, since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*), it has been stated that in the inference "the tree possesses conjunction because it is a substance" (*vṛkṣaḥ saṃyogī dravyatvāt*),
there is a connection with the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) in the case of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*). This is what is meant by the term "result" (*phala*).
The meaning is: by the force of the result characterized as inference.
The counter-positive.

The meaning is that pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists in the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the probandum (*sādhya*), provided that [the absence] is not connected with that absence which has for its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) a probandum that does not co-occur with its own counter-positive; this is due to the aforementioned qualification.

Thus, since the absence of conjunction (*saṃyogābhāva*) does co-occur with its counter-positive, there is no fault—this is the point. Having raised another objection against the relationship of mark and marked (*liṅga-liṅgibhāva*) between two things residing in different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*), he refutes it by means of a *reductio ad absurdum* (prati-bandī), beginning with "But surely... (*nanu*).
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that even when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the restriction to a specific location applies only to the subject (*pakṣa*).
To the question "Why?", he says "by smoke," etc., with the intention that it is because otherwise [the rule] is observed to be different elsewhere.
The phrase "of fire," etc., is connected with the word "siddhi" (accomplishment) ending in the suffix *iti*.
The word *iti* here functions as a reason (*hetu*).
For this very reason, in the *Paddhati*, the relationship of indicator and indicated (*liṅga-liṅgi-bhāva*) is shown to exist among many [signs], such as the rising of the scale-pan and so forth.

And how, even when they are simultaneous, can there be a falling that is occasional due to gravity which is permanent, and a destruction that is occasional due to corporeality which is permanent? *Puṇya-yukta-tarkatāṇḍava* (Third Chapter): How, moreover, even if they are simultaneous, can there be a falling that is occasional on account of gravity which is permanent, and a destruction that is occasional on account of corporeality which is permanent?
"Siddhi" refers to the determination of time.
If it is argued that this is because of their nature as being pervaded (*vyāpti-svabhāva*), then it is the same:
just as "wherever there is taste, there is color" implies identity of place and time,
so too "wherever there is that which is produced by baking (*pākaja*), there is baking" implies identity of place alone.
When there is Kṛttikā, then there is the proximity of the rising of Rohiṇī; this is because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is grasped merely through their simultaneity.

And when there is a river flood at a certain place, there was rain at that same place at a prior time or at a subsequent time; this is because the pervasion is grasped precisely through their difference in place and time.
[Objection: But surely, if there is a lack of co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) with respect to space and time, how can pervasion (*vyāpti*) be apprehended?
For pervasion is grasped only through co-referentiality—either spatially as "wherever this is, there that is," or temporally as "whenever this is, then that is. [Response: This is not so;
for the apprehension of pervasion, which consists in the impossibility [of the probans existing] without the probandum, takes the form "if this is, then that is," and is thus universally applicable.

Having caused the opponent to state the resolution according to the direction given in the *Paddhati*—namely, "because there is a rule that a logical mark (*liṅga*) produces the cognition of the probandum (*liṅgin*) depending on the mode of pervasion (*vyāpti*)"—he says "equally" (*samam*), beginning with the word "pervasion" (*vyāpti*).
He clarifies what was stated as "due to the manifestation of pervasion" with the words: "wherever... there... (yatra yadā).
Having raised the objection regarding the impossibility of the mode of apprehending pervasion (*vyāpti*), he provides the resolution with the words beginning "But surely" (*nanu*).

[Objection: But surely, even in the case of a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), there would be no established distinction between a valid reason (*hetu*) and a fallacious reason (*tadābhāsa*) when there is a relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*). To this, he says: "In this case... [The text continues: ...the nature of being pervaded by itself... (svatavyāptirūpaṇam). (Note: Variants: 1. *jarū* — Ga.Rā.; 2. *ca* is absent — Ṭa.Rā.; 3. *yadedaṃ tadedamiti* — Ṭa.Rā.; 4. *t/ ya* — Ga.Rā.)
Vyāptivāda, Part 15.

— Herein, when there is an impossibility of the reason (*hetu*) being connected with a particular place and time, the non-existence of that reason at that place and time is indeed what constitutes "unestablished" (*asiddhi*);
it does not mean its non-existence in the subject (*pakṣa*).
Thus, when a reason that is connected to a specific place and time is found to be impossible [there], its existence elsewhere in those same places and times constitutes a deviation (*vyabhicāra*);
it is not, however, a presence in that which lacks the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavati*).
Similarly, a reason that exists only elsewhere than in the aforementioned place and time is contradictory (*viruddha*).
But since it does not necessarily subsist in that which lacks the probandum, there is no minor flaw whatsoever.
Therefore, even in the case of a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (vaiyadhikaraṇya), pervasion (vyāpti) certainly exists.
This has been stated by the venerable Bhagavatpāda:

"Even when there is no co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), pervasion (*vyāpti*) certainly exists"— this means that even in the absence of co-referentiality, pervasion in the form of logical impossibility (*anupapatti*) certainly exists.
For this very reason, it will be stated later that "the unestablished nature due to different loci (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhi*) is not a defect."
Thus ends the definition of pervasion (vyāpti) according to our own system. [Note:
This refers to the position that there exists a relationship of the pervaded and the pervader even between things existing at different places and times;
it does not mean "the thesis" (pakṣa).
The sense is that by this [reason], the flood of a river and so forth would be unestablished (*asiddha*). However, it is not so.
It should be understood that [the reason] would be inconclusive due to cases such as a river in flood.
In the phrase "elsewhere than in that place and time," the genitive case is used in the sense of a general relationship (*saṃbandhasāmānye*).
The meaning is "other than those two";
the same applies hereafter as well.
"Thus" (*evam*) is used as a conjunction.

The meaning is that when, in a certain place and at a certain time, there is the non-occurrence of the stated reason without the probandum, "in those two" means "elsewhere than those two," i.e., elsewhere than that place and that time.
Thus it has been said.
Regarding the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he states its meaning for the sake of application to the subject at hand: "co-referentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Thus concludes the definition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) according to our own school’s view. [Note: This will be elaborated upon in the section concerning why the "unestablished due to difference in locus" (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhi*) is not a fault; further details are omitted. [Note: The passage beginning with "ata eva" and so forth is absent in the Gaṅgārāma and Rāghavendra editions.]
Pu-16. *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam* (Third Chapter):
Now follows the refutation of the definition of "crooked pervasion" (*vakravyāpti*) as stated by others.
By this—

The statements beginning with *maṇyuktāni* are commentaries on the phrase "an invariable relation" (*avyabhicaritaḥ saṃbandhaḥ*), and these too are based on the concept of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). Furthermore, they rely on the view that there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of one class of smoke by one class of fire, [defined as] that which is not delimited by the delimiter of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of an absolute non-existence co-located with the locus of the [probans] itself, provided that such a non-existence does not have a counter-correlative co-located with the same locus.
Now, the refutation of the definition of "crooked pervasion" (vakravyāpti) as stated by others. [Section 2] — "As stated in the Maṇi."
The connection with what is to be stated later is that "the fallacious [definitions] characterized by pervasion have been rejected.

And those [fallacies], having been extracted into three categories by way of being elaborations on the non-deviant relation, the non-conditional relation, and the natural relation, are restated here preceded by their internal subdivisions.
[This is explained] by the passage beginning with "the relationship is invariable" (avyabhicaritaḥ saṃbandhaḥ).
"Even there"—that is, even in those [definitions] consisting of the nature of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*);
"even there"—meaning, even in those which contain within them absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
By means of that which belongs to the class of fire, [one infers] that which belongs to the class of smoke.

The meaning is that these definitions of pervasion (vyāpti) are common to all individual instances of smoke and fire—whether co-referential or non-co-referential—just as the fire in a kitchen is like the fire on a mountain.
The counter-correlate.

An absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that is non-co-located with its counter-positive (*pratiyogyasamānādhikaraṇa*)—that is, an absolute absence such as that of a jar which does not reside in the same locus as the probans (smoke) denoted by the word "whatever" (*yat*)—has a delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of its counter-positiveness, such as "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). That which is not delimited (*anavacchinna*) by such [a property], and is therefore not excluded by it, is fire and the like.
The co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of that smoke and the like with any such [fire] whatsoever consists in their residing in a single locus through the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
The meaning is that there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of smoke and so forth by fire and so forth. (This concludes the refutation of the pervasion of the probandum.)
The theory of pervasion (*vyāptivāda*), page 17:

[Statements] such as "pervasion is co-occurrence in the same locus" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and others likewise [apply] only to those definitions that contain the concept of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).

Although the fire of the kitchen and so forth is the counter-positive of an absolute absence that coexists with the smoke of the mountain, its counter-positiveness is delimited by the property of being fire (*vahnitva*).
This is because there is no cognition such as "fire does not exist where there is smoke.
Thus, in the case of the smoke on the mountain, there exists a coexistence with the fire of the kitchen, which is not delimited by that non-delimiting property of being fire.

The point is that even in the absence [of smoke on the mountain], the fire on the mountain is delimited by the universal "fire-ness" (vahnitva) just like the kitchen fire; thus, by taking their co-location, pervasion exists even between smoke and fire that reside in different loci.

In this regard, although the counterpositiveness of the absolute absence co-located with the smoke on the mountain is delimited by "kitchen-fire-ness" (mahānasavahnitva) when residing in the kitchen fire;
Because it is understood that there is no kitchen-fire on the mountain,
the pervasion (vyāpti) of all smoke by all fire is not established.

Nevertheless, this should be explained— following the direction set forth by Pakṣadhara and others— by means of a transposition of the negative particle (*nañ*), such that [the definition] refers to that which is delimited by what is not the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitānavacchedaka*).
In the same way, it should be understood that in the expression "that which has a common locus" (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the phrase "delimited by that" (*yadavacchinna*) is also intended.

Therefore, in the fallacious inference "this [mountain] possesses smoke because it possesses fire," there exists a co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) delimited by "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*), which is not delimited by the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) residing in some kitchen (*mahānasa*) or similar locus that is co-located with fire.
It should be understood that there is no occurrence of the fallacy of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding the pervasion of all instances;

for the property of "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) is indeed the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) of such an absence that is co-located (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the fire in a red-hot iron ball (*ayogolaka*).
Likewise, in the phrase "by that" (*tena*), it should also be explained as meaning "of that which is delimited by that" in relation to "that which is delimited by that."
For this very reason, the use of the word "etc. (*ādi*) has been employed to include such [definitions] as those conceived by the authors of commentaries and others.
Here, "delimitingness" (*avacchedakatva*) means either existing in a locus that does not exceed the counter-positive's own locus, or it is a specific kind of qualifierhood (*viśeṣaṇatāviśeṣa*);
it does not mean the capacity to produce the cognition of being delimited.
Because the state of being a producer (*janakatva*) entails a necessary restriction (*niyamagarbhatā*), it would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). *Pu-18.
Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam (Third Chapter)* [Notes: *ṭa. ṭha.* refer to manuscript variants.]

For those who hold the view that pervasion (*vyāpti*) exists only between specific instances of smoke and fire that share a common locus (*samānādhikaraṇa*), there are such definitions as: "Pervasion is co-occurrence in a common locus with that which is not the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) that resides in the same locus as the [probans] itself, provided that [non-existence] does not have a counter-positive residing in the same locus as the [probans]. And so forth.
Likewise, regarding the phrase "not co-located with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogyasamānādhikaraṇa*):

here, Rucidatta and others maintain that the qualification "co-located with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogisamānādhikaraṇa*) is added to the absence (*abhāva*) in order to avoid the under-extension (*avyāpti*) in the pervasion (*vyāpti*) residing in substanceness (*dravyatva*), etc., where the probandum (*sādhya*) is conjunction (*saṃyoga*), etc.
Pakṣadhara and Śiromaṇi, however, state that this [qualification] is intended to include the inference: "This [tree] possesses monkey-conjunction, because it is this tree."
"Of two [words] in grammatical apposition."
The meaning is: in such a manner as [the pervasion] of smoke on a mountain by fire on that same mountain, or of smoke residing in a kitchen and so forth by fire residing in those very places.
The counter-correlate.

Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of mountain-smoke and the like with that which is not the counter-positive of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that is co-occurrent with the mountain-smoke and has a counter-positive not co-occurrent with it— namely, an absolute absence such as that of a jar, whose counter-positive is not mountain-fire and the like.
In this same manner, the smoke in the kitchen and so forth should also be considered.

[One might object that] there is no pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the pervasion residing in such instances as "the jar possesses odor because it is earth" (*ghaṭo gandhavān pṛthivītvāt*), since individual instances of odor are distinct in each respective substratum, and thus every odor is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) that co-occurs with the locus of earthness (*pṛthivītva*). To address this, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is employed.

By this, the definition proposed by the author of the *Ṭīkā* and others is captured: "co-occurrence with that which is not the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that resides in the same locus as the [property] itself, while not being co-located with its own counter-correlative.
This applies to what follows as well.
Furthermore, although an absolute absence may be non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*), mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) is pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*).

It has been stated that [the definitions] are "lighter" because of the abandonment of the qualifier [“non-deviation”], since there would otherwise be the consequence of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of pervasion residing in substancehood (*dravyatva*) and the like, which are to be established through conjunction (*saṃyoga*). (The refutation of the lack of pervasion in the definition of the cook.)
The Theory of Pervasion (Vyāptivāda), Part 19:

By the addition of qualifiers, there are concise definitions based on mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*): the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of a property with that which is not the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a mutual absence that resides in the same locus as itself.

Likewise, there are definitions such as: "Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of one thing with that which does not possess the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) that is co-located with itself.
It should also be understood that these rely on the view that pervasion exists only between two things that are co-located (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
This is indicated by the phrase beginning with "yatsamānādhikaraṇa... and so forth.
"Yat" refers to the probans, such as smoke;
the mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) that has a common locus with it is the mutual absence of a jar and so forth,
but not the mutual absence of that which possesses fire.
Because there is no cognition such as "the pot and so forth, which possess smoke,
do not possess fire," that which does not serve as the delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of that [absence] is not fire.
Rather, it is [the universal] such as "pot-ness" itself.
The meaning is that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of smoke with that fire.

Although this definition was not explicitly stated in the *Maṇi*, it is presented here because, by virtue of its formulation within the definition involving absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), it is effectively stated even in the definition involving mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*); thus, it is intended [by the author].
He states what was explicitly mentioned by Maṇu in the verse beginning with "tathā yat": "In the same way, that which... and so forth.

Alternatively, for the sake of avoiding redundancy between the two definitions stated by the author of the *Maṇi*, this twofold restatement should be understood as follows, after first refining them: either (1) "the co-existence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of that [the subject] with something which is not the counter-positive of a mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) that has the same locus as itself," or (2) "the state of being that which does not have as its counter-positive a mutual non-existence that has the same locus as itself.
Thus, the two-fold repetition is to be understood.

By the phrase "and so forth" (ādipadena), there is the inclusion of all possible definitions of the form: "the pervasion between two things [A and B] is such that A, which is co-located with something not delimited by that which delimits the counter-correlativity of the mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) co-located with A, is co-located with B."
"Anaupādhika" (unconditioned).

The various formulations of the definition "unconditional relation" (*anaupādhika-sambandha*)—which, even there, ultimately result in the negation of the non-pervasion of the probans by those which pervade the probandum, such as: "Pervasion is the non-coexistence with the absolute absence having as its counter-positive all those things that are not counter-positives of the absolute absences co-present with the probandum"—as well as those which result in the negation of the pervasion of the probandum by those which do not pervade the probans, such as: "all those things which are counter-positives of the absolute absences co-present with the probans."
"Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the co-occurrence with the probandum (*sādhya*) in the same locus as an absolute absence that has that [probandum] as its counter-correlate," and so forth.

Indeed, the non-contingency (*anaupādhikatva*) of the relation between smoke, fire, and the like occurs when there is an absence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) therein; and the absence of a limiting condition—defined as that which pervades the probandum but does not pervade the probans—occurs by virtue of [the condition's] being a non-pervader of those things that pervade the probandum.

Having kept in mind that there are two ways—either by being non-pervasive of the means of proof (*sādhana*) or by not being pervasive of the probandum (*sādhya*)—he says "there too" (*tatrāpi*), following the method stated by Pakṣadhara and others.
The meaning of the phrase ending with "apratiyoginaḥ" (non-correlatives) is "pervaders of the probandum (sādhyavyāpakāḥ)";
the intention is [to refer to] properties such as knowability (prameyatva) and nameability (abhidheyatva).
The meaning of the phrase beginning with "tatpratiyogikatā" (the state of having that as a correlate) is "pervaded by that" (tadvyāpyatvam).
The phrase "of the reason such as smoke" (*dhūmādihetoḥ*) is to be supplied.

This formulation is stated because, if one were to say merely that "the state of being pervaded by that which pervades the probandum" (*sādhyavyāpakavyāpyatva*) constitutes the absence of a limiting condition (*anaupādhikatva*), there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). The same applies hereafter.

In order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of a deviant reason (*hetu*), it should be understood that the terms "as many as" (*yāvat*) and "and subsequently" (*uttaratra ca*) apply here.

Regarding the phrase "as many as" (*yāvantaḥ*): here too, the meaning of the portion ending with "of the counter-correlatives" (*pratiyoginaḥ*) is "those which do not pervade the probans" (*sādhanāvyāpakāḥ*).

The meaning of the phrase "having that as its counter-correlate" (*tatpratiyogika*) and so forth is: "that which is the probandum (*sādhya*) is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*) with respect to that [locus]. (The refutation of the fallacy of over-extension regarding the cook.)

Furthermore, there are definitions of pervasion that take the form of an exposition of the statement "pervasion is an inherent relation" (*svābhāvika-sambandha*), such as: "Pervasion belongs to that which possesses a nature that delimits the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of another";
these are circuitous definitions of pervasion characterized by the co-occurrence of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*).
They have been rejected.
Regarding those [reasons] already mentioned and those yet to be mentioned, which are established for all the world:

some maintain that the subsequent mention of what was stated previously, and the prior mention of what was stated subsequently, is intended to show that since the "pervasion of the probandum" (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) is a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), it must occur first; therefore, the absence of the "non-pervasion of the probans" (*sādhanāvyāpakatvābhāva*), which occurs later, must be stated first.
Others hold that it is for the sake of ease of understanding;

for one must state [the definition] as far as the co-occurrence with the probandum (sādhya-sāmānādhikaraṇya), which is the co-occurrence with the absolute absence of that [probans] having the latter as its counter-correlative (tat-pratiyogitāka).
"That which [is expressed] in grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya)..."

Although the reading in the *Maṇi* is simply "that which possesses the nature of being the delimitor of the relation-ship of that [which is related]," nevertheless, because there is the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)—namely, that the staff, which is delimited by "staffness" (the delimitor of the relation-ship of causehood according to the literal definition of causality), would result in being pervaded by the jar—it is stated as "co-occurrence with that" (*yatsāmānādhikaraṇya*) following the direction explained by its commentator.
The meaning is: smoke’s pervasion consists in its possessing that nature which is the delimitor of co-occurrence with fire; that is, "smokeness."

When it is stated that "the pervasion belongs to that which has co-referentiality with [the probandum]," the term "delimiting" (*avacchedaka*) is employed to avoid the consequence that even a deviant reason would possess pervasion. This definition was already examined in the section refuting the inferability of God (*īśvara*), during the discussion of counter-arguments against the reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*).
He refutes all definitions by means of the fallacies of under-extension, over-extension, and impossibility—[as stated in the verse] "In those [definitions] mentioned... and so forth.
In cases such as rain in an upper region and the resulting flood of a river in a lower region, the pervasion is established through such causal sequences.

If it is argued that "the state of being blue smoke (*nīladhūmatva*) is not a delimiting factor (*anavacchedaka*) because it resides in that which possesses a pervasion established by another delimiting factor," [we reply:
let it be so; nevertheless, this does not prevent over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the other definition.

One might object: "Even according to the literal reading of the definition beginning with 'not co-locating with the counter-positive' (*pratiyogyasamānādhikaraṇa*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) of the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) co-located with blue smoke is delimited by the specific nature of fire produced from chaff and so forth. To one who thinks thus, he replies: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
(Refutation of the definition due to over-extension and lack of pervasion) — The Theory of Pervasion (Vyāptivāda), Part II, p.

23. Furthermore, because the fire of the kitchen (mahānasīyavahni) is delimited by "kitchen-fire-ness" (*mahānasīyavahnitva*), which is the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that co-exists with the smoke of the mountain (*parvatīyadhūma*), the definition is untenable (*asambhava*).

If one were to transpose the negative particle (*nañ*) [in the definition] as "not delimited by the non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity" (*pratiyogitānavacchedakānavacchinna*), then even smoke, which is the probandum (*sādhya*), would be delimited by "knowability" (*prameyatva*)—which is the non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity of the absolute absence co-located with fire—and consequently, fire, being co-located with that [smoke], would also be a pervader (*vyāpaka*) of smoke. [Note:
This occurs] because of the phrase "due to being delimited" (*avacchinnatvāt*).
And thus, there is no co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with that which is not delimited by the delimitor of the counterpositiveness (pratiyogitāvacchedaka) of such an absence;
rather, the point is that it exists only with that which is so delimited.

Now, one might object: even though the fire of the kitchen (mahānasīyavahni) is delimited by such a property, the fire of the mountain (parvatīyavahni) is not delimited by "being the fire of the kitchen" (mahānasīyavahnitva).
If it is argued that by taking its co-occurrence with that [fire], the smoke on the mountain would indeed possess pervasion (*vyāpyatā*), we say no.
For the co-occurrence of the fire delimited by the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of the absolute absence co-occurring with the smoke on the mountain belongs only to the kitchen-smoke;

likewise, since the property of being a fire on the mountain (*parvatīyavahnitva*) is the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of the absence co-occurring with the kitchen-smoke, the co-occurrence of the smoke on the mountain is only with that which is so delimited. Thus it stands.

The intended meaning is that, in no case is the co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of smoke with a counter-positive that is not delimited by the delimitor of the counter-positiveness (pratiyogitāvacchedaka) of the absence in the stated form obtainable; thus, there is the fallacy of impossibility (asaṃbhava).

Having restated the position of Pakṣadhara—who, according to the Navya-nyāya method, maintains that the meaning is "not being delimited by that which is not a delimitor of counter-positiveness"—the author refutes it, beginning with the words "pratiyogitā... (counter-positiveness...).
"Having the form of smoke [is] of the probandum."
The meaning is: "of that which is to be proven (sādhya) called 'smoke'.

In this fallacious syllogistic application—"This [mountain] possesses smoke because it possesses fire"—knowability (*prameyatva*) is not the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that is co-located (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the fire serving as the reason; for there is no such cognition as "there is no knowable thing possessing fire."

And thus, since the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the probandum (*sādhya*)—which is smoke as delimited by that [fire]—also exists in fire, it too would be the pervaded (*vyāpya*); this is the meaning.
Furthermore,

let it simply be that for any given thing (*x*), its pervasion (*vyāpti*) by another thing (*y*) consists in its co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *y*, provided that *x* does not co-occur with the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of *y*.
This is because of parsimony (*lāghava*).

Furthermore, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of a purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) inference, because the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished. [Objection:

But surely, by virtue of the property of being knowable (*prameyatva*), fire does indeed possess the state of being pervaded by the probandum, such as smoke; for that [pervasion] takes the form: "This is knowable because it possesses fire. In this context, if one intends by the term "knowable" the state of being smoke that is itself knowable (*prameyadhūmatva*), then the status of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) consists here in having a non-overextended occurrence (*anatiprasaktavṛttitva*).
This is because even the property of being knowable smoke (*prameyadhūmatva*) is a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of the absence in the form described above.

Even if the property of being knowable smoke were not a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of the absence in the form described above— by taking a specific fire belonging to a kitchen (*mahānasīyavahni*)— nevertheless,

when the phrase "that which is delimited by *yad*" (*yadavacchinna*) in the expression "if" (*yadi*) is intended to mean that which is delimited by a specific locus, then by taking the fire of a red-hot iron ball (*ayogolakīyavahni*), the property of being fire (*vahnitva*) remains a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of an absolute absence that co-exists with it.
