The meaning is "the absolute non-existence of fire and so forth.
"By which" refers to fire and so forth.
The phrase "of which there is co-referentiality" is to be supplied from the preceding context.
The meaning is that there is a pervasion (vyāpti) of that smoke and so forth by that fire and so forth.
Because of its brevity.

The meaning is that because this [definition] consists in the form of unerring co-occurrence (*avyabhicarita-sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it is provided with qualifiers such as "not delimited by a non-delimiter" (*anavacchedakāvacchinna*).

Nor is there a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of the pervasion residing in a reason (*hetu*) where conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), were the phrase "not co-occurrent with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogyasamānādhikaraṇa*) not stated.

The point is that since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is a pervading occurrence (*vyāpyavṛtti*), its absence (*tadabhāva*) likewise lacks co-existence in a single substratum (*aikādhikaraṇya*). (The refutation of the pervasion between the cook and the act of cooking.)
The Theory of Pervasion (Vyāptivāda), p. 25:

Since absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) itself does not exist, the absence of co-location with it is established all the more easily, just like the absence of identity with the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
And this has been stated in the section concerning the yogin.
Furthermore, what here constitutes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)? Is it space alone, time alone, both, the commonality of both, or something following from both?
Not the first, because there would be no pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of the temporal pervasion between "cowness" and "horseness."
For there exists between those two as well the pervasion (vyāpti) that "when there is cowness, then there is horseness.
It is not the second [alternative],
because spatial pervasion fails to apply to the pervasion between cooking and the color produced by cooking (*pākaja-rūpa*), and so forth.

For there is indeed a pervasion (vyāpti) between those two as well: wherever there is color produced by baking (pākaja-rūpa), there is baking. But the third [alternative] is not [tenable], because this [definition] lacks pervasion everywhere except where it is already pervaded by color, taste, and so forth.

Nor is it the fourth [alternative]. For, with respect to the cause consisting of the nature of "cowness," there is an absence of "horseness" in the locus consisting of space; thus, if pervasion were defined by that, it would result in under-pervasion (avyāpti).
If it is argued that in the case of spatial pervasion space is the locus, whereas in the case of temporal pervasion time is the locus—this is not so.
Because there is no following along [of the object].

Relying on the view that "it is precisely the non-existent that appears as having identity with the existent due to the coloring [of the cognition] by the real," he says: "In the case of the identity of the mother-of-pearl and the silver."
"This is that."
Even that which lacks epistemic warrant can be the counter-positive of an absence;
this is because it is excluded from the pervasion of color, taste, and so forth.

The meaning is: "in all cases," such as the rising of Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī, the rising of the river, rain and so forth, and in instances like the cowness of a cow or the horseness of a horse, as well as the color produced by ripening (*pākaja-rūpa*) and the like.
In the form of the nature of a cow.
This refers to such reasons as "this possesses horseness because it possesses cowness," and so forth;
[the word "also" applies] to these two as well, precisely because there is no other possible alternative.
Furthermore,
since pervasion (*vyāpti*) is being defined only at this very moment, [the definition] would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

Moreover, because there is a temporal co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the rising of Kṛttikā and the proximity of the rising of Rohiṇī, it is inappropriate to speak of their lack of co-location (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) in that case.
And because, according to the method stated by me, the possibility of a comprehensive inclusion (anugama) is established.
Furthermore, even in your own view, since eternal substances lack a substratum, there would be no pervasion (vyāpti) such that "wherever there is ether, there is an eternal substance."

If it is argued that time is the locus of space and so forth, because there is also an uncontradicted cognition that "space exists always," then the absolute non-existence of space would not be a purely positive (kevalānvayin) property.
Furthermore, since there is also the cognition that "space is everywhere," space would also have location as its locus.

Now, one might object: "Since space always exists everywhere through its essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*), but does not exist there through the relation of inherence (*samavāya-vṛtti*), then by that [latter] relation, even the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of color and so forth, as well as knowability (*prameyatva*) and the like, would be purely positive (*kevalānvayin*). To prevent this [objection], he says: "As stated by me."
The meaning is as stated by me previously in the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie argument), beginning with the words "of whichever [entity] there is a connection with place and time," and so forth.

He states the lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in other instances regarding the definitions of pervasion (vyāpti) formulated through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), beginning with "Furthermore" (kiñca).

Anticipating the objection that "being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence" (*kevalānvayy-abhāva-pratiyogitva*) and "existing at all times and in all places" (*sadā sarvatra sattvam*) are compatible through a difference in their respective relations, he refutes it by means of a *pratibandi* (reductio ad absurdum), beginning with the words "nanu" and so forth. [If it is argued: "But surely, the absolute non-existence of space (*gaganātyantābhāva*) is a purely positive entity (*kevalānvayin*)."

In that case, since neither color (*rūpa*) and so forth nor knowability (*prameyatva*) and so forth exist anywhere through the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of color, knowability, and the like would also be *kevalānvayin* (universally present) by virtue of that relation.

Furthermore, even the absolute non-existence of space exists everywhere precisely through the relation of essential identity (*svarūpasaṃbandha*), and not through relations such as conjunction; thus, the absolute non-existence of space [is likewise universally present].
(The refutation of the pervasion obtained through the subject-property [pakṣadharmatā]):

The Theory of Pervasion (Vyāptivāda), page 27. Even the absolute non-existence of space (*gaganātyantābhāva*) exists everywhere by way of its own essential relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*) alone, and not through relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Therefore, space—which is the absolute non-existence of the absolute non-existence of space—would also be a purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) entity.
Moreover, the qualification "co-occurring with its counter-positive" (pratiyogisamānādhikaraṇa) is redundant;
for it has been stated elsewhere that conjunction and its absolute absence reside in different parts [of the same locus].

Furthermore, since in your view the nature of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) consists in being an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*), and since that [essential relation] is itself comprised of the capacity to generate a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭapratīti*) which contains within it the necessity (*niyama*) that constitutes pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

Furthermore, according to the view that pervasion (*vyāpti*) exists only between specific instances of the property to be established (*sādhya*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*) that share a common locus (*samānādhikaraṇa*), earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) would not be pervaded by odor (*gandha*).
This is because every single instance of odor is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that coexists with earth-ness in each individual case.
For there is not, as there is for earth-ness, only one single instance of odor that resides in all instances of earth.
"Elsewhere" means in the *Candrikā*, in the treatises such as the *Tattvaviveka*, and in the *Vaiśeṣikādhikaraṇasudhā*.

The phrase "containing a restriction in the form of pervasion (*vyāpti*)" is an epithet for "causality" (*janakatva*); the sense is that causality consists in being a preceding occurrence (*pūrvavṛttitva*) characterized by necessity (*niyama*).
Having set aside the first definition, he states the second definition as well: "Moreover, it being thus..."

If it is argued that the meaning of the definition is "coexistence with that which is not the delimitor of the counterpositiveness of such an absolute absence," and that smell-ness (*gandhatva*) is indeed not such a non-delimiter because there is no cognition that "the earth is not possessed of smell"— then, in that case, there is simply no difference from the previous definition.

If, however, one is somehow satisfied with the conceit of their difference, the author states another fault according to the maxim, "Let the wicked man be content": "Moreover, of the universal cowness... Furthermore, there would be a temporal pervasion (*kālikī vyāpti*) of the universal cowness with respect to individual cows.

At the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), although the destruction of a specific cow (*govyakti*) exists in that which possesses cowness (*gotvavat*), there is no absence of the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the cow-individual;
thus, the temporal pervasion (*kālikī vyāpti*) of earthness (*pṛthivītva*) with smell would be established.
This is because, even though the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of smell exists before the production of smell, there is no absolute non-existence of smell.
Nor should it be argued that by the term "absolute non-existence" (atyantābhāva) one intends merely the absence of a contradictory entity,
since both destruction (dhvaṃsa) and prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) are temporally opposed to their counter-positive;
for if that were the case, the phrase "not co-located with the counter-positive" (pratiyogyasamānādhikaraṇa) would be redundant.
Furthermore, there is no absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of an individual cow anywhere;
for if that were the case, even the temporal pervasion (*kālikī vyāpti*) of "cowness" with respect to "horseness" would not exist.
[The author] refutes the position stated by Pakṣadhara and others, beginning with the words: "And not... absolute non-existence."
Regarding "from time," [it is] threefold.
"At the same time; because it would be redundant."

The point is this: since the absolute non-existence of conjunction (*saṃyogātyantābhāva*) is not incompatible with conjunction itself, if one were to state [the definition] as "that which is not the delimiting factor (*anavacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence that is contradictory to the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*) residing in the same locus (*samānādhikaraṇa*)," then there would be no risk of under-extension (*avyāpti*) in the pervasion (*vyāpti*) residing in substanceness (*dravyatva*), where conjunction is the probandum (*sādhya*).
As for what was said—that the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) [is the cause] with respect to individual cows—that is not correct.

Anticipating the objection that this is because it has the same locus as the absence of another individual cow (*govyakti*), he refutes it with the words: "And not [because of] the individual cow... (*na ca govyakteḥ*).
It is called "pertaining to time."
The meaning is that it is temporal (*kālikī*), as in "when there is cowness, then there is horseness.
He clarifies this with the words "in some cases" (*kvacid*).
(Refutation of the pervasion obtained by the cook:
The Theory of Pervasion, p. 29.
Because even the non-existence of horsehood exists at a certain time while existing in a certain place.
Furthermore, smoke would not even be pervaded by fire,
because fire, by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), is the counter-positive of an absolute absence that is co-located with smoke.

Nor should it be argued that what is intended is the state of being the counter-positive of an absolute absence that is co-located with the probans (sādhana) by way of a mode (vṛtti) included within the body of the pervasion (vyāpti) of the probandum (sādhya), since the pervasion between smoke and fire exists precisely through the mode of conjunction (saṃyoga);
for this would entail the fallacy of circularity (ātmāśraya), as the definition of pervasion is only being formulated at this very moment.

Nor should it be argued that because the absolute absence of fire exists through the relation of inherence (*samavāya-vṛtti*), while fire exists in the same locus through the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga-vṛtti*), this [absurd case] is already excluded by the very term "non-occurrent in the same locus as the counter-positive" (*pratiyogi-vyadhikaraṇa*).

For "non-occurrence in the same locus as the counter-positive" means precisely that the counter-positive does not exist in a certain locus by the very same relation through which the counter-positive exists there.

As for the claim that, although the absolute absence of that *aśvattha* tree exists at that time, it is excluded by the term "non-co-located with its counter-positive" (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*) because it is co-located with its counter-positive—that is not so. For, according to the direction to be stated later beginning with "by whatever relation," that [absence] is also non-co-located with its counter-positive; furthermore, since even the absence of one individual is co-located with its counter-positive at the stage of another individual, the aforementioned fault remains unremedied. Therefore, he raises the objection stated in the *pakṣadharmatā* section: "Nor [is there a fault] regarding the probandum (*sādhya*)" and so forth.
Now, one might object: let there be no such intention regarding the nature of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Nevertheless, fearing that smoke would incur the status of being non-pervasive—due to its co-existence with the absence of fire by way of inherence (*samavāya*), as in the case of a pot—[the author] refutes this, saying: "And not by way of inherence."

Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam (Third Chapter) — By means of that relation, the very non-existence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) therein is indeed "counter-positive-incommensurability" (*pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇyam*).

Otherwise, at that time, because all absences would be co-located with their counterpositives, those [absences] that are non-co-located with their counterpositives (pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa) would be unestablished.

Furthermore, by the term "having a different locus from the counter-positive" (pratīyogivyadhikaraṇa), is it intended that there be a difference of locus from some counter-positive whatsoever, or a difference of locus from all counter-positives?
Not the first.
This [reason] is not valid because it does not pervade the correct inference: "This [subject] possesses the absence of a specific conjunction, because it is a substance.
This is because the conjunction, which constitutes the absence of the probandum (sādhya), is non-co-located with the general absence of conjunction that serves as its own counter-positive.
Nor is the latter [alternative] tenable.

This is because there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the fallacious inference: "This [subject] possesses the absence of the general property of conjunction (*saṃyoga-sāmānyābhāva*), because it is a substance (*dravyatvāt*).

This is due to the fact that conjunction—which is the nature of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*)—lacks the quality of being "non-co-located with all its counter-correlatives" (*yāvat-pratiyogi-vyadhikaraṇatva*), since it is co-located with the counter-correlatives of the absences of specific types of conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣābhāva*).

As for what was said— that there is simplicity (lāghava) in definitions containing mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) due to the abandonment of the qualification "not co-locating with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogy-asamānādhikaraṇa*)—

that is not so. For if the absolute non-existence of conjunction (*saṃyogātyantābhāva*) is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*), then the mutual non-existence of what is conjoined (*saṃyuktānyonyābhāva*) must necessarily also be non-pervasive.
Regarding the phrase "the non-occurrence of the counter-positive" (*pratiyogino 'vṛttiḥ*), the word division is *pratiyoginaḥ* (of the counter-positive) and *avṛttiḥ* (non-occurrence).
The sense is that because fire does not exist by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*), the previously mentioned fault remains firmly established.

Having thus refuted the definition involving absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), he states the following to refute the one involving mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*): "And as for what was said... etc.

(The Refutation of the Attainment of Pervasion by the Cook: The Doctrine of Pervasion, Part 31) [The manuscript variants noted above apply to the respective sections.]
The cognition "the tree is not conjoined with the monkey at its root" is an uncontradicted experience, similar to "the tree is not a pot.
This cognition does not have the absence of conjunction as its object;
rather, it takes the form of a negation of identity, just like the cognition "a pot is not a cloth."
Otherwise, there would be the abolition of mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva),
since contradiction can be resolved by means of a difference in delimiters (avacchedaka), just as in the case of conjunction and its absolute absence.
Now, one might object: "Is this not in contradiction with the recognition that 'the very same tree which was previously devoid of conjunction is now conjoined'? We say no;
for does this recognition establish non-difference, or does it negate difference?
It cannot be the first.

This is because there is also non-difference between those two by virtue of their being that tree. Nor is the latter [alternative] tenable; for it would be impossible to negate [the connection] by saying "it is not conjoined at the root," since that would contradict the cognition of difference.
At the root, there is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) conjoined [with absolute non-existence].
[The author] provides an illustration for the perception of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) with the words "just as 'not'."
The meaning is "to say that it does not exist";
[this results in] the annihilation of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
The point is that in all cases such as "the jar is not a cloth," it is easily stated that the object of cognition is the absolute absence of cloth-ness in the jar.

Now, one might ask: how can there be both identity with the conjoined and difference from the conjoined in a single tree, given their contradiction? To this, he says: "And of contradiction... [and so forth].

The meaning is that just as there is a conjunction of a monkey with a tree delimited by its top and an absolute absence of that same conjunction delimited by its root, so too there is non-difference from the tree conjoined [with the monkey] as delimited by the top, and difference as delimited by the root; thus [the contradiction] is resolved.
He raises an objection against the non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*) of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*).
"Of those two."
The meaning is: "of that which possesses the absence of conjunction and of that which is conjoined.

He states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the claim that mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) also lacks non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*): "Furthermore, at the root... and so forth.

He states—beginning with "Furthermore, by an examination of inferential cognition..."—that even upon careful consideration of inferential knowledge (*anumiti-jñāna*), only the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) as we have described it is the cause, and not that which you have described; therefore, the definition of pervasion proposed by you is not tenable. Furthermore, by an examination of inferential cognition...
[the text continues]. (Note: The variant reading *kiṃ cetyadhikam* found in manuscripts ka, ga, and rā indicates that the word *kiṃ ca* ("furthermore") is an interpolation.)
Otherwise,

if it were not the case that at the root [of the relation] there exists conjunction in the form of the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), and the cognition thereof, then—

according to your own view— the absolute non-existence of mutual non-existence would consist in the very nature of the property that delimits the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-dharma*) of that mutual non-existence.
And because, in the case of manifestation, the conjunction is that which delimits it.

Furthermore, what is the cause of inference? Is it the knowledge of all the aforementioned pervasions (vyāpti) which include absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and so forth, or is it the knowledge of the simpler pervasion consisting solely of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), or is it the knowledge of some [pervasion] at some time?
Not the first, because inference is observed even when there is knowledge of each [pervasion] individually.
Not the second [alternative],
because inference is observed even when there is a cognition of pervasion that contains absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*);
furthermore, parsimony (*lāghava*) has been refuted in the case of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
The third [alternative] is not tenable because it lacks pervasiveness (*ananugama*).

If one were to embrace [the third alternative] on the grounds that it involves a cognition of what is otherwise impossible (*anupapadyamāna-jñānatva*), then since such impossibility itself is necessary and is simpler, let impossibility alone be the pervasion (*vyāpti*); this is the direction of the argument.

Now, an objection: even though inference is observed to arise from a cognition of pervasion characterized by absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva-garbha-vyāpti*), the cause [of inference] is, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), simply the cognition of pervasion characterized by mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva-garbha-vyāpti*).
Since this has been stated in the same way by the author of the Maṇi in his theory of repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*), he says: "In the case of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)."

The point is that since it has been stated that mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*), the term "co-located with its counter-positive" (*pratiyogisamānādhikaraṇa*) must necessarily be included even in that case.
"Thus, 'the direction'—this is the meaning."

Therefore, the definitions of pervasion stated by others suffer from the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) in the following cases: (1) in the pervasions such as that between the rising of a river in the lower region and rain in the upper region; (2) in those pervasions where the logical reasons (*tarka-aṅga*) involve circularity (*ātmāśraya*) and other fallacies; and (3) in negative pervasions (*vyatireka-vyāpti*).

— [The definition of] "absence of a limiting condition" (*anaupādhikatva*) results in either (1) the state of having a probandum that is pervaded by what does not pervade the prover, or else (2) the knowledge of both [the prover and the probandum] at some time, or (3) the knowledge of something or other.
The first three [options] are not tenable,
because inference is observed even from the knowledge of *any* [such thing].
Nor is it the fourth [alternative],
because there is no following through [of the same substratum].
Furthermore, everywhere, what is called "co-referentiality" (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is a relation with a common substratum (adhikaraṇa).

And the nature of being a relation (*saṃbandhatva*) consists in being the regulator (*niyāmaka*) of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭadhī*). Regulation, in turn, consists in producing a qualified cognition while not producing an unqualified cognition. And production (*janakatva*) consists in being a necessary antecedent that is not otherwise established (*ananyathāsiddha-niyatapūrvavṛttitva*). Thus, there arises the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

Nor should it be said that being a restrictor (*niyāmakatva*)—as a relation either as the qualificand or as a qualifier—is the cause of the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) by way of a relational synthesis (*saṃsarga-vidhi*).
Otherwise, it would be impossible for it to function as an obstacle to doubt regarding co-inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Thus, since one must necessarily admit that "relation-ness" (*saṃbandhatva*) is indeed a qualifier (*prakāra*), the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) remains unavoidable.

As for the claim that, because relationhood—in the form of being the determinant of a qualified cognition—must necessarily appear as a qualifier, it must nevertheless appear specifically in the form of "conjunction-ness" (*saṃyogatva*) and so forth;
that is not correct, because if that were the case, there would be a lack of uniformity (*ananugama*). [This is] due to its appearing as inherence-ness (*samavāyatva*).
Furthermore, in the case of an entity (*bhāva*), even the property of inherence (*samavāyatva*) consists in being an eternal relation; thus, the charge of circularity (*ātmāśraya*) remains unrefuted.
Moreover, if "delimitingness" (*avacchedakatva*) means "the capacity to produce a cognition delimited [by it]," then there is the occurrence of circularity and other fallacies.

If, on the other hand, it means "subsisting in no more than [that which is delimited by it]," then since smoke also subsists in less than the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with fire, the final definition would fail to be a valid definition.
In this manner, all the definitions favored by him are to be refuted.

If it is argued that, therefore, "the subject" (pakṣa) is that locus where there is an absence of proof accompanied by the absence of the desire to prove—it is not so.

For even when the desire to prove (siṣādhayiṣā) is absent, inference is observed to occur once the probandum is established— or even when it is not yet established. Indeed, it is seen that for one who has no doubt, who has already ascertained fire from the words of a reliable person,
and who sees a smoke-streak reaching the sky on a mountain peak, an inference arises by the power of fate upon the recollection of pervasion, even though he has no desire to infer.
For a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is not discerning; it cannot remain indifferent by reflecting, "Since this was to be done by me, it has been done by another.
Indeed, a definition must be postulated in accordance with actual experience.
However, there is no violation of experience for the sake of preserving a definition imagined by oneself;
for in this case, there is indeed the experience that not only is fire heard [from scripture], but it is also inferred. Yet, nothing more than this occurs.
Because of its weightiness:
furthermore, being delimited by mutual difference (*anyonyābhāva*) does not constitute causality in terms of positive existence (*bhāvatva*).

For even in cases such as [the presence of] a gem (*maṇi*), there would result the status of being a cause for the absence of mantras by virtue of their mutual absence; this would lead to the collapse of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that the collection of absences of obstructors (*pratibandhakābhāvakūṭa*) is the cause.

With the intention that [if it were otherwise], there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of failing to establish the distinctness of effects (kāryavaijātya) because even the mere difference between grass and other [causes] would entail causality, the objector concludes their own position with the words “therefore” (tasmāt), following the phrase “here is the opinion” (atra matam).

With the intention that this definition also suffers from the fault of being under-extensive (*avyāpti*), he states [the following] beginning with "If it exists," etc., keeping in mind what was said in the *Anuvyākhyāna-sudhā* on the *Bhaktipāda*:

"What fault is there in proving what is already established, if pervasion (*vyāpti*) exists? Translation: With the thought that this definition is also subject to the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*), he refutes [the opponent's position] by stating "If it exists" and so forth, bearing in mind the statement in the *Anuvyākhyāna-sudhā* on the *Bhaktipāda*: "What fault is there in proving what is already established, if pervasion (*vyāpti*) exists?"

The point here is that since both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) exist there, there can be no absence of the qualified (*viśiṣṭābhāva*), whether that absence be caused by the non-existence of one or both of them; therefore, pervasion (*vyāpti*) exists. Nor should it be said that "there is no subjecthood (*pakṣatā*) at all" in that case, because subjecthood is necessary there, as evidenced by the observation of the result in the form of an inference; thus he says: "For it is observed... (*dṛśyate hi*).
Since there might be the objection that experience itself does not exist, he says: "And it exists. (The refutation of the arguments for the destruction of the cooker and the fuel.)
Regarding the discussion on *pakṣatā* (page 69):
If one postulates a desire to infer (*anumitsā*) in this case, then that [desire] must also be postulated in the inference of clouds from the thundering of a jar;
for the sublation by the non-perception of what is perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi-bādha*) is equal in both instances.

And it is not impossible for there to be another determination regarding an object already determined, just as there can be another cut in what has been cut; this applies to an object known by Caitra being known by Maitra,
or to another cognition of that same Caitra at a different time.
For even then, we observe the occurrence of another verbal cognition regarding an object already established by perception,
another cognition in a continuous stream of perception, and,
even when an object has been ascertained through both word and inferential mark, another verbal or inferential cognition arising due to the force of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

[Objection: "In that case, let it be assumed that there is simply a desire to infer (anumitsā) by the force of the result; and thus, since the subject-status (pakṣatā)—which consists in the absence of the qualified [complex] due to the absence of its qualifier, namely the absence of the desire to infer—exists, there is no fault. To this, he says: "In this regard" (atrety).
"By the thundering of the two clouds."

And thus, having accepted the existence of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) therein, the demonstration of its status as the subject (*pakṣatva*) by means of stating a qualified absence—which is occasioned by the absence of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in the form of the proving instrument—would be inconsistent; this is the sense.
To the objection that the desire to infer (*anumitsā*) there would be sublated by the non-experience of what is otherwise fit for experience, he says: "or rather" (*yogya*...).

Because it is appropriate for there to be such a desire [to know], yet that [desire] is not perceived, it is called "non-perception of the perceptible" (*yogyānupalabdhi*), since it is a non-perception of something that would otherwise be perceptible. Is it the case that no other determination exists for anyone at all, or is it that it does not exist for the determiner himself? Even in this latter case, does it not exist at another time, or at that very time? Furthermore, in these instances, is its absence known through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or by the very same means of valid cognition that produced the preceding determination?

He refutes the [opponent’s] successive hypotheses with "It is known by Caitra," etc., showing that once an object has been determined through word and inferential mark, there can be no further determination of it by those very same means. [The opponent argues: "The jar is known by Caitra. Here, the jar is first determined by the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*). Then, based on the cognition "the jar is known by Caitra," one determines that the jar is known by Caitra. Thus, having first determined the jar by the word, one subsequently determines the same jar again by the inferential mark (the cognition). Therefore, since there is a subsequent determination by the same two means, the rule that "an object already determined by word and inferential mark cannot be determined again by them" is not established. To this, he replies: No. For in the case of the cognition "the jar is known by Caitra," the jar is indeed determined by the word "jar. However, the cognition "it is known by Caitra" does not determine the jar itself; rather, it determines the *act of knowing* (*jñāna*) which has the jar as its object. Since the jar is not the object of that [second] cognition, there is no determination of the jar by the inferential mark. Consequently, the jar remains unestablished by the inferential mark, and thus the rule remains intact. Furthermore, the word "jar" does not denote the act of knowing; therefore, the jar is not determined by the word either in that context. Hence, the jar is not determined by both [word and inferential mark] simultaneously. As for the claim that the jar is determined by the word "jar" and then subsequently by the inferential mark "the jar is known by Caitra," this is incorrect. For the cognition "the jar is known by Caitra" does not establish the jar as its own object; rather, it establishes the act of knowing as having the jar as its object. Therefore, the jar is not determined by the inferential mark. Since it is not determined by both, the objection does not hold. Alternatively, the word "jar" denotes the jar, but the cognition "the jar is known by Caitra" does not denote the jar; rather, it denotes the act of knowing. Thus, the jar is not determined by the inferential mark. Since it is not determined by both, the rule is not violated. Or again, the word "jar" denotes the jar, and the cognition "the jar is known by Caitra" also denotes the jar. However, the jar is not determined by the inferential mark because the inferential mark establishes the act of knowing, not the jar. Since the jar is not determined by the inferential mark, the rule remains valid. Thus, the sequence of refuting these various positions is stated: "It is known by Caitra. (Note: The manuscript variants regarding the presence or absence of certain words such as *vastu*, *ghaṭapadam*, *evam ca*, *tatra*, and *api* have been accounted for in the interpretation above.)
Furthermore,

if the accomplishment [of the effect] were obstructed by [the presence of a counter-agent] like a jewel or a mantra, then the absence of that specific [counter-agent] could be established as the cause;
however, that is not the case.
This is because, unlike a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) of a proof, it does not directly have a contradictory object;

because, like the cognition of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it lacks the capacity to disrupt the logical reason (*hetu*); and because, unlike a [counteracting] jewel and so forth, it lacks both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Moreover, if a cognition— even one whose object is not the contradictory— becomes an inhibitor of an inference by virtue of the presence of the auxiliary factor of the absence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) when it has the same object, then the knowledge of the logical mark (*liṅga*), when accompanied by the knowledge of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), would likewise directly inhibit the consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*),
and not through the mediation of the cognition of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Nor should it be argued that if there were no opposition to the established cognition (*siddhi*), the stream of inferential cognitions (*anumiti-dhārā*) would never be interrupted.

[Objection: "In all the aforementioned cases, one must postulate some kind of 'excitant' (*uttejaka*) for the obstructing *siddhi* by virtue of the observed result; otherwise, it would be impossible for the effect to arise while the obstructor is present. To this, he says: "Furthermore... (*kiṃ ca*).

Is the obstructiveness of the [cognition of] proof due to its apprehending the absence of the object to be grasped (grāhyābhāvāvagāhitva), or due to its disrupting another proof (siddhyantaravighaṭakatva), or through positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatireka)? He refutes all three in succession:
having stated that there is no proof for its being an obstructor of proof, he states the refutation as well with the words "api ca" (furthermore).
This is the knowledge of the inferential mark (liṅga).
The meaning is: that perception of the mark (liṅga) on the mountain by one who has already grasped the pervasion (vyāpti) in the kitchen and so forth.

He first raises and then refutes the first objection—namely, that if the established fact (siddhi) were not an obstacle, there would either be no interruption of the inference or the fault of proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatva) would not be a defect—by saying "na ca" (and not).

In the case of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), since established knowledge (*siddhi*) does not act as an obstacle, there would consequently arise an infinite regress of successive instances of verbal cognition even in that instance. (Refutation of the [view that] the cooking is completed)
The Theory of Pakṣatā (pu-71):

[This is because] the consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*), like the cognition that serves as the cause of verbal knowledge, does not persist for two moments, and thus lacks the capacity to be the cause of a continuous stream of inferences (*anumitidhārā*); furthermore, the position that the object possessing the mark (*laiṅgika*) is manifested as being qualified by the mark (*liṅgopahita*) has been refuted.

Nor should it be argued that two distinct inferences would necessarily arise—one at the moment the middle term (liṅga) is perceived and another at the moment of its subsistence—because their respective causes are present;
for there is no certainty regarding such a cause, as an obstruction may occur due to an intense desire to know some other object in certain cases.
Furthermore, if two inferences were to occur simultaneously, this would simply be an accepted consequence, since the causes for both are indeed present.
How indeed have you ascertained that there is never a pair of inferences?
For the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) "I infer" does not have the absence of a second [inference] as its object.

If it is argued that there can be no succession of verbal cognitions because the causal cognition whose object is the word has perished—thereby resulting in an absence of causes—the author replies that this is the same here as well: "of the consideration of the logical mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*)."
Just as in the case of cognition (*jñāna*),

it is said to be "two moments" either by taking the moment of its birth— which is the acquisition of its own being— as a starting point, or by taking the moment of its destruction as a starting point.

Now, one might object that since the form of the inference "the mountain possessing smoke possesses fire" is accepted, the inferential cognition itself must also be of the nature of a *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection); to this, he says: "liṅga... [and so forth].
The meaning is that [the view] has already been refuted in the section on the theory of inference-for-oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
To show that the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) "I infer" itself is the proof for the absence of two separate inferences, he says: "I infer."
He states the second refutation: "But [the charge of] proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
[This concludes the section on the intrinsic nature of validity (*prāmāṇyasvatastva*) within the context of the presentation of inference.
*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam*, Third Chapter, page 72. [End of section.]

It will be explained that the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana) is a defect only in inference for others (parārthānumāna), and not in inference for oneself (svārthānumāna).
Therefore, it is difficult to define [the nature of] the object.
Thus ends the refutation of the definition of the opponent’s position. // 5 //
It will be explained.
In his own view, regarding the discussion on the statement of defects in inference:

by this very refutation of the absence of proof (*siddhyabhāva*) as being the nature of the subject (*pakṣatā*), one should understand that the position of Śiromaṇi—that "the subject-nature consists in the absence of certainty regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) accompanied by the absence of the desire to prove it (*siṣādhayiṣā*)"—is also answered.

This is because the previously mentioned defects persist here as well. Briefly restating these stated defects, he concludes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words: "Therefore... (*tasmāt*).
Thus ends the refutation of the definition of the thesis as stated by Maṇi.
Now follows the definition of the thesis according to our own system.
It is said:

wherever, whenever, and with respect to whomsoever there is the presence of auxiliary factors conducive to the production of that [effect] which is intended by the mark (*liṅga*), there, at that time, and with respect to that person, that [effect] is to be established. — Now follows the definition of the subject (*pakṣa*) according to our own system. (6)

Desiring here to state the definition of the *pakṣa* (the subject) as taught by the venerable Bhagavatpāda in the *Mithyātvanumānakhaṇḍana*—namely, "the *pakṣa* is that which is qualified by the property to be proven" (*sādhyadharmaviśiṣṭaḥ pakṣaḥ*)—and refining the statement made in the *Ṭīkā*, "that which is to be brought about as a cognition by the *liṅga* (probans) is the *sādhyadharma*," he first states the nature of the *sādhya*: "of that which is intended as the *liṅga*... etc.

1. "Therefore, regarding the definitions of *pakṣatā* (the state of being the subject) proposed by others, there are three defects: (i) even when the proof (*siddhi*) exists, if there is no desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*), the resulting impossibility [of inference] constitutes a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*); (ii) if the proof were a sublater (*pratibandhaka*) of inference, there would be no basis for such a claim; and (iii) it would follow that the cognition of the logical mark (*liṅga-jñāna*) would also be a sublater of the inferential consideration (*liṅga-parāmarśa*). These are the three defects. [The reading *ityadhikam* is found in manuscripts Ga, Ṭa, and Rā. 2. *parokta-pakṣatā*—Ṭa."
(Protection of one's own position) The Theory of Subjecthood (pakṣatāvāda), p. 73.
— At that time, for such a person, with respect to the inference of that [object] as qualified by such a probandum, it is the subject (pakṣa).

Nor should it be argued that since the state of being the subject (*pakṣatā*) is also a cause of inference by virtue of being an auxiliary factor (*sahakārin*), how can it be said to consist in the fulfillment of auxiliary conditions? [To this we reply:

The term "regarded as a mark" (*liṅgābhimata*) is stated in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as the fallacious argument "The mountain possesses fire because it is knowable" (*parvato 'gnimān prameyatvāt*).
Its meaning is: "of that which is regarded as possessing pervasion" (*vyāpyatvena abhimatasya*).

The phrase "where, when," and so forth, is stated for the purpose of defining the nature of all probanda (sādhya), whether they are in grammatical apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) or not in apposition (vyadhikaraṇa).

The four occurrences of the words *yat* and *tat* are intended to exclude the fault of treating something as a probandum in another location and so on, by taking into account the attainment of favorable auxiliary conditions (*anukūla-sahakāri-sampatti*) regarding the cognition of another object for another person at another time and place.
The "attainment of auxiliary conditions" means the coming together of auxiliary factors.
The resultant meaning is that "being the probandum" (sādhyatva) consists in being fit to be the object of an inference produced by a logical mark (liṅga).
By this term "probandum" (sādhya), is it intended as a property that is doubtful, or one that is to be made known, or one that is desired to be cognized?
Not the first, because it would contradict the statement in the previous section beginning with "even when there is proof," which asserts that even what is certain is a probandum;
furthermore, for those who maintain the convergence of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa-saṃplava), they admit the operation of inference even regarding what is already certain.
Not the second,
because in the case of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), there is an absence of instruction due to the lack of a person being prompted (*prayojyakartṛ*).
Not the third.
The objection that this would lead to the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of inference (*aniṣṭānumānābhāvaprasaṅga*) and so forth has been removed.

This is because the property residing in the object of the cognition produced by the logical mark (*liṅgajanyapratītiviṣayadharma*) is what is intended by the term "property to be proved" (*sādhyadharma*).

Furthermore, the specific formulation "wherever [the reason exists], whenever [it exists]" (*yatra yadā*) is stated precisely to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) by taking into account other times and so forth.

And thus, it should be understood that at the time of generating the inference of fire on a mountain from smoke residing on that mountain, fire is the *sādhya* (the probandum); at the moment of generating the inference of rain in the upper region from the swelling of a river, rain is the *sādhya*; and at the time of inferring the non-arising of Rohiṇī from the rising of Kṛttikā, the non-arising of Rohiṇī is the *sādhya*, and so forth.
Let it be that the probandum (sādhya) is of such a nature; what follows from that? To this he says: "tādṛśa" (of such a kind).
The meaning is "of the aforementioned form";
"toward him" means toward each individual person.
"Of that," it says.
[This refers to] an entity such as fire.
[Note: *meyatva* is found in Ṭa and Ṭha; *sādhyadharmasya* is additionally present in Ṭha. Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava (Third Chapter). [Page 74]
In my view, *pakṣatā* (the state of being a subject) is not a cause of inference because it consists merely in the fulfillment of the auxiliary conditions for inference.
For even in your own view, *pakṣatā* is a cause only as the absence of the obstacle that is the establishment [of the probandum] (*siddhi*);
and the establishment of something already established does not act as an obstacle.
However, it has been stated that [the mind] is indeed favorable.
If this is so, then subjecthood (*pakṣatā*) would exist only at the stage of the consideration of the logical mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*), and not prior to that;
consequently, how could the consideration of the logical mark have as its object the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*)?
If this objection is raised:

In this case as well, when there is an inference of another object toward another person at a later time, the expression "of that [object] for him at that time" is stated in order to exclude the status of being the subject (*pakṣatā*) for that which is qualified by another object.

If it is objected that "being qualified by the property to be proven" means "being related to the property to be proven," and since this relation exists for the probans as well— by virtue of its being pervaded (vyāpyatā)— there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) to that case, we say no.
This is because what is intended by "qualification" is a relationship characterized by the distinction between property and property-possessor (dharmadharmibhāva).

The term "sādhya" (the property to be proved) is included in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and so forth. If it were stated merely as "the subject (*pakṣa*) qualified by the sādhya," then—since in reality even the mountain qualified by fire would be the sādhya—it would follow that anything other than that [fire] qualified by it [the mountain] would be the subject. To prevent this, the word "dharma" (property) is employed.
Nor should it be said that fire alone is the probandum (sādhya) and not the mountain;
for the mere nature of fire has already been established.
If it is argued that fire is established in its form as being related to the mountain because it was previously unestablished in that specific relation, then [it follows that] just as the mountain...

Fire is the probandum (sādhya) by virtue of its relation [to smoke], and likewise the mountain is also a probandum precisely by virtue of its relation to fire; for even when only the essential nature [of the subject] is established, the establishment of the qualified [probandum] is equal in both cases.

Now, one might object that in the Nyāya system, the definition of "subjectness" (pakṣatā) as consisting in the fulfillment of the requirements for inquiry is possible; therefore, he says: "In your view."

"It has been stated" refers to the previous refutation; thus, the sense is that even in your own view, the status of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) does not possess the nature of a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*).
"But is it not so? [he asks].
The meaning is: "provided that *pakṣatā* consists in the perfection of the auxiliary conditions for inference. [This concludes] the definition of its own nature (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*).
The Theory of Pakṣatā (Subjecthood), Part II—75. What is the nature of this [subjecthood], and how so?

For the fact that the "consideration of the mark" (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) has as its object the property of being a pervader residing in the locus of that subjecthood which exists at a time prior to itself and at its own time, does not constitute [the definition of pakṣatā].

However, the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*), which exists in reality at its own time, has as its locus the property of having the pervader as its object; and at the time of the consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*), the state of being a subject certainly exists. Since, even in your view, the cognition of the state of being a subject is not the cause of inference, what inconsistency is there here?

Even the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) are merely instances of the subject (*pakṣa*) when the aforementioned auxiliary conditions are present; when those conditions are absent, even the subject is nothing but a non-subject (*apakṣa*).
For "subject-ness" (*pakṣatva*) is not a genus (*jāti*).

Intending exactly this, in the *Mithyātvānumānakhaṇḍanaṭīkā*, on the occasion of explaining the root text’s statement “the subject (pakṣa) as qualified by the property to be proven (sādhyadharma),” it was stated: “that cognition which is to be produced by the logical mark (liṅga) is the property to be proven.
[Question: How is it that [the cognition] has the property-ness-in-the-subject (pakṣadharmatā) as its object? [Answer:

The meaning is that since the property which exists in the locus of the subject-status (pakṣatā) must necessarily exist at the time of the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) of the subject-status, the state of having that [property] as its object is what constitutes having the property-ness-in-the-subject as its object.

Now, one might object: since the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) exists at the time of the reflective cognition (*parāmarśa*), that cognition cannot have it as its object; and since the state of being a subject occurs at the final moment, it is impossible to even conceive of a cognition of the state of being a subject after that point. Thus, it would follow that the cognition of the state of being a subject is not a cause [of inference]. To this, he says: "But the cognition of the state of being a subject... [etc.].
"Even in your own view," [it is said].
The meaning is that this is not merely my own view;
the intention is that since [the cause] consists in the absence of an obstructer, and since the absence of an obstructer is a cause by its very existence as a positive entity (svarūpasat).

[Objection: But in this way, since the attainment of the aforementioned auxiliary conditions might occasionally occur even in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and so forth, and since that [attainment] might occasionally fail to occur even in the subject (*pakṣa*), there would be the fallacies of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and under-extension (*avyāpti*). To this, he says: "In the similar instances... (*sapakṣa...*) [Note: *liṅga* — Ga, Rā; *tattvavi-* — Ṭa, Ṭha; *yaddharmatāvi-* — Ṭa.]
In the *Sudhā* as well, it is stated that, in reality, the subject (*pakṣa*) is the object of inference (*anumiti-viṣaya*).

For there, by means of the suffix *-tavya* and the word "object" (*viṣaya*), what is intended is precisely the fitness (*yogyatā*) for being the object of inference, which consists in the attainment of the aforementioned auxiliary conditions.
Alternatively, what is intended by "being the subject" (*pakṣatva*) is being the object of an inference by virtue of possessing the pervader (*vyāpakavatva*), in both treatises.

By qualifying [the definition] with "possessing the pervader," there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the pervader itself or to the delimiters of the pervasiveness (*vyāpakatāvacchedaka*), even though these too may be objects of that inference.
And according to this view, even at the stage of the consideration of the logical mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*), [the definition applies].
There is no *pakṣatā* [as a causal factor]; rather, it exists only at the time of inference (*anumiti*).
Even in your own view, at the time of inference, there is no *pakṣatā* characterized by the absence of certainty (*siddhi*).

In this position, however, the fact that the consideration of the logical mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) has the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) as its object means that it has as its object the state of possessing the pervader (*vyāpyavatva*) with respect to the locus of the *pakṣatā* that is simultaneous with the result produced by itself.

In the definition of the probandum (*sādhyalakṣaṇa*), because the word "cognition" (*dhī*) does not intend to specify valid cognition (*pramiti*), it includes even that which belongs to the counter-example (*vipakṣa*);
this is also stated in the *Sudhā*.
The meaning is as stated in the *Sudhā* [commentary] during the discussion on why the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the section on Devotion (*bhaktipāda*) is not a fault.
He demonstrates what he himself has stated by showing its grounding in the root text with the words "tatra hi" ("for there...").
The meaning of "hi" (for) is [to be understood] in the two cited statements.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that fitness (*yogyatā*) itself is of the nature of attainment (*saṃpatti*).
Having stated one position by relying on the view of fitness, he states another definition by relying on the presence of the result (*phalopadhāna*), saying "or else" (*yadvā*).

However, some [hold that] even in the case of a treatise (*grantha*), what is intended by "subjecthood" (*pakṣatā*) is simply the fitness to be the object of an inference;
and this fitness is the absence of a cognition that—though residing in the same locus [as the probandum]—is regarded as valid and has the absence of the probandum as its object.

And thus, in the case of one who asserts non-momentariness in the world, there is the absence of such a cognition regarding momentariness, which is regarded as valid though it resides in a different locus.

And even when there exists for the proponent a perception that is not accepted as a valid cognition (*pramā*) regarding the same locus— namely, a perception of non-momentariness— the world may still properly serve as the subject (*pakṣatā*) in the momentariness-inference of the proponent of momentariness, provided that [the opponent] possesses such a perception of momentariness. [Regarding the term] "regarding the same locus" (*samānādhikaraṇa*):...
The meaning is: that which exists in the locus where the inference arises.
The meaning is: the absence of a cognition of the absence of the probandum (sādhya) which is co-located with what is intended as valid knowledge (pramātvena abhimata).
If one were to say merely "absence of cognition," there would be an impossibility [of definition].

Even if one were to say that "non-existence" means the absence of the cognition [of the probandum], the same fault remains because [such a cognition] exists [in the opponent]. When it is specified as being "of the nature of valid knowledge," since there is no necessity that the mutual cognitions of the absence of the probandum residing in the proponent and the opponent be of the nature of valid knowledge, the term "intended" (*abhimata*) is stated so that *pakṣatā* (the state of being a subject under investigation) would not occur even when such a cognition exists.

Even if it were stated that "there is an absence of such a cognition regarded as valid," this would still result in an impossibility by taking into account the cognition of another person or opponent who occupies a different locus; therefore, the entire phrase beginning with "occupying the same locus" (samānādhikaraṇa) is meaningful.
He demonstrates the definition of "subjecthood" (*pakṣatā*) as residing within the object of definition by means of its application to inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), stating:
"And thus... (*evaṃ ca*).

The connection [of the argument] is as follows: for the proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), the inference of the momentariness of form—namely, "whatever exists is momentary, like a lamp and so forth; and this world exists"—is correctly characterized by the world being the subject (*pakṣa*).

Now, the cognition of the non-momentariness of the world in the form of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) exists both for the proponent of momentariness and for the proponent of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikavādin*);
however, in that case, it is not accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) by the proponent of momentariness.

furthermore, in that case, even though the state of being a subject exists, an inference does not occasionally occur because—according to your own view—the causal complex for it, such as the consideration of the logical mark (liṅgaparāmarśa), is absent, just as in the case of perception following doubt.

Thus ends the definition of the thesis according to our own view. [Verse 6] But for another [opponent], who maintains the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*) and accepts that [the reason] as being a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with existence (*sattva*) in the person who infers.
Furthermore, for one who maintains the non-momentary theory (*akṣaṇikavādin*), [the reason] "because of existence" (*sattvāt*) would be incongruent in its locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

Thus, even when there is a cognition of the absence of such a probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), the status of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) is appropriate because of the absence of a cognition that is intended to be a valid knowledge (*pramā*) residing in the same locus; this is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "for both the proponent of non-momentariness and the proponent of momentariness," the ellipsis is "by virtue of its existence.
This means [existence] in the form of direct perception, such as recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) and so forth.

[Objection: But if this were the case, then even in the kitchen and similar locations, there would be "subjectness" (*pakṣatā*), because the capacity to be the object of an inference of the aforementioned form exists there as well.

And thus, since there would follow the erroneous application of the term "sapakṣa" (similar instance) to its effects, as well as the application of the term "pakṣa" (subject) and the resulting inferences, he says: "smoke," etc.
The reason why it is not even designated as a "subject" (pakṣa) is that it is not an object of inferential cognition (anumiti).
"From the consideration of the mark," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: in that case, just as there is no inference even when both the memory of a disintegrated pervasion and the perception of the mark (*liṅga*)—such as smoke—are present, because of the absence of the "consideration" (*parāmarśa*) consisting in the perception of the mark as qualified by the pervasion; or alternatively, even if consideration is present, it does not occur because the causal complex for perception (*pratyakṣa-sāmagrī*) is more powerful.
On this point, some hold that the seed of dissatisfaction [with the definition] is its being overly cumbersome (*gaurava*).

Others maintain that, since there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of the designation "subject" (*pakṣatva*) and the occurrence of inference even when—by chance—the conditions for consideration (*parāmarśa*) exist in a kitchen or similar location, yet the causal complex for perception (*pratyakṣasāmagrī*) is absent.

The meaning is as follows: after thus defining the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other factors employed in inference, the nature of the "obstructing factor" (*pratibandhaka*), which has now reached its turn, is being defined.
By this, it is stated that the definition of the "limiting condition" (*upādhi*) prior to the mention of the "subject-ness" (*pakṣatā*) in the *Maṇi* is misplaced and untenable;

for the knowledge of the limiting condition is of two kinds: that occurring at the time of grasping the pervasion, and that occurring at the time of the application of inference subsequent to the grasping of the pervasion.
In that regard, it was stated with the first intention—that [it is] because it acts as an obstacle to the knowledge of pervasion (vyāpti).
Because it acts as a counter-position to the second [type of fallacy], it functions as a defect by obstructing inference.

Furthermore, the manner in which it obstructs the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is clearly explained in the discussion on the "seed of the defeater" (*dūṣakatābīja*) regarding the *upādhi*, namely that for a reason (*hetu*) that abandons the pervader of the probandum (*sādhya*), the abandonment of the probandum itself is necessarily entailed.

Keeping in mind the statement from the *Anuvyākhyāna-sudhā* on the *Yuktipāda*, namely, "But the pervasion of the probans is [limited] by the exclusion of that which pervades the probandum," he states the general definition of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) as follows: "The probandum... and so forth.

In this context, by the term "sādhya" (the probandum), it is not intended—according to the direction previously stated—that there be the status of being an object of a cognition produced by a logical mark (*liṅga*).

Now, [one might object]: in an inference such as "Air is perceptible by touch because, while not being the locus of unmanifest color, it is the substratum of a perceptible touch, like a jar," there is an *upādhi* (limiting condition) such as "visibility" (*cākṣuṣatva*), which pervades the probandum (*sādhya*) as delimited by the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), namely "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*). Furthermore, in an inference such as "Inherence (*samavāya*) is inherent (*samaveta*) because it is a relation (*saṃbandhatva*), like conjunction (*saṃyoga*)," there is an *upādhi* such as "being a quality" (*guṇatva*), which pervades the probandum as delimited by the probans (*sādhana*), namely "relation-ness. [Response: This is not so. In the first case, since the *upādhi* "visibility" does not exist in the subject (*pakṣa*, i.e., air), it cannot be a true *upādhi*. In the second case, since the *upādhi* "being a quality" is absent from the probans "relation-ness," it likewise fails to qualify as an *upādhi*. Therefore, these are not valid examples of *upādhi*. Furthermore, in the case of the inference regarding air, the *upādhi* "visibility" is not even a necessary concomitant of the probandum; rather, it is merely a property that coincides with the probandum in certain instances. Thus, the definition of an *upādhi* remains unrefuted.

If [the definition were merely "that which is not present where the probandum is absent"], then at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), since smoke from the kitchen (*mahānasīyadhūma*) and the like would lack that status [of being absent where the probandum is absent], there would be an over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) regarding such adjuncts (*upādhi*) as moist fuel (*ārdrandhana*).
However, it will be clarified later that [an adjunct] is simply that which possesses the property that delimits the pervaderhood (*vyāpakatāvacchedakadharma*).

In the inference of smoke and so forth, the phrase beginning with "existent" (*sat*) is included in order to exclude things like "having a fan" (*vyañjanavatva*) from being considered adjuncts. In that very context...
The statement "not pervading the probans" (*sādhanāvyāpaka*) is made in order to exclude [qualities] such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) from being considered limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
By the word "probans" (*sādhana*), that which is intended to be the probans is meant;
the same applies to the word "probandum" (*sādhya*).

In this context, since invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) itself is accepted as pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is no mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), because the definition of pervasion as "the absence of a limiting condition" (*anaupādhikatva*) is disregarded.
He raises an objection in order to explain the response given in the *Sudhā* to the doubt that the definition previously stated might be under-extended: "But surely... (*nanu*).

Tactile sensation (*spārśana*) is that which is cognized by the sense organ of touch (*tvigindriya*). The term "existent" (*sat*) is included to ensure non-deviation with respect to fire residing in heated water; the qualifier "consisting of the subtle element" (*tanmātra*) is included to ensure non-deviation with respect to space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.

The logical connection is that there is no over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) with respect to the limiting condition (*upādhi*) such as "being visible" (*cākṣuṣatva*). Although the universal pervasion of the pure probandum (*sādhya*) is absent— because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the quality of touch itself (since "wherever there is tangibility (*spārśanatva*),

there is visibility" does not hold for touch)— nevertheless, since one observes the pervasion in jars and the like that "wherever there is tangibility in something that is a substance (*dravyatve sati spārśanatvaṃ*), there is visibility," [the condition is valid].

Because there exists the property of being a pervader of the probandum as delimited by the property residing in the subject (*pakṣadharmāvacchinnasādhyavyāpakatva*), there is a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in that case. [This concludes] the definition of an upādhi other than [the two types mentioned] by itself.
The critique of the definition of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) [on page] 81:
There is also non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of a limiting condition such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), which pervades the probandum (*sādhya*);
for in that instance, "tangibility" (*spārśanatva*) and so forth alone constitute the probandum.

By the term "sādhyapadena" — [it is meant that] although "producedness" (kṛtakatva) does not pervade the pure probandum because of its deviation in the case of universals (jāti) and so forth— since where there is inherence (samavetatva) there is producedness— nevertheless, given that it is a relation, wherever there is inherence, there is producedness.

The meaning is that there is no pervasion (avyāpti) in the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) due to its being perceived [as non-pervasive], and also in the case of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) which pervades the probandum as qualified by the probans.
Here, "being qualified" (*avacchinnatva*) should be understood as "co-referentiality" (*samānādhikaraṇatva*). He clarifies the lack of pervasion with the word "therein" (*tatra*).

The meaning is that in the two aforementioned inferences, the property of being tangible (*spārśanatva*) and so forth is not delimited; thus, because the stated definition applies, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).
If it is argued that these two should not be included as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),
but rather only that which pervades the pure probandum (*śuddhasādhyavyāpaka*), we say no.

The meaning is as follows: in the inference—namely, that the scripture beginning with "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it possesses a reliable speaker (*āpta*) and other favorable conditions, such as the one stated in the verse, "When there is the attainment of favorability among the speaker, the listener, and the connection"—the property of being the speech of a reliable person (*āptavākyatva*) is accepted as a *upādhi* (limiting condition). This is because it pervades the subject delimited by the probandum (*sādhya*), and because the seed of the fault to be explained later applies equally to all *upādhis* that pervade the subject delimited by the probandum.

Although there is no harm even if one does not accept a *upādhi* (limiting condition) in that case— since the inference is already defective due to the sublation (*bādha*) of the probandum and the reason by the fact that *samavāya* lacks any basis in valid cognition (*aprāmāṇika*)— nevertheless, following the maxim that "one need not adhere to a specific example," the intent is to demonstrate an *upādhi* that pervades the probandum as qualified by the reason, as in the argument "destruction is perishable because it is produced" (*dhvaṃso vināśī janyatvāt*), where "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth serve as such an *upādhi*; for other examples of this kind are possible.

Since this [reason] is well-known in the opponent's own view (*paramata*) and is merely restated here in the *Sudhā* commentary, the example shown pertains specifically to the position of *samavāya* (inherence); thus, there is no fault. [Note: In the case of arguments such as "absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is perishable because it is produced," the property of being an entity (*bhāvatva*), which pervades the probandum as delimited by the probans, is added; however, in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*), this is not so.]
Pu-82. *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (Third Chapter):

In the treatise (*śāstra*), in such arguments as "the color and other qualities of earth-atoms are eternal because they are specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of atoms, like the color of water-atoms," the status of being a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is accepted even for that which has "unequal pervasion" (*viṣamavyāpta*), such as the absence of being a specific quality of earth.

This is because, even in the absence of equal pervasion (*samavyāpti*), it is possible to bring about a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*) and so forth by the mere fact of being a pervader of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka*) and so on according to the method to be explained hereafter; and furthermore, because the underlying cause of its capacity to refute remains the same.

Furthermore, even though the specific meaning of the word's component parts—namely, "producing a reflection" (pratibimbajanakatva)—is absent in the case of the prover (*sādhana*) regarding its own property in the form of being pervaded by the probandum (*sādhyavyāpyatva*), the use of the term *upādhi* is justified through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), just as in expressions such as "done for the sake of gain" (*lābhādyupādhinā kṛtam*).

Furthermore, the definition of a *upādhi* (limiting condition) in the treatise is not for the sake of worldly convention, but rather for the purpose of refuting inference; therefore, let the term *upādhi* be technical (*pāribhāṣika*) when applied to a case of unequal pervasion (*viṣamavyāpti*).

To explain: the definition of a *upādhi* (limiting condition) is "that which, while being a pervader of the *sādhya* (the probandum), or while being co-locatable with the *sādhya*, does not pervade the *sādhana* (the probans) that deviates from the *sādhya*.

Here, the first "being" (*sat*) clause is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to such things as a non-locus or something contradictory to the *sādhya*, which are entirely devoid of the conventional usage of *upādhi*.

The qualifier "deviating from the *sādhya*" is included to prevent the undesired consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [properties like] "possessing a wick" being an *upādhi* in the case of a reason such as "smoke," and so forth.

That too has been refuted by this very [argument], because the usage of "limiting adjunct" (*upādhi*) occurs even when this [definition] is unknown, and because it obstructs inference; these are the reasons already stated. This is because the deviation [of the reason] caused by the deviation [of the probans] from the limiting condition (*upādhi*) exists even in the case of the pure probandum (*śuddhasādhya*).
