For whatever is to be reduced to absurdity is precisely what is intended [by the opponent].
"Unacceptability" (*aniṣṭatva*) consists precisely in being sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabādha*).

For this very reason, they say that "the state of being the thing to be entailed" (*āpādyatva*) is the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) of the absence (*vyatireka*) which is the object of the cognition that refutes what is intended as the entailment (*apādaka*). [The phrase] "they say" means "the logicians (*tārkika*) say."
He clarifies the state of being destructible by the aforementioned knowledge with the words: "For it is destroyed."
The meaning is that in the absence of that, there is no finality in the opposite case.

The meaning is that [the reasoning] would be a fallacy because it lacks one of the five constituent parts mentioned in the verse: "Pervasion, non-frustration by tarka, termination in the opposite case, and undesirability/non-conformity—these are the members of tarka. Thus, due to the deficiency of even a single member, it would be a semblance (ābhāsa).
Having set aside the charge of non-establishment (asiddhi), he states the refutation of sublation (bādha) with the words "evam" (thus).
"These very ones."
The meaning is: because only that which is sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is to be established as the consequence (*āpādya*).
That which is intended as the reason for the consequence (*āpādaka*), namely "the state of being without fire" (*niragnikatva*)—[this is] indeed sublated by that very means of valid cognition.
For what is undesirable must be established [as the probandum]; [this is] according to the *Pramāṇagādharāja* and the *Vacaspatya*.
— [Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava, Third Chapter, p.
146] — Nor is "the absence of smoke" (*nirdhūmatva*) the probandum in this case.
For if that were the case, there would not be the cognition "it is so" nor "it is thus"; rather, there would be the cognition "this is smokeless.
Furthermore, the object of the cognition "this is smokeless" is not coextensive with the object of the cognition "it is thus smokeless."
In that case, it would belong to the additional [word], because the meaning of both words is also indicated.

For this very reason, there is no "contradiction with one's own tenet" (apasiddhānta) either; for that [fallacy] occurs when one establishes something contrary to one's own tenet, rather than when one points out a consequence.

Therefore, in an inference in the form of a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga), non-establishment (asiddhi), sublation (bādhā), and contradiction with one's own tenet (apasiddhānta) are indeed ornaments.
But not the refutations.

For this very reason, it has been stated that this [inference] is a *prasaṅga-anumāna* (reductio ad absurdum) precisely because of its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) to a *sādhana-anumāna* (positive proof-inference).

Indeed, even among *sādhana-anumānas*, one observes mutual dissimilarity between those that are purely positive (*kevalānvayi*), purely negative (*kevalavyatireki*), and both-positive-and-negative (*anvayavyatireki*).

[The phrase] "the absence (*vyatireka*) which is the object of that cognition—namely, the cognition of 'possessing smoke'—which serves as its destroyer" means that the absence is the state of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) to that which possesses smoke.
When the subsumer (*apādaka*) is sublated by the cognition of the absence of the subsumed (*āpādya*), the latter’s status as the subsumed is destroyed.
For instance, the state of being without fire (*niragnikatva*) is sublated by the cognition of the presence of smoke (*sadhūmatva*), which is the absence of the absence of smoke (*nirdhūmatva*).
This is because the argument results in a reductio (*viparyaya*): "This is not smokeless; therefore, it is not without fire."
The meaning is that otherwise, it would follow that inference (tarka) lacks existence.
Now, one might ask: "In proving the absence of smoke, how is there no sublation (bādha)? To this, he says: "And not here."
And he refutes the fault of contradicting one's own tenets (apasiddhānta) previously mentioned with the words "for this very reason."
The meaning is that this [cognition] "this is smokeless" arises precisely from a non-probative [means].
Now, one might ask: since it differs from inferential proof (*sādhana-anumāna*), how can this be considered inference? To this, he says: "Precisely for this reason."

Its exclusion [from the category of non-existence] has been stated; if [it is argued that it is excluded] because of its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) from the nature of being characterized by spatial direction (*diś*), time (*kāla*), and so forth—[then we reply:
there is no inclusion of that [dissimilarity] within [the definition].

Tarkavādaḥ, p. 147: Even though there are internal differences among these [types of inference], they possess the nature of inference because they function as means of cognition through the force of pervasion (vyāpti); this is equally true for the proponent of *tarka* (reductio). 1.
If it is asked: "In that case, since sublation (*bādha*) and other such factors would not be defects, how can there be validity [of the inference]?"—listen.
For a doubt may arise in two ways regarding the possibility of smoke existing without fire:

either because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of non-smokiness with respect to the state of being without fire is simply absent, or because, even if the pervasion exists, non-smokiness is present in the subject (*pakṣa*).
This is the dissimilarity.

The meaning is that "dissimilarity" (vaidharmya) consists in the form of being empty of the counter-example (vipakṣa), being empty of the similar example (sapakṣa), possessing both of these, and so forth.
“That which is present in all or some of the similar instances (sapakṣas),
is absent from all dissimilar instances (vipakṣas), and pervades the subject (pakṣa), is a purely positive (kevalānvayin) reason.”
This is the intended meaning of the phrase "ityādeḥ" (of such [statements]).
By this, the statement from the *Paddhati*—namely, that "the non-establishment of the probans (*apādaka*) is not a defect," and so forth—is to be understood as explained.

Having restated the objection that "because they possess the general definition of inference (*anumāna*), the purely positive inference (*kevalānvayi*) and others are indeed inference," he states their similarity with the words "teṣu" (among them).
How so?

The meaning is as follows: since the result consisting of the cognition "absence of smoke" has a sublated object and is therefore non-valid, and since the cognition "absence of fire" is its instrument, how can that which produces non-validity—having an unestablished object and being of the nature of an error—possess validity, which consists in being the instrument of a means of valid cognition?
The relationship between the result and the instrument is not thus;
rather, it is quite otherwise.

And in that regard, since both knowledge as the result and knowledge as the instrument are of the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*) alone, the author— desiring here to provide a threefold resolution according to the *Sudhā* commentary on the *Lakṣaṇa-ṭīkā*, beginning with the words "niragnikatvam" and so forth— states the introductory context (*upoddhāta*) with the verse beginning "śṛṇu" and so on.
It has been stated that "reasoning (*tarka*) is the limit of doubt," because its function is to remove doubt; thus, it was said, "for doubt...

In that regard, the first [type of doubt] is dispelled by the statement, "If it were without fire, then it would be without smoke," which demonstrates that the absence of smoke (*nirdhūmatva*) is the pervader (*vyāpaka*).

This is because it is established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that words such as "if" (*yadi*) and "then" (*tarhi*) convey a pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the form of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) regarding the meaning of the word with which they are co-occurrent; as in the cases: "If the gavaya is like a cow, then the cow is also like a gavaya," "If he is not at home while alive, then he is outside," and "If there is smoke, then there is fire."

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Sudhā* that the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is expressed simply as "if this, then this. However, by the word "yadi" (if) used therein— the meaning is that doubt is to be removed by reasoning (*tarka*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "If..."

"The cognition of similarity residing in the remembered [object] arising from the cognition of similarity residing in the perceived [object] is analogy (*upamāna*); this is the example of analogy according to the *Śābara-bhāṣya*, namely:
'If it is a gavaya...'"

The example of the means of valid cognition known as presumption (*arthāpatti*) is as follows: "If [a person] is alive, the absence of that living being in the house leads one to postulate his existence outside; this is the case when it is said, 'if he is alive'."
An example of a well-known inference (prasiddhānumāna) is: "If there is smoke..."
By the phrase "and so forth" (ādipadena), there is the inclusion of such statements as: "If, between Caitra and Maitra, one of them is Caitra, then the other is Maitra," and so on.
"For this very reason" (ata eva).
Because the capacity to convey pervasion (vyāpti) is established by linguistic convention precisely in cases where [the word] has "if" (yadi) as its initial member.

"Since Rohiṇī is near its rising because Kṛttikā has already risen"—when this is said, there is no proof [for the claim]. For in this matter, only the authoritative word (ājñā) is the means of establishment.

Thus, the meaning is that in the *Anuvyākhyāna-sudhā* on the section concerning devotion (*bhaktipādīya*), the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigraha*) is stated by the words "yadi" (if) and so forth.

Now, one might object: "In this case, the two words 'syāt' (might be) and 'ac' (unconditioned) located in the locus of the consequence (*āpādya*) and the probans (*āpādaka*) would be redundant, because there is no [logical] operation (*kṛtvābhāva*). To this he says: "By the word 'yadi' joined with... [and so on].
The meaning is "by that which is joined with the word *yadi*. (The inclusion of that [word] within the [compound]...)

For in the case of its opposite, at the very limit of the final conclusion of the reasoning, there is likewise an understanding [of the truth].
By that very same statement, the second [type of reasoning] is also excluded.

For you yourself agree that a statement such as "if a guest should arrive, then he ought to be fed" is a mere possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) and not a *tarka*, because it lacks a conclusive reversal (*viparyaya-paryavasānābhāvāt*).
And in this case, the absence of smoke is the logical mark (*liṅga*) which possesses the pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) with respect to the absence of fire.
The cognition of that [absence] is the instrument (*karaṇa*).

With respect to the absence of the state of being without fire (*niragnikatva*), the pervadedness (*vyāpyatva*) of the absence of the state of being without smoke (*nirdhūmatva*) is the mark (*liṅga*), and the cognition thereof is the result (*phala*). Both of these are indeed of the nature of valid knowledge (*pramā*).

"By that very [word]" means: by the word *syāt* joined with the word *tarhi*, the existence of the absence of smoke in the subject (*pakṣa*) is established; thus, the subject itself is also refuted—this is the meaning.

[Objection: "In that case, then, an undesirable understanding would also arise in instances such as *bhojayitavya* (should be fed), because the suffix *tavya*, which is a synonym [for *anīya*], is present. To this, he says: "If [he is] a guest... etc.
"It is merely a conceptual presumption."
The meaning is "merely fitness.
This applies to you as well.
The sense is that it is exactly so according to the statement of Maṇikaṇṭha. To the question, "Let that be so; how, however, does this constitute validity? he says: "And here... [atra ca].
"An ascetic."
The meaning is that the object to be inferred is the thing;
thus, both [the subject and the property] are included.

The meaning is that there are two [types of knowledge]: the knowledge of the mark (*liṅgajñāna*) and the knowledge of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgijñāna*). Because of the rule that in the absence of a cause there is necessarily an absence of the effect,

For this very reason, since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the absence of the lack of smoke by the absence of the lack of fire has been established precisely through the force of the reductio (*prasaṅga*), and because [the argument] culminates in its contrapositive (*viparyaya*), the statement "this is smokeless" merely demonstrates its presence as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*);
then, by the statement "therefore, it is not without fire," the probandum (*sādhya*) is stated.

by which both [cognitions] would be invalid.

the sense is that by the statement "if [it] were without fire," etc., that doubt is dispelled, and thus the mark (liṅga) consisting of the nature of the pervader (vyāpakatva)—namely, the absence of smoke—is not unestablished (asiddha). To this, he says: "of the absence of the pervader" (vyāpakābhāvasya).
The meaning is that the absence of the state of being smokeless [serves as the reason] for cognizing the absence of the state of being without fire, which is its pervaded (vyāpya) form.
Regarding this, he states the indicator: "For this very reason" (ata eva).

[Objection: But if it has been stated that there is no defect in the *tarka* when one anticipates such issues as unestablishedness (*asiddhi*) or sublation (*bādha*), then how can it be said that there is an absence of unestablishedness and so forth by the method just described? To this, he says: "But the statement regarding unestablishedness, etc. (*asiddhyādyuktistviti*).
(Its inclusion is not within that):
the statement of *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum), p. 151.

— In order to demonstrate the pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) of "the absence of smoke," those two forms—the state of being without fire and the state of being without smoke—which are respectively the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*), are presented by means of the *tarka*-statement with that intention.
Therefore, since the object embraced by each respective [reasoning] is not sublated, reasoning is not invalid.

Intending exactly this, it is stated in the *Sudhā*: "If [the opponent argues] that there is no unestablished nature (*asiddhatva*) regarding the absence of sacrificial fires (*niragnikatva*) and so forth because they are [in fact] adorned [by them], then [the author replies] that the words 'if' (*yadi*) and 'it would be so' (*tathā sati*) would not be used, nor would the word 'but' (*iti ca na syāt*) be spoken.
This is the position."

Furthermore, it has been stated in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇaṭīkā* that in an inference in the form of a reductio (*prasaṅga*), there is no defect such as contradiction with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇavirodha*) regarding the probandum or the consequence; this is also stated in the *Sudhā*: "Because sublation (*bādhā*) and departure from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*) are not defects in an inference in the form of a reductio."
Intending this very point, it is stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna*:
"Stated for the sake of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*), it does not refute the established doctrine (*siddhānta*)."

Thus: *praśaṅga* (the objection) is the demonstration of the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) residing in another [entity], which serves as the mark (*liṅga*) for the positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) that constitutes a member of the inference to be supported.
Because it has that as its purpose—that is, because it necessitates it—it resides in the heart and so forth—as stated in the *Sudhā*.
The meaning is: "as stated in the *Bhaktipādīya-sudhā*. Thus it is said.
In the *Anuvyākhyāna* on the *Bhaktipāda*, he states the meaning in accordance with his own position, beginning with the words "prasaṅga" (consequence), etc.

that is intended with reference to the third alternative (*pakṣa*) which will be stated later.

And this is appropriate; for, according to the maxim of the "strength corresponding to the Yakṣa," even the absence of smoke must be accepted as a property of the subject (pakṣa), since it is precisely that which is related to the subject that constitutes the probans.

In that case, smoke, taste, and so forth, serve to establish fire, color, and so on, only when they are known to be related to the subject through relations such as inherence in what is conjoined (saṃyuktasamavetatva).

Just as in the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), and so forth, since even the property of "being without fire" is accepted by the opponent as residing in the subject (*pakṣa*), it is appropriate that the relationship [of the reductio] consists precisely in the acceptance [of that property], because only what is known as such can serve as the subsumer (*apādaka*).
// [Regarding the term] "to be stated" (*vakṣyamāṇa*)...

Refuting sublation (*bādha*) and non-establishment (*asiddhi*) by means of another method, and while accepting—according to the opponent's own way of speaking—the instrumentality and result of the cognitions of "being without fire" and "being without smoke," he states the validity of *tarka* (reductio): "Or rather... (*yadvā*).
"Having the form of a yakṣa."

The meaning is that, according to the principle that the offering should correspond to the yakṣa’s nature— namely, a *bali* for one who is fierce, an *atibali* for one who is extremely fierce, and a small *bali* for one who is mild— the word "smoke" (*dhūma*) [is used].
The meaning is: smoke and taste [serve as indicators] of that and its like;

Moreover, it is observed that even in the case of an inference based on a means of proof such as the rise of the Kṛttikās and the subsequent flooding of a river, although there is no [such flood] in the subject (pakṣa)— namely, the region above the rising Rohiṇīs—

there exists the property of being situated below the region defined by the subject, which is co-temporal with the probandum (sādhya) residing in the subject; and according to your own view, even in the case of knowability (*prameyatva*) in the form of "knowability" and so forth, there exists a mediated relation (*paraṃparā-sambandha*), such as being inherent in the cognition that is proximate to the subject in its own nature, through the word which serves as the subject.
In this view, the validity of the *tarka* consists in the fact that the absence of fire and the absence of smoke are accepted—or must be accepted—as being present in the subject (*pakṣa*).

[Objection: But how can something other than conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*) function as the relation constituting "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*), since such a thing is never observed? To this, he says: "And it is seen," etc.

The meaning is that it is an inference taking such forms as: "the rising of Rohiṇī is imminent because Kṛttikā has already risen," and "the upper region will have rain because there is a swelling of the river in the lower region."

The connection with the subject (*pakṣasaṃbandha*)—in the form of being proximate to the completion of the phase whose nature is the rising of Rohiṇī, and in the form of occurring at the same time as the probandum—is observed in the case of the mark (*liṅga*) which is the rising of Kṛttikā. Nor can this be accepted as a desired consequence (iṣṭāpatti), because it contradicts experience; such is the meaning.
[This applies] to your position.

It is nothing other than that.

Validity.

The connection [of the words] is with "reasoning" (*yukti*). Regarding the phrase "as being for the sake of a reductio ad absurdum" (*prasaṅgārthatayā*), he says "or rather" (*athavā*) in accordance with the statement in the *Sudhā* commentary.

Because it exists, and because in that form the instruments and results— namely, the cognitions of "absence of fire" and "absence of smoke"— which have that [proposition] as their object, are valid (*pramā*), it is correct [to say that the inference is not a means of valid knowledge].
And this position is stated in the *Paddhati* because, in that context, the meaning of the term "establishment" (*siddhi*) consists merely in the opponent's own admission.
Alternatively, the phrase "if he were without fire" means "if there were an acceptance of being without fire";
and such an acceptance is indeed already established.
Otherwise, even *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) would not arise.
Thus, the meaning of "it would be smokeless" is that it must be accepted as being smokeless;
for *āpādana* (the drawing out of a consequence) is the making known of something as something that must be accepted.
Nor, however, is it an establishment of actual existence, as in the case of [the statement]:

"If you eat poison, then you will die. Furthermore, in the absence of an admission [of the probandum], the capacity for such an admission—consisting in the contradiction with one's own actions and so forth—is not sublated.
Now, one might ask: even if it is made known that [the object] must be admitted, how is the sublation (bādhitatva) of that admission refuted? To this, he says: "And not... (na ca).

The necessity of accepting smokelessness (*nirdhūmatva*) is indeed the fitness for acceptance; this consists in the contradiction with one's own action (*svakriyāvirodha*). When, having accepted the effect in the form of smoke, one accepts the absence of the cause in the form of fire, there arises a contradiction with one's own action in the form of engaging with the cause for the sake of the effect. Thus, it is stated in another manner that "this smokelessness must be accepted."
And thus, the meaning is that it is not sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Alternatively, why would the knowledge of what must be accepted be undesirable?
Since it is precisely the undesirable that is to be brought about as a consequence, he says: "And not... (*na ca*).

The meaning is as follows: since it was previously stated that "there must be smoke," if one were to accept the absence of smoke, there would be an inconsistency with one's own action (*svakriyāvirodha*). Thus, the "unfitness for acceptance" (*aṅgīkārāyogyatā*) remains uncontradicted; therefore, the production of an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*) does not fail to occur.

Pu-178. *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam* (Third Chapter):

Because there is an absence of both doubt and the desire to prove [the probandum] due to the fact that the probandum is already ascertained, it is impossible for a single part [of the subject] to possess the status of being the "locus" (*pakṣa*) according to your own view.

Nor should it be argued that even when there is a certainty regarding a jar’s difference from others by virtue of its being a jar (*ghaṭatva*), there may still be doubt and so forth concerning it by virtue of its being earth (*pṛthivītva*).

For when there is a certainty regarding the difference from others in a specific form, any doubt regarding it in a general form must necessarily have as its object either that specific [property] or another specific [property].

Otherwise, even if there were a certainty regarding this mountain’s possession of fire by virtue of its being a mountain (*parvatatva*), there would result a doubt regarding it on that mountain by virtue of its being a mountain; consequently, one seeking fire would not engage in unhesitating action toward it.

Nor is the non-establishment of the probandum (sādhyāprasiddhi) merely in the form of doubt regarding the subject (pakṣa) itself, because that would entail the impossibility of its being a subject (pakṣatvāyogāt).

He states [the objection] with the words beginning "But then," and so forth.

The meaning of the probandum (*sādhya*) is: that which is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the difference residing in that entity which is distinct from the twelve categories beginning with fire (*tejas*).

Thus, the connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: since the difference from water and the differences from the twelve categories beginning with fire are established in a single locus by way of generality, the state of being distinct from thirteen [categories] is established either through perception or through inference; this is what is suspected here as well, because the same logic applies, just as it was stated in the *Maṇi* (Gangeśa’s *Tattvacintāmaṇi*) in the *Prāmāṇyavāda* section to establish the establishment of the cognition of validity (*prāmāṇya-anumiti*) by means of ensuring the well-known status of validity. He introduces this with the words "vyāghātādi" ("contradiction, etc.").

The meaning is as follows: since there are thirteen types of non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) that constitute the probandum (*sādhya*), if the probandum were unestablished, it would be impossible to negate it by saying "the probandum is not established. Therefore, the person who negates it must have already understood the probandum in a general sense. Thus, when one says "it is not established," it is like saying "this is not denotable" (*anabhidheya*); it is said out of fear of the punishment of contradiction with one's own words (fire striking itself).

If it is argued that even when the probandum (*sādhya*) is established through general cognition (*sāmugdhya*), there is no certainty regarding a specific individual—whether it be the subject (*pakṣa*) or something other than the subject—that "this [individual] possesses the probandum," we say: no.

For even in the absence of certainty regarding a specific individual, the negative inference (*vyatirekin*) proceeds; if, prior to this, there were certainty that "something possesses the probandum," that very thing would constitute a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and thus the status of the inference as a negative one (*vyatirekitva*) would be destroyed.

Otherwise, even if there were certainty that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is broken by a limiting condition (*upādhi*) somewhere, if one did not ascertain the specific location where the pervasion is broken—thinking "it is here"—then even a fallacious reason (*sopādhika*) would become a valid reason (*saddhetu*).

Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava (Third Chapter) When an object has been ascertained precisely as being authoritative, an inquiry into a specific means of knowledge for that [object] is as futile as an inquiry into a specific attribute of something already known to possess that attribute.

Furthermore, because even that which is ascertained as possessing a common property by means of a general valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), the status of being a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*) would be undermined.
Therefore, negative inference (vyatirekyanumāna) is not logical. Furthermore, how can a positive entity be made known by a negative concomitance (vyatirekavyāpti) that pertains to non-existence?

If it is argued that, regarding the capacity to convey meaning (*gamakatva*), what is essential is simply the nature of pervasion (*vyāptitva*) as accompanied by both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekavyāpti*),
and not specifically the nature of positive pervasion (*anvayavyāptitva*) because of the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*), we say: no.

If that were the case, since the fact of being produced would then result in making known impermanence through a pervasion residing in smoke (rather than in the property itself), one must state that what is essential is the possession of a pervasion residing in the [probans] itself. Thus, in a positive inference (*anvayi*), the essential pervasion resides in the [probans] itself;
however, in a negative inference (*vyatirekin*), it resides in the absence.

If it is argued that there is no over-extension [of the definition] because the relationship between the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and the substratum (*anuyogin*) serves as the regulator, we say no;
for this would result in the definition of a logical mark (*liṅga*)— namely, "that which is pervaded" (*vyāpyam*)— being inapplicable to the negative inference (*vyatirekin*).
Having taken what was stated [in the previous verse] to heart, he refutes the *vyatirekin* [reason] by means of another method, saying: "Furthermore, by that which resides in non-existence... etc.
And there is no over-extension [of the principle].
The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) indicates impermanence through a pervasion (*vyāpti*) based on smoke.
"The counter-correlate."

The meaning is that there is a relationship of counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and substratum (*anuyogin*) between the absence and the presence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*), as well as between the probans (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*).

For, just as in the case of fires produced from grass, fire-sticks, or jewels, no internal distinction is experienced among the inferential cognitions (*anumiti*) produced by the two aforementioned causes— such as the consideration of the middle term (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) and so forth.

Furthermore, the postulation of such a distinction is improper, as it would involve a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*) and because it cannot be established through non-perception of the capable (*yogyānupalabdhi*).
Of the intermediate distinctness.
This must necessarily be accepted; otherwise,

because the two sets of causal conditions would lack mutual invariable concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*) with respect to their status as causes for cognition, it would follow that the specific intermediate species delimited by being produced by those respective [causes]— which are pervaded by the universal "fire-ness"— could not be admitted even in the case of fires produced from grass, fire-sticks, or gems.
Furthermore, that universal (jāti) is not perceived;
therefore, such a conceptual construction is not tenable—this is the intended meaning.
The phrase "in the case of fires produced from grass, flint, and jewels" serves as a negative example (vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta) according to the opponent's own system.
In that regard as well, because [the existence of] a sub-class has been refuted in the second chapter;
others hold that, according to our own view, this is merely a positive example (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*).

The meaning is that even if it is not being experienced, the postulation [of a difference] based on the distinctness of the causal complex (*sāmagrī-vaijātya*) involves a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*), since the distinctness of the complex can only be established once the two complexes have been proven to exist.
The meaning is that the capacity for proof as stated by you regarding the negative-only (vyatirekin) inference remains unestablished even now.

Furthermore, if negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) were to directly produce cognition, then the redundancy (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇatva*) you accept as being an obstacle to inference by way of obstructing the knowledge of pervasion would not be an obstacle at all.

This is because, even if the positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) is disrupted by such redundancy, the negative concomitance— being an indivisible absence (*akhaṇḍābhāva*)— is not disrupted by it, and thus lacks redundancy.

Moreover, in this way, your intended position—that the seed of the defeater (dūṣakatābīja) for a contradictory [reason] is its being the counter-positive of the absence that pervades the probandum—would not be established.
To explain: does the cognition of the aforementioned counter-positiveness obstruct inference by way of obstructing the cognition of non-deviation?
Or is it by way of obstructing the cognition of concomitance?
Not the first,
because that would result in the inclusion of the contradictory (*viruddha*) within the "overly pervasive" (*sādhāraṇa*).
The meaning of "being a prover" (*gagamakatva*) is "being a generator of an inference" (*anumitijanakatva*).
Regarding the point that the qualification is useless.

In cases such as "the mountain possesses fire because it possesses blue smoke," the presence of a redundant qualifier (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇatva*) would indeed lead to inference, since it obstructs inference only by obstructing the cognition of the pervasion residing in smoke as defined by fire.
This is because the absence of the qualified entity—namely, the absence of "blue smoke"—is not a redundant qualifier;
the meaning is that this absence is an indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) whole.

To the one who argues that "negative pervasion (vyatirekavyāpti) is the direct means of proof only in the case of the purely negative inference (kevalavyatirekin), whereas elsewhere it is employed by way of removing the cognition of deviation and not directly," he replies with the words "Moreover" (api ca).
"So be it."
The meaning is that negative concomitance (vyatirekavyāpti) possesses the capacity to produce knowledge directly.
"It is as you have intended."
The meaning is that this was stated in exactly the same way in the *Hetvābhāsa-saṃgraha*;
[the question is] "What is non-deviation?"

For the sublated (bādhita) and the counter-balanced (pratipakṣita) [reasons] are direct impediments to inference because they involve the apprehension of the absence of the object to be grasped (grāhyābhāva).
The three— contradictory (viruddha), established [by another means] (siddha), and inconclusive (vyabhicārin)— are impediments to inference by way of obstructing the reflective judgment (parāmarśa),
which is the instrument of inference.
Not the second [alternative] either;

for although the knowledge of the absence of the probans (*hetu*) in all instances possessing the probandum (*sādhya*) obstructs the knowledge of positive concomitance (*anvaya-sahacāra*), there is an absence of the knowledge that "the probans exists in all instances where the probandum is absent," which would obstruct the knowledge of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*).
Therefore, negative inference (vyatirekyanumāna) is not tenable.

For investigators, however, the presentation of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is as follows: for instance, the presentation of the establishment of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhya*), or the deficiency of the probans (*sādhana*), and so forth, serves as a means to establish a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) that undermines the inference, rather than being a direct refutation.
Furthermore, the capacity to obstruct the final cognitive reflection (*parāmarśa*) occurs by way of having as its object the absence of the objects of that reflection;
and those two objects are the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
Among these, "unestablished" (asiddhi) is [a fallacy] by way of contradicting the property-of-the-subject (pakṣadharmatā);
the other two are by way of contradicting pervasion (vyāpti).
And pervasion consists of two components: non-deviation (avyabhicāra) and concomitance (sahacāra).

In that regard, the meaning is as follows: in a case of contradiction (*viruddha*), does the cognition of being the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakībhūtābhāvapratiyogitva*) function by way of obstructing the cognition of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), or by way of obstructing the cognition of co-presence (*sahacāra*)?
It is "common."
The meaning is "inconclusive due to being common" (*sādhāraṇānekāntika*).
By providing an explanation of the phrase "of the cognition of contradiction," the [author] specifies it as "the cognition of the absence of the reason in everything that possesses the probandum."
"Positive concomitance."
The meaning is: "in the reason (hetu), there is concomitance (sahacāra) in the form of co-occurrence with the probandum (sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇya).
[This is said] because that [concomitance] is not disrupted.
And thus, the point is that since the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) can be known there through the constraint of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*), an inference would indeed occur.

Or, for example, the presentation of an illustrative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) is by way of demonstrating the pervasion (*vyāpti*) which is a constituent part of inference, but not as a direct constituent part itself.

Likewise, it should be understood that [the example] functions as a means of establishing the positive concomitance (anvaya-vyāpti), which is a constituent of inference, but not as a direct constituent [of the inference itself].

Although in an inference based on both positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatirekin), negative pervasion (vyatirekavyāpti) does not establish positive pervasion (anvayavyāpti)— since the latter is established there from other means— nevertheless, even when an inference clearly exhibits deviation (vyabhicāra), it either remains silent like a suppressed condition (upādhi), or it persists by dispelling the very suspicion of deviation regarding the positive pervasion itself.

As for the statement in the *Sudhā* that the inference based on negative concomitance (*vyatirekin*) lacks the five required features (*pañcarūpatā*), and that this [objection] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to inferences such as those based on elimination (*pariśeṣa*),

which serves to refute the objection of a bystander that the negative inference is not a valid means of knowledge— that was intended merely to point out to the opponent that if "unestablished qualification" (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) were considered a logical defect,
then the negative inference (*vyatirekipramāṇa*) would cease to exist. This is what was introduced there.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "deviation and so forth," one should understand that "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*) is included as a prover of the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*), and "deficiency of the probandum" (*sādhyavaikalya*) is included as a prover of the "unestablished pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*).

Having thus restated the objection that the presentation of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is useless in the case of a positive-negative inference (*anvayavyatirekin*), and keeping in mind the statement from the *Paddhati* beginning with "In a positive-negative inference, however, negative pervasion is simply not required," he provides the rebuttal with the words "Even though... (*yadyapi*).
Anticipating an objection regarding the contradiction with the *Bhaktipādīya-sudhā*, he refutes it by stating the intended meaning in three ways, beginning with "yā tu" (as for that which...).
Thus ends the refutation of the purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*). [End of] Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava (Third Chapter).

It should be understood that this is intended either (1) by resorting to the perspective of others, or (2) with the intention that [the reason] is employed as a means of establishing negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*),

or (3) with the intention that it is not a form of inference because it lacks the five characteristics (*pañcarūpatā*), but rather because of the lack of co-location (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

Furthermore, inference is of two kinds:
for oneself (svārtha) and for others (parārtha). Among these, that which does not depend on instruction from another is for oneself.
That which depends upon it is for the sake of another. // 20 // Now follows the refutation of the restriction to five members and so forth. // 21 //
Explaining what was stated in the *Paddhati*—namely, that "inference is again of two kinds: for oneself (*svārtha*) and for others (*parārtha*)"—he says: "Again," and so forth.
The word "again" (punar) is used with reference to the division previously mentioned.
The meaning is that inference (*anumāna*) consists in the cognition of a mark (*liṅga*) qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*). "Therein" (*tatra*) means among those two.

It does not depend on instruction from another—that is, it does not require instruction provided by others in the form of "this [subject] possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire," and so forth; thus, it is "independent of instruction from another" (*paropadeśānapekṣam*).
The term "knowledge of the mark as qualified by pervasion" (*vyāptiviśiṣṭaliṅgajñānam*) is the substantive (*viśeṣya*), and it is to be construed here and in what follows.
(Refutation of the five-fold division: The doctrine of division [is as follows].—195.

It being established that even the instruction of another, consisting of a statement that expresses a logical mark (*liṅga*) together with its capacity [to prove the conclusion], is metaphorically designated as "inference for others" (*parārthānumāna*), [the following applies]:

Regarding that instruction from another, the ancient Naiyāyikas maintain that there are ten members: (1) the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), (2) doubt (*saṃśaya*), (3) the capacity [for knowledge] (*śakya-prāpti*), (4) the purpose (*prayojana*), (5) the removal of doubt (*saṃśaya-nirāsa*), (6) the proposition (*pratijñā*), (7) the reason (*hetu*), (8) the example (*udāharaṇa*), (9) the application (*upanaya*), and (10) the conclusion (*nīti*).
The Mīmāṃsakas, however, hold that there are three members: either the proposition and so forth, or the example and so forth.
The Buddhists maintain that there are only two [members], namely the example (udāharaṇa) and the application (upanaya).

Since the nature of instruction for others was not mentioned in the manual (paddhati), he cites what was stated in the *Anuvyākhyānasudhā* on the section concerning "Reasoning" (*yukti*), saying: "It is reasoning alone that has been declared," namely, "possessing capacity" (*sasāmarthya*).

The meaning is that *paropadeśa* (instruction by another) is a statement that generates the cognition of a logical mark (*liṅga*), such as smoke, which is accompanied by the capacity consisting in its presence in a location appropriate for pervasion; or, alternatively, pervasion itself is the capacity, and the statement generating the cognition of the logical mark accompanied by that [pervasion] is *paropadeśa*.
And that [instruction] takes such forms as "this mountain possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire.
The inclusion of the term "speaker" (pratipādaka) at the end is for the purpose of excluding mere sentences from being considered "instruction to another" (paropadeśa).

The inclusion of the phrase "consisting of a sentence" (vākyātmaka) is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (ativyāpti) to the contact of the mind with the eyes and other such general causes for the cognition of a competent logical mark (liṅga).
In the phrase "there is smoke," the term "sāmarthya" (capacity) is used to exclude over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Since the *Paddhati* states, "Because it produces that [cognition], even instruction for others is metaphorically called inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) in some cases," he says "parārthā" (for others).
The meaning is that it is so "metaphorically designated."

As for the claim that "a statement expressing a probans (*liṅga*) endowed with its capacity is not an *upadeśa* (instruction) because it would over-apply (*ativyāpti*) to that very same statement," that is not correct.
[The definition] "a statement expressing a probans endowed with its capacity" — [is intended to exclude such cases].
1. śaktya — Rā. 2. ya nigamanānīti — Ka.Ga.Ṭa.Rā. 3. kā āhuḥ — Ka.Ga.Ṭa.Rā. 4. vā — Ka.Ṭa.Rā. 5. ya eveti — Ṭa. 6. dvāviti — Ga.Ṭa.Rā. 7. sasā — Ṭa.Ḍa.

That is not so; for since the first five [members] do not consist of words, they lack the very status of being members of a sentence (*vākya-avayava*), and furthermore, there is no reason for the aforementioned rules [regarding their number].
Now, an objection:

since the cognition of the logical mark (*liṅga*) qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*), its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), and so forth, must be expressed through a sequence of expectations (*ākāṅkṣā*), otherwise there would be the fault of deficiency;

and since the very expectation for a reason (*hetu*) does not arise if the probandum (*sādhya*) is not presented, the thesis-statement (*pratijñā*) is therefore necessary for the purpose of presenting that [probandum].
Because a sentence [denying existence] expresses a sequence of phonemes of that kind (i.e., a sentence containing a negative particle), it does not express such a probans (liṅga).

Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that the cognition of the absence of a jar would be a cognition of the jar, and the conventional usage regarding the absence of a jar would be a conventional usage regarding the jar.

If it is argued that "the cognition of a jar" is that which apprehends a jar without delimitation by anything else, then "instruction from another" would be that which conveys such a logical mark (liṅga) without delimitation by anything else.
And there is no such over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in this case; for otherwise, the response would be a mere quibble (chala). This is the intended meaning.
"Regarding the word 'ādyā' (the first)": this refers to the initial [stage].

The meaning is as follows: the fivefold [requirements] consist of (1) *jijñāsā* (the desire to know), such as the doubt "Does this possess fire or not?"; (2) *prāptiyogyatā* (fitness for attainment), which is the possibility of attainment; (3) *prayojana* (purpose), which is the well-known removal of the hesitation regarding whether it possesses fire or not; and so forth.

In this regard, since the nature of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth— such as "the statement of the subject is the proposition" and "the mark is the reason"— is already evident from the *Mithyātvanumānakhaṇḍana*, its commentary, the *Tattvabhāvaprakāśikā*, the *Pramāṇapaddhati*, and other works, I shall not state their specific definitions here. Rather, I shall explain that exactly five members must be employed in their proper sequence, neither fewer nor [more] than three.

The [reasons] to be employed are neither fewer nor more; having kept in mind the arguments from the *Anuvyākhyāna-sudhā* on the "Chapter on Reason" (*Yuktipāda*) regarding the refutation of the position held by those who maintain the restrictive rule that "only two reasons are to be employed, not more," he states the reason: "In the stated restrictive rules... etc.

With the thought that "the very desire [to know] is the cause," he raises an objection in the manner of the *Sudhā* and according to the reasoning stated by Maṇi and others, beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*).
(The Refutation of the Fivefold Argument)
Vibhāgavāda, p. 197.

Then, when there arises the inquiry, "By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this [reason] to be known?", the statement of the reason, such as "because of smoke," merely establishes the nature of the middle term (*liṅga*) as that which causes the other [the probandum] to be cognized. Subsequently, when there is a desire to know its capacity, the example (*udāharaṇa*) is presented first for the purpose of demonstrating the invariable concomitance (*vyāpti*).
The application (*upanaya*) is for the purpose of demonstrating that the subject possesses the property [previously established];
then, the conclusion (*nigamana*) is for the purpose of bringing about the unity of the statement so that everything may ascend into a single cognition.

Alternatively, when the object of knowledge has been presented by the thesis (*pratijñā*) in the fifth member, and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the form of a logical mark (*liṅga*) has been stated by the reason (*hetu*) for the purpose of ascertaining that [object], then the examples (*udāharaṇa*) and so forth are required for the purpose of removing doubts, because it is only when that [reason] is free from all suspicion of defects that it can ascertain the object of knowledge.

In that context, the exclusion of contradictory (*viruddha*), inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and irrelevant (*anavadyasita*) reasons is accomplished by the example (*udāharaṇa*) which demonstrates pervasion (*vyāpti*). The exclusion of the unestablished (*asiddha*) is accomplished by the application (*upanaya*). Furthermore, the conclusion (*nigamana*) serves to restrict [the reason] to that very [subject] and not to anything else, since its commencement—even when the [reason] is already established—is for the sake of a definitive rule; thus, by restating the reason, it prevents the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).
With the words "Or else" (*yadvā*), he restates another position as stated in the *Sudhā* commentary, beginning with "others say" (*para āhuḥ*).
By the term "not determined" (*anadhyavasita*), the uncommon inconclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason is grasped.

He refutes this according to the method stated by Sudhākarin, beginning with the words "In the first case," etc. [The example: "Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire"—this is the instance (*udāharaṇa*).

The *haṃsa-vāda* (the "Swan's Speech") has completed [the section] with the following: "For the purpose of demonstrating that the property resides in the locus starting from the subject (*pakṣa*), there is the application (*upanaya*): 'And this [subject] possesses smoke pervaded by fire. [The conclusion (*niṅgama*) is: 'Therefore, it possesses fire indeed. [Notes on variants: 1. *pradarśanārtham agnivyāptadhūmavāṃścāyam ity upanayaḥ* — Ṭa. 2. *tasmād agnimān eveti ni-* — Ṭa. 3. *pakṣe iti nāsti* — Ṭa, Rā. 4. *te pi* — Ga, Rā. 5. *ṣāśaṃ* — Ka, Ṭa, Rār.

—Since the statement "it possesses fire, but not one devoid of fire" serves as a restatement of the thesis (*sādhya-anuvāda*), it excludes both sublation (*bādha*) and the counter-thesis (*satpratipakṣa*); how then can there be an absence of a reason (*hetu*) when the rule of five members is maintained?
It is said:
first of all, the initial position is not tenable;
for the statement of a proponent does not, by virtue of being the speech of a trustworthy person, cause the cognition of a probans qualified by pervasion and so forth.
By what sequence of desire could there be a fixed order of the members?
Because the two disputants would lack mutual confidence;
otherwise, the thesis alone would suffice.

However, it serves as a means of establishing [the probandum] for a person who has already grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, whereas for one who has not grasped the pervasion and so forth, it is useful by generating a desire to know (*jijñāsā*) regarding them.

And thus, only so much should be stated as is required for the recollection of the qualified mark (liṅga) to occur—whether by means of the pervasion (vyāpti) and the presence of the reason in the subject (pakṣadharmatā), or by means of the pervasion and the establishment of the location appropriate to it; otherwise, there would be the fault of prolixity.

And that [inference], "That mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke, like a kitchen," occurs either by means of merely stating the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and a partial example (*ekadeśadṛṣṭānta*),
or— according to the system of others— by means of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of being a locus-feature (*pakṣadharmatā*).
He states his own view: "By means of pervasion and the establishment of a suitable location."

Now, one might ask: "By how much does the recollection of the previously mentioned form of the logical mark (liṅga) come about? To this, he says—beginning with "And that [recollection]"—that it occurs through the seven modes described in the *Paddhati* and other works. // 1 //
The connection is with the word "being born" (jāyamānā).
For an *udāharaṇa* (example) is the statement of an instance preceded by the expression of pervasion (*vyāpti*). [Note: 1.
This means by the mere statement of that which is an instance, which is a part of the *udāharaṇa*.]
"By way of an example.
[The reading] "udāharaṇeti" is an addition found in manuscripts Ṭa and Ṭha. (The Refutation of the Fivefold Negation)
The Theory of Distinction (Vibhāgavāda), p. 199.

Either by a mere thesis containing the reason—such as "the mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke pervaded by fire"—or, since the thesis is established through the very dispute itself, when the question "Why does the mountain possess fire? is asked, [the answer is] "Because of its possessing smoke pervaded by fire."

Or, when asked what proof there is for a mountain’s possession of fire based on the mere presence of a cause, [the answer may be given] either by the mere statement of the logical mark (*liṅga*)— namely, "the state of possessing smoke pervaded by fire"— or by the mere statement of an example containing the reason along with the proposition, such as "the mountain possesses fire, like a kitchen which possesses smoke," or by the mere application (*upanaya*), namely, "smoke, which is pervaded by fire, exists on the mountain."

Since it is experienced as arising merely through the conclusion— such as "the mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke, which is pervaded"— what is the use of the restriction to five members?

For in the first case, since the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) certainly occurs for one who is proficient in the logic of inference at the point where pervasion was grasped, there is no deficiency [in the argument].
Furthermore, the word expressing pervasion—namely, "whatever possesses smoke, that possesses fire"—does not exist even within the other part of the example (*udāharaṇa*).

In this context, the meaning is: by means of the mere statement of the example, "like a kitchen," while omitting the portion of the statement of pervasion, "whatever possesses smoke, that possesses fire."

Establishing the manner in which the recollection of pervasion arises within all the aforementioned positions, he refutes defects such as incompleteness with the words beginning "For in the first... and so forth.
[Objection: But how can there be a recollection of pervasion (vyāpti) in the absence of a word that expresses pervasion? To this, he says: "The word expressing pervasion," etc.

The point is that in the case of the probandum (*sādhya*) "whatever it may be" (*yo yaḥ*), there is no word expressing the existence [of the probans] in all loci of the probans (*sakalasādhanādhikaraṇasattva*), which is what constitutes pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Furthermore, in both common worldly usage and in the scriptures, one who is learned and has observed the employment of qualifiers containing the probans (*hetugarbhaviśeṣaṇa*) certainly understands that "the state of possessing smoke" is the probans; thus, there is no deficiency [in the definition].

In the third case as well, the reason "because of possessing smoke" does not lack purpose, since it is connected with the word "fire" present in the question. Nor is there a deficiency due to the absence of a formal thesis,
because the probandum is established by the very fact of the dispute.

Nor should it be said that the counter-argument is interrupted by the binding of a convention (*samayabandha*), because the probandum (*sādhya*) is presented once again by the question "How [do you know] it possesses fire? which arises immediately after the binding of the convention.
As for the first position, however, it [establishes] its own side...

Since the inquiry "Prove it" and so forth has already been set in motion, the proposition (pratijñā) is indeed required there for the purpose of presenting the probandum (sādhya), which constitutes one's own position.

Now, one might object: even so, the statement of the reason, which serves to satisfy the expectation for a mere reason, ought to be in the form "because of smoke" (*dhūmāt*) and not in the form "because of possessing smoke" (*dhūmavattvāt*). And thus, since the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is not obtained, there is once again a deficiency in the third [member].
If it is argued that, in my view, this [connection] is obtained through the *upanaya* (application), we say no;

for by the statement of the reason (*hetu*), which serves to satisfy the expectancy as to what the reason is when the subject (*pakṣa*) possesses the property to be proven (*sādhya*), the connection of the reason with the subject must also be made known.
It is precisely for this reason that the *upanaya* is redundant.
1. *viśeṣaṇapadaṃ na* — Ga. Ṭa. Rā. 2. *ve ca sā* — Rā. 3. *abhāvāt pu* — Rā. (The Refutation of the Fivefold Negation; The Doctrine of Division, p. 201)

In the fifth [member] as well, by the phrase "like a kitchen," there is the presentation of pervasion (vyāpti), and by the qualification of the example "like smoke," there is the presentation of the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā); thus, there is no deficiency.

Nor should it be argued that if the words of a proponent were to be followed in the same manner as the words of a reliable authority (*āpta*), then there would be no occasion for pointing out a defeat (*nigraha*).

For even the words of a proponent must be followed when they function as indicators (*jñāpaka*)—provided one sets aside their aspect as means of valid cognition (*pramāpaka*)—in accordance with the conventions established by worldly usage and the treatises.

Otherwise, if someone says "he has fire" (*agnimān*), one might raise the objection of "shifting the subject matter" (*arthāntara*) by taking the word "fire" (*agni*) to mean "variegated root" (*citramūla*).

Furthermore, in your own position, there could be no pointing out of defeats such as deficiency (*nyūna*) and so forth; for in your view, the worldly convention itself serves as the ultimate limit regarding what constitutes deficiency and the like.
In my position, however, the pointing out of defeat finds its scope precisely in the transgression of the conventions established by the world.
That is to say, it is futile;
[this refers to] the aspect of being a means of valid cognition.

The point is that, just as in the case of the words of a trustworthy person (*āptavākya*), even though there is an absence of being a producer of valid cognition (*pramāpakatva*) in the words of a disputant (*vādivākya*), there still exists the mere quality of being a communicator (*jñāpakatvamātra*); for it has been established in the theory of semantic competency (*yogyatāvāda*) that even a sentence whose meaning is sublated possesses the capacity to convey understanding.
"Citramūla and so forth."
If it is argued that one would be defeated by means of a quibble (*chala*) when such a statement is made, [we ask] why that is so?
If it is argued that it is because of the consideration of the context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, the point is that this applies equally to the present case as well.
"Established in the world."
The intended meaning is that only those who follow the manner we have described conform to the conventions of the world and the true dharma (*saddharma*).

Now, one might object: "In the *Sudhā* on the section concerning logical reasoning (*yukti*), it was stated that only one of the two—namely, the connection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) or the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—need be expressed;
for it is understood that the statement of pervasion is not strictly necessary."

Since there is a contradiction between the two—the denotation and the cognition—regarding the previously mentioned positions, he refutes that contradiction by restating what was said in the *Sudhā* and expressing fourfold intentions, beginning with the words "yātu sudhāyamānam" and so forth.

As for the claim in the *Sudhā*: "One should observe some such thing as similarity (*sādṛśya*), relation (*saṃbandha*), and so forth, which is useful for the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)," etc.

The statement that "when either the pervasion (*vyāpti*) or the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is stated, there will be a recollection of the other" is indeed seen in the world as being like the expression "recollection of the word-meaning by means of a portion of the word. Alternatively, it may intend an external formal application (*bāhyaprayoga*), or it may intend a formal debate (*vādakathā*).

It is intended either as referring to a specific person possessing the memory of two parts based on a single statement, or as having the sense of *kaimutya* (a fortiori), but not with the intention that only one of the two is the actual subject matter.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇayaṭīkā*: "Recollection is indeed seen even by means of a single part of a word, let alone by means of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth.

And for this same reason, in the *Brahmatarka*—the connection [of the text] begins with the words: "Or rather, they have the intention of employing half-sentences of that [verse], beginning with 'sa' (he)... and so on.
He causes it to be played.

The meaning is that, because his status as a trustworthy authority has been established and because there is no ground for defeat, both [the premises] can be recalled even when only one part is mentioned.
By way of *kaimutya* (a fortiori).

The meaning is that this expresses the intention of a *kaimutya* (a fortiori) argument: "If even by the mention of a single part there arises a recollection of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) together with its capacity, how much more so by the seven previously mentioned modes, since the words required therein are present?
For this very reason, it says "and therefore."
The meaning is: "precisely because the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth is necessary.
The word "suggested" (*sūcita*) is to be construed [with this].
[This occurs] in the *Brahmatarka*.
In the *Tattvanirṇaya*, it is stated:
"Reasoning (*yukti*) is a mark (*liṅga*) possessing pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth;
it is described as that which has the form of a proposition (*pratijñā*) and which brings about recollection (*smṛti*) and other such mental states."
In this same manner, the [sections] beginning with "having the form of a reason" (*heturūpika*) and "having the form of an example" (*dṛṣṭāntarūpika*) are also to be explained.

[Notes on the variants: 1. *yattu* — corrected to *ga.rā.* 2. *śāditopi* — corrected to *iti śodhitam-ṭa.* 3. *smaraṇādikami* — corrected to *iti śodhitam -ṭa.* 4. *dartha vākyaprayo* — *ga.ṭa.rā.* 5. *ṇānyasmṛ* — *ga.ṭa.rā.* 6. *satyasya vākyārtha* — *ṭha.*
The refutation of the fivefold division of speech (*pañcāvayava-bhaṅga*): the doctrine of differentiation (*vibhāga-vāda*), page 203. *Sā* refers to the middle of this sentence.
Reasoning consists of the form of the proposition, the form of the reason and the example,
likewise the form of the application, and finally the nature of the conclusion.

Thus, having asserted that each of the five members constitutes inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), the statement "merely by relying on pervasion" indicates that the expression of pervasion is required in every case.

In the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇayaṭīkā* as well, by the statement, “The phrase ‘relying upon pervasion’ (*vyāptim āśritya*) is a presentation of an alternative position,” it is indicated that the mention of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs even in the initial thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth.

In the *Pramāṇapaddhati* as well, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is stated in the application (*upanaya*) as "this smoke, which is pervaded [by fire], exists on the mountain," and also in the conclusion (*nigamana*) as "because it possesses smoke that is characterized by pervasion and so forth.
By the word "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*), the statement of that [pervasion] is indicated.
It is stated that "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) is mentioned for the purpose of grasping a portion of the illustrative instance (*udāharaṇa*).
The metaphorical usage of "consisting of the conclusion" (*nigamanātmikā*) is intended to mean [the application] possessing the memory produced by the conclusion (*nigamana*).
Although the reasoning (*yukti*) is singular, it is stated to be metaphorical with the intention of referring to the diversity of those factors that generate its memory.

In all these cases, it should be completed as follows: "having the form of a thesis containing the reason" (*sapratijñaheturūpikā*), "having the form of an example containing both the thesis and the reason" (*hetugarbhasapratijñadṛṣṭāntarūpikā*), and "having the form of a conclusion containing the thesis" (*sapratijñopanayarūpā*).
This is because of the implied remainder of the sentences beginning with "having the form of the thesis and the reason" (*pratijñāheturūpā*) and so forth.
"Regarding the reality of Viṣṇu."
The phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) is to be supplied [from the previous context].

Here, although it might be understood that—relative to the previously mentioned position consisting of a proposition (*pratijñā*) and an application (*upanaya*)—the present [position] has as its purport the form of an application accompanied by a pervasion (*vyāpti*), it is stated that "it applies to the proposition and so forth as well" because the same logic holds true for them.
The intended meaning is that this follows the method previously stated by the author himself.

1. In this context, what was originally *ity atra* has been corrected to *ity etat*—as found in manuscript Ṭa. 2. The term *pramāṇapadaṃ* is not present in manuscripts Ga, Ṭa, and Rā. 3. [The phrase] ending with *sapratijñānigamanarūpetye* is found in manuscript Ṭha. 4. However, the passage beginning with *garbha* and so forth is found in manuscripts Ṭa, Ṭha, and Ḍa.

—204— *Tarkatāṇḍava* with the *Nyāyadīpa* (Third Chapter): Even in the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is stated: "The proposition (*pratijñā*) contains the reason (*hetu*), or it may be alone."

In the case of a proof, there is merely the reason (*hetu*) within the proposition (*pratijñā*), while the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) contains the proposition and the reason. Thus, by the word *hetu*—which signifies the statement of a logical mark (*liṅga*) in the form of a pervasion (*vyāpti*)—it is indicated that the expression of pervasion occurs in every instance. Furthermore, in the *Sudhā*, it is stated that "instruction" (*upadeśa*) is a sentence that generates the cognition of a logical mark together with its capacity [to prove].

Alternatively, the reason is simply "because of possessing smoke," and not "because of possessing smoke that is pervaded. This should be understood as applying to the other members of the syllogism as well.
Nevertheless, there is no deficiency,
because it is possible to state the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth in the third and subsequent stages according to the sequence of the opponent's expectations;
and you yourself have accepted that statements should be made according to the sequence of expectation.
"In the nectar," it is said.

The meaning is that this was stated in the *Sudhā* commentary on the occasion of explaining the *Anuvyākhyāna* of the *Yuktipāda*, which says: "But that [inference] is indeed the pervasion (*vyāpti*) as it is remembered.
The same applies to the other members [of the syllogism] as well.

It has been stated that each of the five members, beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*), when accompanied by some element such as the reason (*hetu*), constitutes an "instruction for another" (*paropadeśa*).
Among those seven previously mentioned types of sentences that constitute instructions for another, the component that is the reason (*hetvaṃśa*) is devoid of the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*);
the meaning is that it is to be expressed in its own right alone.
"From the third [moment] onwards."

"Because it possesses smoke," etc., is the first stage of the proponent (1). "Pervasion does not exist [for you], so how can there be pervasion? is the second stage of the proponent (2). "Whatever possesses smoke... is the third stage of the one stating the expression of pervasion (3). "How is there the presence of the pervaded in the subject, or its occurrence in a suitable location? is the fourth stage of the opponent (4).

The proponent who states the application (*upanaya*)—saying, for example, "Smoke pervaded by fire exists here"—is at the fifth stage (*kakṣyā*); thus, the discourse proceeds in this manner through the third, [fourth, and fifth stages]. (This concludes the refutation of the five-membered syllogism.)
Vibhāgavāda (Pu-205):

Furthermore, in your view, even though the opponent may desire to know the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other elements in the second and subsequent stages, you maintain that the proponent must state them all at once within the first stage by means of the five-membered great sentence; however, this is not my position.

For if that which is intended to be stated later were to be stated at the very beginning, there would follow the undesirable consequence of stating everything that ought to be said right from the start, until the conclusion of the entire discourse.

Furthermore, even if there were a rule for simultaneous utterance, since the *upanaya* and *nigamana* as accepted by them are each capable of expressing the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth individually, what is the purpose of the other members?
Therefore, the first position is not tenable.
Nor is it the second [position], that there is a restriction to five members for the sake of dispelling all doubts;
for it has already been stated that [the reason] at the very outset is precisely that which dispels all doubts.
"But for me, it is not so"—this is incorrect, because even that which is intended to be explained later ought to have been stated at the very beginning; therefore, he says: "Later on."

He states "moreover" (kiñca) to show that even according to the opponent's own system, the other two members [of the syllogism] are redundant, as the conclusion is established by either the application (upanaya) or the conclusion (nigamana) alone.
But by stating the five members [of a syllogism], the cessation of dispute would not occur;
and the same would apply to the examples and so forth.
He explains this according to the direction stated in the *Anuvyākhyānasudhā*, beginning with the words "At the very outset," and so forth.

If it is argued that a single "great sentence" (mahāvākya) is defined as consisting merely of the employment of the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayavaprayoga*) because such intermediate doubts— consisting of defects like fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) and so forth— are dispelled by it alone; then, why is it that the proposition (*pratijñā*) "the mountain possesses fire" dispels the doubt "does the mountain possess fire or not?", while the statement of the reason (*hetu*), "because it possesses smoke," dispels the doubt "how does it possess fire?"?
How is its pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth [established]? [Note:

In inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), since that [objection] is removed by the employment of the five-membered syllogism alone, it would follow—due to the consequence of sealing off the entire discussion—that the whole discussion which removes it would itself have to be considered an inference for the sake of others;
for even each individual member, such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth, possesses the capacity to remove intermediate doubts.

Furthermore, according to the aforementioned method, since even a single member [of the syllogism] expresses both pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), that member also possesses the capacity to remove all doubts.
Moreover, on this view, the "extraction of thorns" (*kaṇṭakoddhāra*) would not need to be performed separately.
Therefore, both positions are untenable.
Moreover, even the restriction to the five-membered syllogism and so forth must be established by inference alone against one who holds a contrary view,
since that [restriction] is not an object of perception or other such means of knowledge.
For if it were established solely through the employment of the five-membered syllogism, there would be the undesirable consequence of redundancy when addressing opponents such as the Mīmāṃsakas.
Because, in order to avoid that [objection], if one attempts to prove the ontological reality of the restriction to five members, there would be an infinite regress;
and furthermore, if one were to employ a syllogism with three members or fewer according to that same logic, it would result in the fallacy of deficiency (*nyūnatva*) on your part.
Thus ends the refutation of the objection regarding the function of the example as a negator of doubt.

The meaning is this: since an intermediate doubt is dispelled by the statement of each individual member in such a manner, the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the other members would also individually constitute great sentences (*mahāvākya*) consisting of instruction for others.

Just as in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), even in this position, because the removal of all fallacies is possible through the reversal [of each member], every other member would be redundant; therefore, he says: "Moreover, according to the stated method... (*kiñcoktarītyā*).
And that [inference] is by the method stated in such passages as "that mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke";
the phrase "of that too" refers to this.
The meaning is: even for each individual member [of the syllogism], such as the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), or the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

If one were to state an inference even when there is a restriction to only three or five members, or even when there is an absence of the pair [of middle and conclusion], one should address such a person as follows: "Tell me what you mean by this."
And by means of the reasoning stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna-sudhā*, he refutes the position that [the syllogism] must consist of five members, stating: "Moreover, [regarding] 'the five-membered'..."
Because it is not an object of perception and the other [means of valid cognition].
It should also be considered that there is an absence of scriptural authority (*āgama*). (The Refutation of the Fivefold Negation)
Either it should be employed according to the method of each respective school (*tattanmatarītyā*),
or it should be employed as long as there is cognition of the middle term (*liṅga*) qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth.

Furthermore, since you have accepted that when the Mīmāṃsakas and others—acting under a formal agreement (*samayabandha*) made for the sake of establishing their own desired restriction on the number of syllogistic members (*avayava*)—employ only three members and so forth, it is not necessary for them to remember the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other such factors; therefore, you yourself must abandon the restriction to five members.
Likewise, the Mīmāṃsakas and others must also abandon their own preferred restriction. How, then, can such a restriction be maintained?
Because there would be an infinite regress.

When you have established [your position] against the Mīmāṃsaka— who maintains the rule of three members— by means of an inference endowed with five members, adhering to the restriction of five members, and the Mīmāṃsaka has declared that this constitutes an "excessive" point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), you must again demonstrate, for the sake of refuting the fault of excess, that the restriction of five members alone is the ultimate truth, by means of an inference endowed with five members.

The meaning is that even there, when that previously mentioned defect has been pointed out by you, the same must be established again by another inference; thus, because of this infinite regress (*anavasthā*), it is according to that method— that is,
according to the method of the Mīmāṃsakas.
Thus it is by the Mīmāṃsakas and others.

When an inference consisting of three members (*avayava*) is stated by a Mīmāṃsaka and refuted by a Naiyāyika on the grounds of deficiency, even the proof of the necessity of the three-membered rule must be carried out by means of such a [three-membered] formulation itself; thus, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, when a Mīmāṃsaka states an argument according to the Nyāya system, if one were to claim that it contains an excess according to one's own view—that it should be formulated according to the specific rules of each respective school—and so forth, then once the Naiyāyika has made a five-membered formulation according to the Nyāya system, he would have to state for you [the Mīmāṃsaka] the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti-smṛti*) and so on.
