In the case of the first [type of] probative inferences, such as "because of being unestablished" (*asiddhatvāt*), this is not unestablished because it lacks the characteristics [of an unestablished reason]; in the case of "thorn-removing" (*kaṇṭakoddhāra*) inferences, when there is disagreement regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), and so forth of the reason employed in the first stage, in the branch-inferences (*śākhānumāna*) belonging to the second and subsequent stages which establish those [points], the two disputants,
for the sake of establishing their respective intended objects of knowledge (*prameya*) within the course of the debate, [employ] the five-membered form.

Since you yourself have abandoned the restriction even in cases where [the object] is not explicitly stated— such as in the forms of *pariśeṣa* (presumption by elimination), *arthāpatti* (presumption from implication), and so forth, as well as in inferences based on secondary branches (*upaśākhā*)— how can that restriction apply elsewhere?
Indeed, if one does not accept pervasion (*vyāpti*) because [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), incapable of proving [the probandum], and so forth,
then the rule of the three members [of a syllogism] must necessarily be abandoned.
Thus, the meaning is that the Buddhist must likewise abandon his own accepted rule.

He establishes the refutation of the restriction [regarding the five-membered syllogism] even by means of a counter-argument (*pratibandī*), stating: "Furthermore, this is not so," because since [the structure] is determined in some cases, the restriction to five members and so forth should not be accepted even in the initial inferential establishment.
The meaning is that it is exactly so because [the distinction] is manifest even in the case of the jewel at the end of the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
[This applies] to the inferences regarding the branches (*śākhānumāna*).
First, the inference employed for the purpose of establishing the primary object of cognition (*prameya*) is the "primary" one, which stands in the place of the great trunk of the tree;

the inferences employed as auxiliaries to it, or as refutations of it, are the "branch-inferences. Furthermore, the inferences employed for intermediate objects of cognition interspersed therein are the "sub-branch-inferences. It is for this reason that it was stated [in the previous verse]: "among the branch-inferences and the sub-branch-inferences."
Having caused him to recite the answer through another's mouth, he said, "It is equal," beginning with the word "nanu."

Regarding the point that there is no employment of further members [of the syllogism] when there is no dispute, he states another defect: "Furthermore, in the case of a purely positive (kevalānvayin) [reason]," and so forth.

209. — Because pervasion (*vyāpti*) therein is admitted by both parties due to the [opponent's] lack of qualification for debate, only the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) need be demonstrated.

If that is so, then since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*) is also accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas, and since no suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) arises there— either in that case where the probandum is purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) or in the case of a logical reason (*hetu*)— then in those instances too, it would suffice merely to demonstrate the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

Furthermore, since the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) is present in all cases in the case of a purely positive reason (kevalānvayihetu), only the pervasion (vyāpti) would need to be demonstrated therein.

Furthermore, if the proponent must establish even those things—such as pervasion—that are already accepted by the opponent, then he must likewise establish the demonstration of pervasion for the sake of proving that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) or non-probative (*asādhaka*).

Moreover, if one accepts that even an unestablished reason can be probative, it is easy to say that the disputant lacks the qualification for debate; thus, the inference of non-probativeness would be rendered futile.
And if even for one who accepts that [reason], the inference of non-probativeness against one who is in disagreement regarding its lack of authority is fruitful,
then the demonstration of the pervasion between "unestablishedness" (asiddhatva) and "non-probativeness" (asādhakatva) is likewise fruitful for one who is in disagreement regarding it.

Furthermore, what would be the status of the secondary and tertiary inferences (*śākhopaśākhānumāna*) in this case? Since there is no mutual consensus regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in those instances, one must simply state the method as I have described it; let it be exactly so for the primary inferences (*mūlānumāna*). Regarding the phrase "the method as I have described": it refers to the aforementioned approach.

The meaning is that one should follow whichever among the seven previously mentioned types [of inference] applies, starting with "only as much as is required for the cognition of that" (*yāvatā tadbodhaḥ tāvanmātram*).
Alternatively, it may take the form of observing a commonality within the same class (*sajātīya-anvaya-darśana*).
1. *matāvapi* — ka, ga, rā. 2. *kartavyam* is added — ka, ga, rā. 3. *vyāpti pra-* — ka, ga, rā. 4. *khādyanumā-* — ka, ga, ṭa, rā. 5. *neta* — ga; *nepita* — ṭa, rā.

Moreover, since it is observed that a statement spoken by a reliable person (*āptokta*), such as "there is smoke on the mountain because it is pervaded by fire," is a means of valid cognition (*pramāpaka*) for a logical mark (*liṅga*) characterized by pervasion and so forth, how could that very same statement uttered by a proponent not be a means of making [the object] known?

Furthermore, even by you, when there is a lapse in memory regarding the restriction to five members (*pañcāvayava*) as you have postulated, a lack of restriction to members is improper due to the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); since the impropriety of the lack of restriction to members is being established by this much alone, there is a contradiction with your own practice (*svakriyāvirodha*).
[Objection: But if this is so, how can one point out defects such as deficiency (*nyūna*) in the view that maintains there is no fixed rule [regarding the number of members]? [Response: No;

for according to the opponent’s own view, since there are only three members—either ending with the example (*udāharaṇa*) or beginning with the example—how could one point out defects such as "out-of-order" (*aprāptakāla*)?

Furthermore, since the property of being delimited by the relation of positive concomitance (*anvayitāvacchedakatva*), or the possession of fitness (*yogyatāvatva*), exists even in the member stating the reason (*hetu*), it is that very [member] which generates the knowledge of the mark (*liṅga*) that is the cause of inference; thus, the other members are indeed redundant.
With the thought that the possibility of removing all suspicion of defects arises by that much alone, he says: "Moreover, by fire... (5).
He says that the position of restriction must be abandoned because of contradiction: "Furthermore, by you also... and so forth.
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is: "because it is being established by this much alone.

"By this much alone" means by the two members consisting of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) alone. In that regard, the reason is as follows: "that which is imagined by you," and so forth.
It is indeterminate.
The meaning is: "of that which is the irrationality of the position consisting of the restriction to five members.
He states the answer by way of a counter-argument (pratibandī): "ending with the example" (udāharaṇāntam).
The sense is that, just as in his own view, the lack of restriction is equally present in that [other] view as well.
"Unattained."

The meaning is that "reversal of sequence" (*kramaviparyāsa*) refers to the pointing out of a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "untimely" (*aprāptakāla*). The connection for the phrase "how so? is with the statement "pointing out deficiencies and so forth.

Furthermore, how is the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) in the illustration [to be understood]? There is the repetition (*vīpsā*) of the words *yat* and *tat*, and the specific removal of thorns (*kaṇṭakoddhāra*). In the Naiyāyika system, the non-establishment of the inference (*asādhakatānumāna*), the mention of the condition (*upādhi*) by its own name, and the pointing out of irregularity (*aniyata*) constitute the pointing out of deficiencies (*nyūnatā*) and other such fallacies.

If it is argued that [the definition] follows the binding of the convention (*samayabandha*), then the same applies to the present case as well. Or rather, one should state [the definition] by relying on this particular position among the positions mentioned, or according to the path understood by everyone in worldly treatises (*lokaśāstra*): namely, that the presentation of the mark (*liṅga*) qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*) and presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) must be stated for as long as it takes.
Or because the commitment (samaya) must be bound;
for this very reason, it is stated in the Brahmatarka:
"In this regard, it is said that 'it attains separate validity only through reasoning' (*yukti*);

here, in the context of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), the essential factor is precisely the capacity to present the logical mark (*liṅga*) as qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*) and its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), which is what is denoted by the word *yukti*. Furthermore, it has been stated that the proposition (*pratijñā*) alone comes first because it presents the probandum (*sādhya*)."
That is not so;
for in some cases, the explanatory passage (arthavāda) possesses primacy even over the injunction,
just as in the Bhaṭṭa school’s doctrine, the illustrative example possesses primacy.
The term *aniyata* follows each [word] individually;
for that very reason, he recites the subsequent [formula]: "By agreement" (*samayena*).

The meaning is as follows: if there were an agreement that "only up to the example (udāharaṇa) should be stated by you," and one were to point out a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) because of a departure from that [agreement] by employing the example and so forth;
however, since there is no such agreement in the case where no restriction is accepted, he says: "In the aforementioned positions... [i.e., *uktapakṣeṣu*].
And by the words "that too" and so forth, [it refers] to the seven positions previously mentioned.

Indeed, with the passage beginning "nanu yāvatā," he also refutes that sequence consisting of the prior and posterior order of the members such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) which was previously suspected; this is indicated by the words "yacceti."
"Also because of the [status of] an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) even with respect to an injunction (*vidhi*).

Because [in statements such as] “Since the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts not having that as their purpose are useless; therefore it is said to be non-eternal,” and “For this very reason, the vital breath [is Brahman],” and “The means of knowledge is purposeful because of its capacity for activity,” there is the possibility of the reason being presented first— both by virtue of its primacy in the conclusion and by the logic of what is accepted in worldly and scriptural usage.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that the object to be established (*sādhya*) is presented by the very fact of the dispute itself.

"Prajāpati alone was this [universe] in the beginning. He desired: 'May I create offspring and cattle. He extracted his own omentum (*vapā*), offered it into the fire, and from that a hornless goat (*tūpara*) was born."

The meaning is that, for instance, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) comes first in such texts as: "He became [the universe]; he offered it to his own deity; from that, indeed, he created offspring and cattle; therefore, he who desires offspring and cattle should offer this hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati. Thus, the *arthavāda* is primary.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "Bhaṭṭa, etc.," the Buddhists are included.
Since the reason (*hetu*) comes first, he cites the sūtra of Jaimini from the section on *arthavāda*: "Of the sacred tradition... (*āmnāyasya*).

Because the Veda is the means of making known actions characterized as dharma and adharma, those portions which do not have that as their purpose—namely the *arthavādas* which do not convey action—are purposeless. Therefore, because they lack meaning, the collection of *arthavādas* is said to be "non-eternal" (meaning non-authoritative), like something impermanent; such is the meaning of the sūtra of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
In that very context, he cites the Vyāsasūtra: "For this very reason," etc.
The meaning of the Sūtra is that the referent of the word "prāṇa" is Brahman precisely because of the indicative mark (liṅga) which allows no other possibility.
In that very context, he cites the Gautama Sūtra: "In the activity... and so forth.
The meaning is that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which penetrates the object because it generates an activity directed toward a fruitful purpose.
This is the conclusion.
Therefore, the meaning is that [the rule applies] even in the member called the conclusion (*nigamana*), namely "therefore the mountain possesses fire.

Here too, the meaning is "even in the context of a proponent’s formal inference" (*kathaka-anumāna-prayoga*). He asks: "If there is no necessity for the proposition (*pratijñā*) itself, how can there be a necessity for its being first? To this he replies: "In the context of debate," etc. (*vivāda-*, etc.).

1. *ke śāstre ca prahateno*—ka.ga.ṭa.rā. 2. *nātrāpi he-*—ka.ga.ṭa.rā. 3. *tataḥ ‘niyamavismṛtidaśāyām’ ityādyevāsti*—ga.rā. 4. *alabhata tataḥ*—ṭha.ḍa. 5. *va i-*—ṭha. 6. *vayai*—ṭha.ḍa. (The Refutation of the Fivefold Argument)
Regarding the theory of sequential division (vibhāgavāda), page 213:
[The reason for stating the probandum first is] because in the question "Why does the mountain possess fire?", there is a lack of logical connection (*ananvaya*) with the proposition (*pratijñā*).

Furthermore, even by you, in a state where the rule regarding the priority of the proposition as conceived by you has been forgotten, there is a contradiction with your own practice (*svakriyāvirodha*), since the reason (*hetu*) is sometimes stated even before the proposition.

For this very reason, the restriction that the statement of the reason (*hetu*) must be second in order is also refuted. Furthermore, the claim that the statement of the reason must be devoid of possessive suffixes (*matup* etc. in order for the application (*upanaya*) to be meaningful has already been refuted previously.
Moreover, [the absence of such suffixes] contradicts the author's own commentary (*bhāṣya*), which states: "It is earth because of its connection with earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*)," and so forth.

As for what was stated—that there is figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word "fire" within the proposition (*pratijñā*), in the word "smoke" within the reason (*hetu*), and in the cognition thereof—otherwise, since smoke is not a cause with respect to fire, the use of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) would be improper.

Now, against one who asserts that the very dispute—"the mountain possesses fire" versus "the mountain is without fire"—is itself the form of the proposition (*pratijñā*) regarding one's own and the opponent's positions, he states its lack of necessity by another method: "of the mountain... (*parvatasya*).
"For this very reason."
The meaning is simply that the primacy of stating the reason (*hetu*) has already been demonstrated.
As for the claim in the *Maṇi* and other works that in formal debate one should employ only "because of smoke" (*dhūmāt*) and not "because of possessing smoke" (*dhūmavattvāt*),
this is because the possessive suffix (*matup*) is redundant.
Regarding the statement that "the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) is understood through the application (upanaya)," he refutes it with the words "of the application."

The inclusion of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the expression "matup and so forth" is intended to ensure the meaningfulness of the examples; the point is that this includes the apprehension of the absence of pervasion (*vyāpty-āhitya*), since the formal argument "because it possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire" has already been demonstrated.
"How much more so," and so forth.
The sense is: "Is it not so that [the definition] still functions to satisfy the expectation for a mere reason (hetu), etc.?"—this is the meaning expressed by the passage beginning with those words.
Thus, by his own statement.

In the *Gotamasūtrabhāṣya*, the meaning is that since the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*)—namely, the connection with the subject—is already included within the statement of the reason (*hetuvacana*) itself, to claim that the statement of the reason is devoid of the possessive suffix is contradictory.
He refutes other points as well stated by [Śrīdhara] Maṇika, beginning with "And that which... (*yacca*).
The meaning of "one who possesses fire" (agnimān) is "the cognition of fire";
and the meaning of "from smoke" (dhūmāt) is "from the cognition of smoke."

That is not so; for in the case of smoke, there exists the nature of being a "cognizer-reason" (*jñāpaka-hetu*), which consists in its being the object of the cognition that generates the cognition of fire.

If it is argued that being a "cognizing cause" (*jñāpaka-hetu*) consists precisely in being the producer of a cognition having that [object] as its content—and that this belongs only to the cognition of smoke (*dhūma-jñāna*), not to the smoke itself—that is not so;
for the status of being a cognizer residing in the cognition of smoke does not, first of all, belong with respect to fire (*vahni*).
This is because the expression "fire from the cognition of smoke" is never employed.
Nor is it [the cause] with respect to the cognition of fire;
for in that case, only the status of being a productive cause (*kārakahetu*) is possible.

Furthermore, just as the term "differentiator" (*vyāvartaka*) is applied to a staff and so forth—which are the objects of a cognition that is the cause of a cognition of exclusion—so too is the term "indicator of fire" (*vahnijñāpaka*) applied specifically to smoke, which is the object of a cognition that is the cause of a cognition of fire.

In the case of a *jñāpaka-hetu* (informative cause), the ablative (*pañcamī*) is primary (*mukhya*) precisely because of its frequent usage, such as in constructions where there is no dependence on the connection with an "impossibility" (*anupapatti*). Otherwise, it would be non-primary only in the case of a *sādhaka-hetu* (productive cause). The meaning is that when the noun-base (*prātipadika*) such as *dhūma* ("smoke") indicates cognition (*jñāna*), the ablative expressing the sense of causality (*hetutva*) becomes primary.
He explains [this] according to the direction stated starting with "the lord of sacrifice" (yajñapati) and so forth: "smoke," etc.
"Exclusion."
The meaning is that, in the case of one distinguished by punishment, the exclusion is of one who has not been punished.

Now, one might object: "Could the use of the word 'indicator' (jñāpaka) with respect to smoke be due to metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā)? To this, he says: "And in the case of an indicative reason (jñāpakahetu)."
The meaning is: "because the primary sense is untenable.
He states the objection [to the claim] that even in such a usage there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*), with the words "otherwise": *anyathā*.

Alternatively, one might object: "Is it not the case that, according to the maxim *nanv anyāyaś cānekārthatvam* (‘Indeed, it is illogical for a word to have multiple primary meanings’), one must accept that [the term] has its primary sense in only one place and a secondary sense elsewhere? To this, he says: "Otherwise... (*anyathā*).
(The Fivefold Breakdown of the Ablative Case):
Even though the ablative case primarily denotes the efficient cause (*kāraka-hetu*), let it be understood as having a secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) specifically in the ablative.

But it is not the case that there is no indication by secondary function (lakṣaṇā) when the primary meaning is the word *dhūma* (smoke), nor is it a rule of the grammatical tradition (*kuladharma*) that secondary function does not apply to nominal suffixes (*sub-vibhakti*).
This is evident in Vedic passages such as, “He sprinkles the sacrificial oblations with the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings.”
Furthermore, this is observed in such [propositions] as "In your view there are twenty-four qualities" and "There is one inherence," for in your system,
plurality and other such numbers expressed by case-endings (vibhakti) in words like "qualities" do not exist within the qualities themselves or other categories.

Or, even if—according to your view—the ablative case were primarily used only for the causal factor (*kāraṇahetu*), nevertheless, it would follow that in other instances, such as the indicative cause (*jñāpakahetu*), its usage would be merely figurative (*lākṣaṇikī*). To this he says: "only for the causal factor."
Now, one might object that figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is not appropriate when a case-ending (sup-vibhakti) is present; therefore, he says: "And not... (na ca).
Since there is no perception [of such a rule] anywhere, it is not a grammatical characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) for the case-ending *su*; therefore, he says: "In the Veda."
"With the remnant of the prayāja offerings."

Regarding the sentence "with the remnant of the *prayāja*" occurring in the context of the *Vājapeya*, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, because the second and third case endings indicate that the remnant serves as a consecration for the sacrificial oblation (*havis*),
the meaning is that one should consecrate the oblation with the remnant of the clarified butter (*ājya*) which is the substance employed as a means in the sacrifice named *prayāja*.

However, since the remnant requires only a disposal (*pratipatti*), and in accordance with the natural sense of the nominal stem (*pratipadika*), [one should dispose of] the remnant of the clarified butter used as a means in the sacrifice named *prayāja*.

The meaning is that since it is established in the thirteenth section (adhikaraṇa) of the first quarter of the fourth book— concerning the rule "one should place [the portions] upon the oblations" (*haviṣṣu sthāpayet*)— that "there should be a distinction of vessels due to the separation [of the acts], as in the case of the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) during the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*)," it is observed that the third and second cases are accepted as having the sense of the object (*karman*).
Furthermore, the inclusion of the qualifiers "twenty-four" and "one" is for the purpose of dispelling the misconception that the plural and singular numbers are not intended to be significant.
"Because of the perception of that."
The meaning is: because it is observed by means of the definition of number residing in the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) and so forth.
On the contrary,

when the reason (*hetu*) is stated, in the example (*udāharaṇa*), and in the application (*upanaya*), one must state that the very cognition which serves as the means of comprehension possesses the property of having pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth as its object, for the sake of making that cognition itself the instrument of proof.
But it is not the case that the logical mark (liṅga) possesses [the property of] pervasion and so forth.
Furthermore, by means of a constituent member (avayava), only a cognition that is an auxiliary factor for inference must be produced;
and it is the cognition of the mark (liṅga) alone that is such an auxiliary factor,
not the cognition of the cognition of the mark.
Nor is there figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word "fire" (*vahni*).

For fire’s status as the object to be made known (*jñāpyatva*) is established simply through its syntactic connection (*anvaya*) either as the object of the cognition included within the "causality of making known" expressed by the ablative case, or as that which is to be made known in relation to the causality of making known itself.

Furthermore, in expressions such as *caitramātā* ("Caitra’s mother"), Caitra is seen to be connected as the produced (*janya*) with respect to the generativity (*janakatva*) inherent in "motherhood," which consists in being a generator qualified by femininity.
Even in the case of an example, such as "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire," it is either by the first part alone,
or it is simply the cognition of the mark (liṅga).
But it is not the cognition of the mark [that is produced];
rather, according to the view that [cognition] is characterized by knowledge, it is the cognition of the cognition of the mark itself that must be produced,
just as the cognition of the riverbank is produced by the word "Gaṅgā."
The point is that this [perception] is not a factor in inference.

Having refuted [the existence of] the "characterization by cognition" (jñānalakṣaṇā) in the case of the reason (hetu), he now refutes it in the case of the probandum (sādhya) as well—starting with "But not... (na tv iti).

The meaning of "with respect to" (*prati*) is the cognition of fire, which is included within the state of being an indicator (*jñāpakatva*), defined as being the object of the cognition that produces the cognition of fire.
[This is expressed by the phrase] "by way of being indicated" (*jñāpyatayā*).

The meaning is that the status of being a cognizer (jñāpakatva), in the form of being a producer of knowledge, exists only with respect to the status of being a cognized object (jñāpyatā), which consists in being the object of the knowledge produced by that [cognizer].
Now, one might ask: "In the first alternative, how can there be a syntactic connection with only a part of the word-meaning? To this, he says: "And it is observed."

He refutes even the member consisting of the example (*udāharaṇa*) as intended by the opponent, stating: "Even in the case of the example... [The section titled] *Pañcāvayavabhaṅga* (The Refutation of the Five Members). (Note: Variants from manuscripts: 1. *na tu* etc. is absent in Ṭa and Rā; 2. *bdenala* in Ka, Ga, and Rā; 3. *vijñāpyat* in Ga, Ṭha, and Rā; 4. *sāvasāya* in Ka and Rā.)
The theory of distinction (vibhāgavāda):
[This is] because pervasion (vyāpti) is established by the latter member alone, as in the case of "in the kitchen" (mahānase), [and thus one of the two members is redundant].

If it is argued that for this very reason the statement of the example is superfluous, we say no; for it would be impossible to establish an agreement (*samaya-bandha*) that even what is useless should be stated.
This applies to whichever person...
If it is argued that there is no recollection of pervasion (vyāpti) by means of the first member, and thus the statement of the example for its sake is also unnecessary, we say no;
for if that were the case, the fixed order of the members would not be established.

As for the claim that the word "whatever" (*yat*) implies a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) for the sake of the sense of totality included within the pervasion—that is, the state of possessing the probandum for every single possessor of the probans—that is not correct. [This is illustrated by examples such as:
“A cow must not be touched with the foot,” and “If both sacrificial offerings of someone should meet with ruin.”

Just as in the case of [the Vedic injunction] "one who raises a weapon against a Brahmin should be punished with a hundred [strokes]," the [conclusion] is established even without a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) by the general statement alone, namely, "whatever possesses smoke";
[the author] objects: "For this very reason..."
This is because the apprehension of pervasion has already occurred by means of the mere initial portion;
"conventional" (sāmayika) means that which is produced by the binding of a convention.
Regarding the term "member" (avayava):
The meaning is that our position is established because there is no fixed rule regarding the number of constituent members [of a syllogism].
Regarding the word "cow": with the intention that "whatever is a cow, it must not be touched with the foot," it is stated in the Veda, "A cow must not be touched with the foot.

Similarly, in the passage, "If both the evening and morning oblations of anyone should meet with affliction or destruction due to worms, insects, and so forth, he should offer five *śarāva* measures of rice for Indra," although it should have been said "of whichever person," the word "whose" (*yasya*) is used only once.

Therefore, the meaning is that in such passages as "Whosoever should threaten a Brāhmaṇa—that is, should make an effort to kill him—one should know him to be a denizen of hell called Śatayātanā," the expression is made without the repetition (vīpsā) of the word *yaḥ* (whosoever).
[Notes: 1. *dhīstaṃ* – *ga*, *rā*. 2. *bdādau* – *ga*, *rār*. 3. *chati atha yo* – *ṭa*, *rā*.]

In the inference of non-difference—"This is non-different from that, because it is the locus of the unique properties of that, like that"—there is an absence of distinct instances in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), and because there is no need for distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). *Pu — 218. Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava (Third Chapter)* --------------------------------------------------------------------------- "This is non-different from that, because it is the substratum of the uncommon properties of that, like that"—in such an inference of non-difference, since there is an absence of distinct individuals in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), and because there is no requirement for distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), [the reason is not inconclusive].
In some cases, however, repetition (*vīpsā*) serves the purpose of clarity;
for this very reason, in such [syllogisms] as "the subject of dispute is distinct because it is liberated—whatever is thus, is so," the Master did not employ repetition in his statement.
The application (*upanaya*) is also already implied by the statement of the reason (*hetu*).

Furthermore, in an *upanaya* such as "and this [subject] possesses smoke pervaded by fire," which is accepted by you, the portions consisting of the restatement of the pervasion established in the example (*udāharaṇa*) would be redundant.
The conclusion (*nigamana*) as well is already implied by the proposition (*pratijñā*).
Nor is that for the purpose of a summary, because it does not depend upon such [a summary] when there is no intervention by many dissimilar objects of cognition;
otherwise, after each individual removal of a thorn, [one would have to conclude] "therefore, all... [and so on].

Now, one might ask: how then is it that expressions of repetition (*vīpsā*) are used in such passages as "O Lord of the World, abandon whatever sin [I have committed] against me," or "Whomever my beloved gazes upon"? To this, he says: "In some cases... (*kvacid iti*).
"In the words of the Teacher."
In the *Tattvodyota*, he refutes the status of the "application" (*upanaya*) as a member of the syllogism, stating: "The application also... and so forth.
And he refutes the fifth member as well, stating: "the conclusion also."
This is for the purpose of concluding [the section].
The meaning is that this is for the purpose of bringing together, by means of a single cognition, those things which have been stated in separate sentences.
[This applies] to each one individually, beginning with "the thorn," and so forth.

Having stated, "This [reason] is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because it lacks the characteristics thereof," one would have to provide a separate conclusion for each, saying, "Because it is free from the unestablished, this is a prover"; and having stated, "This is not contradictory (*viruddha*), because it lacks the characteristics thereof," one would say, "Because it is free from the contradictory, this is a prover.

Likewise, immediately after stating, "This is not a fallacy (*ābhāsa*), because it is devoid of the characteristics thereof," one would say, "Therefore, because it is free from all defects, this is a prover."
1. *ktiḥ* — ṭa. 2. *rāyānaṃ* — ka. 3. *namrasya* — supplied as such — ḍa. 4. *sādhakaṃ* exists [in this form] — ḍa.
(The defects of the self and so forth) The Discourse on the Defects of Inference, page 219.
Furthermore, the conclusion (*nigamana*) would necessarily have to state such things as, "Because it is free from defects, this is a valid proof.
Nor is it for the purpose of dispelling doubts regarding sublation (*bādhā*) and so forth;

for all defects that contradict [the thesis] are already excluded by the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) and the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) stated in the example (*udāharaṇa*) and the application (*upanaya*).
Therefore, the restriction to five members and so forth is not logical.

The refutation of the restriction to five members, etc. // 20 // Likewise, even in the inference that constitutes a refutation—such as "this [reason] is non-probative because it is unestablished" (asiddhatvāt)—there would follow a conclusion such as: "Therefore, because it is unestablished, this is non-probative," or "Therefore, because it is fallacious, this is non-probative. Now, one might object: "In some cases, even that is indeed accepted there. To this, he says: "Necessarily" (niyatam).
The word "that" (tat) means the conclusion; the sense is that it follows the manner previously described.
The refutation of the restriction [to] five members and so forth. // 21 // Now, the fault in the inference as intended by [the opponent] himself. // 21 //
Now, the fallacy of inference is stated. // @--------------------------------------------------------------------------- Now, the fallacy of inference as intended by [the author] himself. // 22 //
It has been stated that "inference is the establishment [of the probandum] when there is no defect.

Since the establishment [of the probandum] as being free from defects is easily understood only when the defects are known, he says "Now, inference is the establishment when there is no defect" (2), and then, extracting the defects of inference from those mentioned in the *Paddhati* and other works starting with "What are the defects of establishment therein?", he explains them. Thus: "Now... (atha).

In this way, by the word "atha" (now/then), he indicates the logical connection (*avasara-saṅgati*) [of inference] immediately after the statement of all the faults already employed. (Note: The various manuscript variants provided—such as *noktadau*, *doṣoktyanantaraṃ*, *nopayuktadauṣoktyanantaraṃ*, etc.—all converge on the same meaning: that the word "atha" serves to signal the transition to the next topic following the exhaustive discussion of the aforementioned defects.)
Pu-120. *Tarkatāṇḍava* with the *Nyāyadīpa* (Third Chapter):
That which, despite being intended as a logical mark (*liṅga*), does not produce valid cognition (*pramā*) when present, is a defect of inference (*anumānadoṣa*).
And this absence of the capacity to produce valid cognition is common to [marks] that produce doubt or error, as well as those that do not produce any cognition at all.
And that [inference] is threefold,
by way of the distinctions of thesis (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Here,
by the word "inference" (*anumāna*), that which is intended as the inferential mark (*liṅga*) is expressed.
Thus, this [criticism] is a statement regarding a defect in the teacher alone, and not a defect in the words as well.
Even though that [defect in the words] may ultimately be a defect in the meaning through a mediated succession, the point here is that only a direct defect in the meaning is being stated.
This is merely an illustration.
It should also be understood that the faults of the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are likewise being stated.
Alternatively, the meaning is that the faults of inference are stated here by way of extraction as being limited to this much.
The subsequent statement regarding the faults of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is for the purpose of distinguishing them from the faults of inference.
Or else, by the word "inference" (*anumāna*), what is meant here is the inferential mark (*liṅga*) together with its auxiliary components in the form of the proposition and the example.
The meaning is that this is its defect.
For this very reason, later on, a general definition common to the three defects—namely, those of the proposition and so forth—is stated.
That which exists in reality.

Since it is a rule that a logical mark (liṅga) possessing [the characteristics of] pervasion and so forth necessarily generates valid cognition, the phrase "that which is intended as a logical mark" (liṅgābhimata) was used instead of simply saying "logical mark" in order to exclude the impossible case.
This is to be construed with the phrase "by means of its own cognition.
The meaning is that the nature of a defect consists in being that which leads to the non-generation of valid cognition by that which is intended as a logical mark.

He states that there is pervasion because [the absence of the probans] exists in that which produces mere knowledge, as well as in that which produces doubt and error—namely, "and the absence of being a producer of valid cognition."
By the word "and" (ca), there is the inclusion of that which does not produce knowledge.

The intention is that the statement in the *Paddhati* and other works— "That in the presence of which the cognition intended as a logical mark (*liṅga*) does not arise, or produces doubt or error"— is for the sake of clarity.
To state that not all fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) mentioned by others constitute defects of the reason, but only some of them do, he provides a classification, saying: "And that... (sa ca).
The proposition.
The grasping of that meaning [of the thesis] occurs through the two terms "proposition" (*pratijñā*) and "reason" (*hetu*). Alternatively,
since the defect of the object itself implies the defect of the statement that makes it known, only "proposition" and "reason" were mentioned.
[The faults of inference: The discussion on the faults of inference, page 221.
Among these, the contradiction of the subject matter asserted in the proposition (*pratijñā*) with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the fault of the proposition.
It is of two kinds:
1) contradiction by a stronger means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
and contradiction by a means of valid cognition of equal strength.
Because that which is weak is incapable of action,
and equality of strength is merely a matter of overweening pride.
Furthermore, both are threefold,
due to the distinctions of contradiction with perception, inference, and scripture.
Contradiction with inference is also twofold.
[The fallacy is classified] by that very reason and by another reason.
Of these, the first is called *prakaraṇasama* by others,
while the second is called *satpratipakṣa*.

It should be understood that this definition follows the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa*, which states: "Contradiction is threefold, according to the distinction of the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)," and so forth; this applies even to the subsequent statement of the definition. The meaning is: "of that," namely, of the subject (*dharmī*) qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), which is the object of the proposition.

One might argue that there should be three types [of contradiction] because there also exists contradiction with a weaker means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, he says: "of that which is of inferior strength."
Since it is impossible for two things to be of equal strength when they appear as two distinct forms of a single entity, he says: "equal" (samam).
Furthermore, it is of three kinds.
Contradiction with equally strong perception, contradiction with stronger perception,
and contradiction with equally strong inference.
The meaning is that [the contradiction] is threefold: contradiction by a stronger inference, contradiction by an equally strong scripture, and contradiction by a stronger scripture.
He speaks, dividing even the second among the three types: "Inference... and so forth.
But surely, in both cases, the three-featured reason is "equal to the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*), and thus it is of equal strength; yet that is not correct, as in the case:
"Sound is impermanent, because it is a quality."
In the argument "Sound is eternal because it is a quality," for the proponent of non-eternality, the color and so forth of a jar constitute the similar instance (sapakṣa),
whereas for the proponent of eternality, that very same thing constitutes the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa).
Thus, it is not logical for a single entity to possess both presence in the similar instance and exclusion from it.

Therefore, suspecting that because it is illogical for two pervasions determined by both [the probandum and the negation of the probandum] to reside in one and the same [locus], contradiction would be impossible by that very reason, he refutes this, saying: "And not in the first case."

Nor is the first [alternative] impossible; for, just as it is possible for both the pervasion of the probandum and the pervasion of its absence to reside in a single reason within a single thesis through mere misconception (*abhimāna*), so too [the two] may coexist. *Pu-222. Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava (Third Chapter)* --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Nor is the first [alternative] impossible; for, just as it is possible for both the pervasion of the probandum and the pervasion of its absence to reside in a single reason within a single thesis through mere misconception (*abhimāna*), so too [the two] may coexist.
A defect of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) is the absence of the capacity of the reason to produce valid cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*).
It is of two kinds: non-establishment (*asiddhi*) and lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). Non-establishment is the absence of the reason at the appropriate location.

The absence of pervasion (*avyāpti*) is the lack of *vyāpti*. It occurs in three ways: (1) when the probans (*sādhana*) has no connection with the probandum (*sādhya*) even though it exists; (2) when it has a connection with the absence of the probandum as well as with the probandum itself; and (3) when it has a connection with the absence of the probandum alone.
As in the case of two pervaders.
The meaning is "like two reasons that possess counter-arguments.

It should be understood that for a single reason, the proponent has the conceit (*abhimāna*) that it is pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*), while the opponent has the conceit that it is pervaded by its absence; thus, even the presence [of the reason] in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and so forth is merely a matter of conceit.
Having thus examined the defect of the thesis, he states the defect of the reason: "of the reason" (hetor iti).
The meaning is "of the indicative mark" (liṅga).
[The word] "by virtue of the capacity" (sāmarthya) [is used].
The meaning is the absence of the capacity characterized by existing in a location appropriate for pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Since a division [of fallacies] would be impossible in the absence of a recurring universal (*sāmānya*), he states this himself—though not mentioned in the *Paddhati* and other works—beginning with "vyāptī" (pervasion).

The meaning is the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the form of "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*). The triad beginning with "of the probans [occurring] only with the absence of the probandum" and so forth is also designated by opponents, respectively, by the terms "uncommon inconclusive" (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*), "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*), and "contradictory" (*viruddha*).
[The faults of inference: The discussion on the faults of inference, page 223.
The fault of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*) is its lack of suitability for the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
It is of two kinds:
deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) and deficiency of the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*).
Among these, the first fault, known as contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇavirodha*), is common to both perception (*pratyakṣa*) and scripture (*āgama*).
The other two, however, are unique to inference.
For it is stated in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇaṭīkā*:
"In this case, contradiction with one's own thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*) is common (*sādhāraṇa*);
the other two, however, are uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*)."

Nor is there any deficiency in the classification of defects of the reason (*hetudoṣa*). For the [fallacies] intended by others—namely *savyabhicāra*, *viruddha*, and *vyāpyatvāsiddhi*—are included within *avyāpti* (lack of pervasion). Furthermore, *bādha* (sublation) and *pratirodha* (counter-thesis) are not themselves defects of the reason, as will be stated later; likewise, *āśrayāsiddhi* (unestablished locus) and *vyadhikaraṇāsiddhi* (unestablished due to different substrata) are not defects provided that pervasion exists.

However, in my view, the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) is not a defect in inference for one's own sake (*svārthānumāna*); furthermore, in inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), it is subsumed under the category of irrelevance (*asaṅgati*).
This applies to both the absence of favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*) and the presence of counter-reasoning (*pratikūlatarka*).

And because the [flaw of the] *upādhi* is included within the [category of] non-pervasion (*avyāpti*). Having examined the flaws of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), he states the flaw of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) with the words "vyāptīti" (regarding pervasion).
By the word "apprehension" (grahaṇa), valid cognition (pramā) is meant.
That [example] in the presence of which pervasion cannot be ascertained is a defect of the example (dṛṣṭāntadoṣa).
Having thus defined the three types of contradiction, he explains their distinction with the words "therein" (tatra).
"Between [the faults of] contradiction with the proposition, the reason, and the example, the other two... [as stated].
Regarding the faults of the reason and the example:
in order to state the result of the analyzed classification, he says—"And not... etc.

The sense is that there are many other sub-varieties of those [fallacies] mentioned by others—namely, the *savyabhicāra*, *viruddha*, *satpratipakṣa*, and *bādhita* as stated in the *Maṇi*, and so forth—which have not been enumerated here.
To the question "Why is there no deficiency [in the classification]? he replies: "Those intended by others..."
The connection of both these two words [“asabhāṅgatā” and “iti”] is with the phrase “because they will be explained later,” just like the subsequent word “iti.
Thus ends [the section on] "asabhāṅgatā."
Contradiction (*virodha*) and inconsistency (*asaṅgati*) are two defects of meaning; among these,
it is contradiction alone that is elaborated here,
and not inconsistency.
Because it has been stated that [the fallacy of] *satpratipakṣa* (counter-balanced) is included within *avyāpti* (non-pervasion),
and because [fallacies such as] *vyarthaviśeṣaṇa* (useless qualification) and so forth are included within *ādhikya* (redundancy).
Therefore, there are only two defects of the reason: non-establishment and lack of pervasion.
This is a fault of one's own preferred inference (svābhimatānumānadoṣa).
This [objection], namely that "it is a lack of expectancy" or "a lack of connection," has been elaborated upon in the *Paddhati* and other works, and is therefore omitted here.

The sense is that the objection regarding "the acceptance of what is already established" (*iṣṭāpatti*) is entirely irrelevant because it results in proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhanatva*), as stated in the definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇalakṣaṇa*) and elsewhere.
Because it has already been stated.
The meaning is that this has already been stated in the discussion concerning the statement of the reason for the defectiveness of a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

Regarding the term "useless" (*vyartha*): although it has been stated in the *Anuvyākhyānasudhā* on the *Bhaktipāda* that "if the qualifier is useless, or if one [of the two] is unestablished, there is indeed the non-establishment of the qualified," and furthermore that "the uselessness of the qualifier constitutes a fallacy because the qualified entity lacks pervasion (*vyāpyatva*)," [the following applies].
Nevertheless, since it has already been stated that this [objection] is indeed included within another more significant one, there is no fault in speaking thus.
The defects of inference as conceived by [the opponent] themselves.
// 22 // Now, in our own system, there is no confusion between sublation (*bādhā*) and the like with the fallacies of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and the like. // 22 //
Now, at the time when there is the cognition of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) in the subject (*pakṣa*), is the reason (*hetu*) uncognized or cognized?
[Now follows] the non-confusion of *bādhā* (sublation) and other fallacies with *vyabhicāra* (inconstancy) according to our own system. // 23 //
The claim that the fault of the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*) is distinct from the faults of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) is incorrect.
This is because, with the underlying intention that it can be subsumed under the two faults of the reason—namely, non-establishment (*asiddhi*) and lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*)—it is said:
"Even when there is a contradiction with one's own statement, [the reason] certainly does not attain the status of a prover."
Thus, explaining what was stated in the *Yuktipadīyānuvyākhyānasudhā*, he raises an objection with the words "But surely... (*nanu*).

It should be understood that the phrase "the cognition of the absence of the probandum" (*sādhyābhāvapramiti*) is stated with reference to contradiction by a stronger means of valid cognition (*prabalapramāṇavirodha*),
whereas the phrase "at the time of the knowledge of the absence of the probandum" (*sādhyābhāvajñānadaśāyām*) is stated with reference to counter-argument (*pratirodha*).
(Regarding the first [point], beginning with "svate-bādi-":
The discussion on the defects of inference. Page 225.
In the first case, there is no establishment of valid cognition (*pramiti*).

If it is argued that since the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is known in the second case alone, there is no example of a defective [reason] unconfounded with the already established defects such as deviation, and therefore what is the point of postulating *bādha* (sublation) and *pratirodha* (contradiction) as defects? We say:
no, because there is no defect in either of the two cases.
For instance— let us consider the first [case] for now.
Indeed, the non-establishment of the cognition to be produced (pramiti) acts as an impediment to inference by way of obstructing the efficacy of the means of knowledge (karaṇa),
and its presence depends upon the statement of the reason (hetu).

Obstruction (*bādha*) and the like are direct impediments; they are also presented through the cognition of the thesis (*pratijñā*). However, when internal means such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) are already present and established—@---------------------------------------------------------------------------
The deviation is known.

When there is a contradiction with a stronger means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the knowledge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is of the nature of certainty (*niścaya*); however, in the case of a contradiction between two equally strong [means], it should be understood as being of the nature of doubt (*saṃśaya*).
For this very reason, the general statement "known" (*jñāta*) is used.

It might be argued that doubt regarding a deviation (vyabhicāra) pertaining to the subject (pakṣīya) is indeed favorable [to the inference] and not contrary to it; for if it were contrary, it would follow that the entire domain of inference would be abolished. To this we say: no.

For while a doubt concerning deviation arising from its own nature (svārasika) may be favorable, a doubt induced by a contradiction with a means of valid cognition (pramāṇavirodha) and the like is contrary to it.
Otherwise, there would follow the absurd conclusion that even a suspected "limiting condition" (upādhi) would not be a defect. This is the intended meaning.
"In both cases as well."
The meaning is: the two alternatives consisting of the nature of being unmeasured and the nature of being measured.
Regarding the term "capacity" (sāmarthya):
The meaning is: "by way of subverting the capacity consisting in being located in a suitable place.
The underlying idea is that [the cognition of the contradictory] acts as an inhibitor precisely in that manner, because it does not apprehend the absence of the object of the inference.
Regarding the phrase "the statement of the reason":
The meaning is that it does not arise from the mere assertion [of a thesis].
"Dependent upon the thesis."
The meaning is that this is because of the statement in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa-ṭīkā*: "Because it does not manifest by mere assertion."
226. *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (Third Chapter):
When a sublation (*bādha*) or similar defect has been established, it is proper to wait for the non-establishment (*asiddhatva*) of its opposite;
otherwise, even when a point of defeat (*nigraha*) that is to be grasped as stated has been reached, one would have to wait for a point of defeat that was not so stated.
Or rather, let there be a second [type]:

for the reason (*hetu*) is cognized in the subject (*pakṣa*) by another cognition that is ignorant of the report of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), whereas the absence of the probandum is [cognized] by a sublation (*bādhaka*) that is ignorant of the report of the reason.
However, the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) consisting in the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the reason with the absence of the probandum is not [cognized] by anyone at all.
This is because there is no cognition of the reason existing in that which lacks the probandum (i.e., the locus of the absence of the probandum) with respect to that [subject].

Thus, at the time when sublation (*bādha*) and so forth are present, even if a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) exists, it does not reside in the mind; therefore, due to its immediate presence in the mind and its intensity as it subverts the object of cognition, sublation and the like alone constitute the defect.

This is just as in cases such as "the mute is a speaker," where, despite the contradiction with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇavirodha*), the defect is only the contradiction with the words of the proposition (*pratijñāpadavirodha*), as it immediately presents itself to the mind.

And just as in the case [of the fallacious argument] "the mother is barren because she is an object of cognition," even though there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the fault is primarily the contradiction with the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*) itself;

or, let us grant that there is the specific cognition that "the reason exists in the subject which lacks the probandum" (*sādhyābhāvavati pakṣe hetuḥ*). Nevertheless, the cognitive element "the probandum is not in the subject" is a fault independently of the cognitive element "the reason is in the subject."
The meaning is that this is because of the statement in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa-ṭīkā*: "Because of the expansion of the mouth of the three."
It is said: "While being spoken."

In cases such as "I am ignorant," a contradiction with one's own action (*svakriyāvirodha*) is stated; this is a contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavirodha*) regarding what is to be apprehended, and because it is apprehended immediately after being uttered, it is called "apprehended by what was said" (*uktagrāhya*).

Previously, assuming that the deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—in the form of the reason’s co-occurrence with the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*)—had not yet arisen, the status of sublation (*bādhādi*) and other fallacies as distinct defects was explained.
Now, even while accepting that deviation has arisen, he states that sublation and the others are still distinct defects: "Or let it be... (*astu vā*).

1. When the two [reasons] are established, [the following occurs]: ... (The establishment of the nature of wisdom in the Vākyapadīya and the Raurava; the discussion on the defects of inference, page 227).

Because it deprives [the object] of its objective domain, the reason (*hetu*) exists within the subject (*pakṣa*). However, since the aspect of cognition that is the probandum (*sādhya*) does not exist within the subject, the defect is dependent precisely upon that aspect of cognition;
for that [aspect], when independent of it, is a quality (*guṇa*).

And so, just as in the case of being common [to both sides], even though it occurs in the similar instances (sapakṣa), its occurrence in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) alone constitutes a defect; likewise, even when there is knowledge of the reason in the subject (pakṣa), by distinguishing between what is attained and what is not attained, only that portion consisting of sublation (bādhā)—which is the certain cognition of the absence of the probandum in the subject—constitutes a defect.
In our own system, there is no confusion [of fallacies] such as contradiction, non-deviation, and so forth.
// 22 // [Regarding the term] "common" (sādhāraṇa):
The meaning is that it is the "common" (sādhāraṇa) inconclusive [reason] whose nature consists in occurring in both the similar class (sapakṣa) and the dissimilar class (vipakṣa);
that is to say, its very nature is to occur in the dissimilar class.

Since the presence of the reason in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) is conducive to inference, whereas its mere presence in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is detrimental, it is that [latter] alone which constitutes a defect; this is stated in the *Maṇi* and other texts on the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
Thus, [the objection] is "already attained or not yet attained" (*prāptāprāpta*).

The meaning is: by distinguishing between what is obtained and what is not obtained—that is, the portion consisting of the cognition of the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva) which is obtained as a defect, and the portion consisting of the cognition of the existence of the reason (hetusattva) which is not obtained as a defect.

In our own system, there is no confusion between sublation (*bādha*) and inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*). // 23 // Now follows the demonstration that sublation and counter-inference are defects of the thesis (*pratijñā-doṣa*).
Some, however, say that sublation (*bādha*) and counter-argument (*pratirodha*) are defects of the reason (*hetudoṣa*).
Now follows the demonstration that sublation and counter-argument are defects of the thesis (*pratijñādoṣatva*).

Now, even if sublation (*bādha*) and contradiction (*pratirodha*) do not constitute defects of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) in the form of unestablishedness (*asiddhi*) or lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*), let it be granted that there is a distinct defect of the reason in the form of having a sublated object (*bādhitaviṣayatva*) and so forth, as stated by the author of the *Maṇi* and others.
To the question of how, then, these can be defects of the proposition (*pratijñādoṣa*), he says "Some, however... in order to establish that point.
The logicians (*tārkika*) and others.

[End of] *Tarkatāṇḍava* with the *Nyāyadīpa*, Third Chapter. [Page 228] (Note: The textual variants provided—*rāsaṃ* for *rasaṃ* and *ṭa.rā.* for *ṭha.ḍa.*—indicate differences in manuscript readings regarding the section title and folio numbers.)

Just as there is no cutting of space because it is inherently unfit for cutting— even though the axe lacks defects such as bluntness— so too, even when the eye and other senses are free from defects such as cataracts, the non-arising of perceptual valid cognition occurs solely due to defects in the object, such as extreme distance, extreme proximity, confusion with similar objects, or resemblance; likewise,

in the case of a sentence such as "sprinkle with fire," even in the absence of verbal defects like lack of denotation or deficiency, the failure to produce a valid cognition arises solely from a defect in the meaning, namely its unfitness (ayogyatva).

Just as there is no production of verbal valid cognition [in cases like "the pot is impermanent because it is knowable"], and just as in inferences such as "the pot is impermanent because it is knowable" the invalidity is due solely to a defect in the reason (*hetu*) even though there is no defect in the object of cognition (*prameya*),

so too in inferences such as "all fire is non-hot because it is knowable," although there is no defect in the reason, the non-production of inferential valid cognition must be explained as being due solely to a defect in the object of cognition— namely, its unfitness for proof because the subject matter contradicts another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara-viruddhatva*).

Keeping in mind what is stated in the *Anuvyākhyānasudhā* on the *Yuktipāda*—namely, "Contradiction also would be of three kinds: contradiction with the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*), absence of the probans (*liṅga*), and lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*)"—he states, with an illustration, that even when the instrument (*karaṇa*) is faultless, in cases where the effect does not arise due to a defect in the object (*artha-doṣa*), it is the defect [of the object] alone that must be asserted as the cause. [He says: "Even if the instrument is flawless, in a situation where the result fails to arise because of a flaw in the object, it is precisely that flaw which must be designated as the cause; this is illustrated by the following example:"
Regarding the axe: 5. Thus it is said.
He brings together.
The meaning is: "due to defects in the object, such as similarity or subtlety, as in the case of milk and water, or a heap of beans and individual beans.

Having cited the production of a heterogeneous [cognition] and the production of a perception of a homogeneous [object] in the form of a word as examples, he provides an example of the production [of cognition] in the form of internal inference—namely, "it is impermanent."
The object of cognition.
The meaning is: "even in the absence of a defect in the probandum" (sādhyadoṣa), that is, "even in the absence of a defect in the reason" (hetudoṣa).

The sense is that, because all [entities] possess the nature of *tejas* (luminosity), there is no locus for deviation (*vyabhicāra*) other than that; thus, since the defect of deviation is absent, defects such as the unestablished (*asiddhi*) cannot even be suspected. (Vāpra-royoḥ-prajñā-dotva-sanam)

Furthermore, since sublation (*bādha*) and counter-inference (*pratirodha*) possess objects that are contradictory to what is apprehended by inference, they can—without depending on looking over another's shoulder—directly obstruct the fruit of inference, namely the inferential cognition itself, just as in the case of perception; thus, it is possible for them to function as such through the logic of "catching the crane. (Anumādoṣavādaḥ, p. 229)
It is unreasonable to postulate an obstruction to the result by way of producing a deficiency in the instrument [of cognition].
Otherwise, once perception has been sublated by a defect in its object— such as similarity— one would have to postulate a defect in the instrument, such as a cataract or the like.

Now, against the opponent who argues that even if the probans is stated to be defective by virtue of its being the prover of the counter-correlative of an absence known to reside in the subject (pakṣa)— which is the nature of sublation— the non-arising of inferential valid cognition remains logical, [the author] states another defect according to the method explained in the *Lakṣaṇa-ṭīkā*, beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
"In perception and so forth."

The meaning is as follows: just as in the perception "the conch is yellow," the perception "the conch is white" acts as an inhibitor because its object is directly opposed to that which is being apprehended;

and just as between the two verbal cognitions "the jar exists" and "the jar does not exist," there is a relationship of the inhibited and the inhibitor due to their having contradictory objects, so it is here.
"Bakabandha" (the crane-binding).
When someone asks another for a means to obstruct [the opponent's argument], he says:

"When butter is placed on the head of a crane, as the butter melts from the heat of the sun and falls between its eyes, when the crane closes its eyes, it is then bound. Just as there is a binding at that very moment when the butter was placed there, so too, even the postulation of a defect in the reason (*hetudoṣatva*) by way of producing a deficiency in the instruments of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, is like that method of binding the crane.

Alternatively, the meaning is: "by means of producing a deficiency in the state of having pervasion (*vyāpti*) as its object, within the instrument which consists of the act of reflective consideration (*parāmarśa*).
[From the *Tarkatāṇḍava* with the *Nyāyadīpa*, Third Chapter, page 230]
Furthermore, that which is known to be a subverter of an inference by virtue of being established in a certain [probandum] is a defect (doṣa) of that [inference].
Otherwise, even the abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*) and so forth would constitute the abandonment of the reason (*hetuhāni*) and so forth.

For instance, contradictions with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) and the like, which depend upon the thesis "Sound is eternal," as well as the fallacies of contradicting a tenet (*apasiddhānta*) and so forth, which depend upon the thesis "The phoneme is non-eternal" as employed by the Mīmāṃsakas, would [absurdly] be defects of the reason.
Furthermore, sublation (*bādha*) and the like do not function as impediments [to inference] by being known as residing in the reason (*hetu*),
because they impede the inferential cognition only when they are already perceived prior to the presentation of the reason immediately after the thesis (*pratijñā*).

Furthermore, if it is assumed that sublation (*bādha*) consists in establishing the counter-positive of an absence known to reside in the subject (*pakṣa*), then the cognition of that sublation as residing in the reason (*hetu*) would have to be postulated; however, it has already been stated that such a postulation is improper because of its complexity (*gurutvāt*). Moreover, since there is no evidence for it, it is improper to regard it as a defect of the reason. Thus, he states the general principle—preceded by the refutation of the opposing view—with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).
The proposition.

*Pratijñāhāni* (abandonment of the proposition) is the relinquishing by the proponent of that very thing, in that same manner, as it was previously asserted; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), *pratijñāntara* (shifting the proposition), *pratijñāvirodha* (contradiction of the proposition), *pratijñāsannyāsa* (renunciation of the proposition), and so forth are included.

When the subject of the thesis has been stated previously in an unqualified manner, such as "sound," the addition of a qualification to the part to be proven—such as "it consists of phonemes and is eternal"—is *pratijñāntara*.
Mutual contradiction is a contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*).
Denying what one has stated oneself is the abandonment of the proposition (*pratijñāsannyāsa*).

The meaning is that even points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) such as the loss of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*) would, by way of having abandoned the proposition and so forth, constitute the loss of the reason (*hetuhāni*) and the like.
There may be defects in the cause.
The meaning is that [the fallacy] exists as residing in the reason (*hetu*) by way of such forms as having contradictory propositions (*viruddhapratijñakatva*).
Having established the pervasion (*vyāpti*), he states that it does not exist in the subject (*pakṣa*) with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
And because there is a subverting proof (bādhaka), it is not reasonable to assume that this is a defect of the reason (hetudoṣa); thus he says: "If, moreover... (yadi ca).
Alternatively, against one who maintains that even sublation (*bādhādi*) is a defect only when known as residing in the reason (*hetu*) and not otherwise, he states the refutation: "If, moreover...

In that case, let it be postulated that the cognition of both "unestablishedness" (asiddhi)— defined as proving a counter-positive of an absence known to reside in the subject (pakṣa)— and "non-pervasion" (avyāpti)— defined as proving [the probandum] while lacking pervasion— should likewise be based on their residing in the probandum (sādhya).
Furthermore, sublation (*bādhā*) and the like are common to perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of valid cognition;
however, in the case of a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), the criterion is being a defect unique to the reason.
Otherwise, even lack of attention on the part of the mind and so forth would have to be considered a fallacy of the reason.

If it is argued that even in the case of a common [inconclusive reason], since it acts as an obstacle to inference by being known as such, sublation (*bādha*) and the like constitute fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) because they differ from lack of attention (*manonavadhāna*) and other such factors—this is not so.

For in your own view, the probandum (*sādhya*), which is the object of the establishment of the probandum that constitutes an obstacle to inference, would also have to be classified as a fallacious reason.

Furthermore, he states that these are defects of the reason (hetudoṣa) according to the logic indicated in the *Lakṣaṇaṭīkā*: "contradiction with the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*) is common [to both types of fallacies], while the other two are uncommon. He says this by adding: "Moreover, there is sublation (*bādhādi*) and so forth."
Obstruction (*pratirodha*) and so forth are the categories [of defects].
To the question, "Why, by that much alone, do they not constitute a defect of the reason (*hetudoṣa*)?", he says: "The reason... (*hetu*...).
"Otherwise."

The meaning is that even a defect common to perception and other means of knowledge constitutes a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Anticipating an objection regarding this disparity, he refutes it with the words beginning "But surely" (*nanu*).
"Even for one who is practicing [the path]," it says.
The point is that if the probandum were an obstacle to the establishment [of the proof], then the probandum itself, by virtue of being known, would also be an obstacle.

He raises an objection, suggesting that the fact that sublation (*bādhā*) and so forth are common to perception and the other means of valid cognition is itself unestablished; if this were the case, they would not constitute defects of the logical reason (*hetu*). He begins with "But surely" (*nanu*).

Objection: [It may be argued that] there is a distinction [between perception and inference]: 1) in the case of perception and the like, the non-validity of the cognition produced is merely understood through sublation, as seen in cases such as the confusion of directions; whereas 2) in the case of inference, the very production of the cognition is obstructed. Furthermore, 3) since verbal testimony can be a cause of cognition even for that which is absolutely non-existent, and 4) since a fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*) must necessarily be a cause of that [cognition], these [cases] avoid being common [to both types of error]. [Reply: Even so, [the objection remains untenable]. 3) Because verbal testimony is a cause of cognition even with respect to what is absolutely non-existent, and 4) because a fallacious mark must necessarily be a cause of that [cognition], [inference] shares this commonality [with perception]. Since the sublation of the object (*viṣayabādha*) is indistinguishable [in both cases], the claim that "only a pseudo-word (*śabdābhāsa*) indicates a non-existent object, and not a pseudo-logical mark (*liṅgābhāsa*)" is merely a technical convention (*paribhāṣāmātra*). Furthermore, even after the onset of sublation, one observes the restatement: "That which was inferred by you is non-existent."

Furthermore, that which consists in the sublation of either the pervasion (*vyāpti*)— which is the nature of the capacity of the means [of proof]— or the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), is alone a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Sublation (*bādhā*) and the like, however, are not such,
because they do not touch upon the means [of proof].
The meaning is: by sublation, that is, by contrary cognition.
It is simply origination.
The meaning is that the very arising of the inference is what is obstructed by the sublation (bādha).
He says—“of the fallacious word”—to show that the obstruction of its arising is itself unestablished, such that there would be the fault of being over-exclusive (asādhāraṇya).

Since it has been established in the discussion on *yogyatā* (semantic competency) that a statement from a proponent containing a non-existent object—such as "there is a rabbit's horn"—can produce understanding in an opponent, just like a statement such as "there is a cow's horn" which produces understanding;

[one might object]: "Granted that a fallacious word (*śabdābhāsa*) lacks the power to produce cognition because one has the experience that 'what was understood from the word is false' immediately after the sublation (*bādhā*) occurs, but this is not the case for a fallacious logical mark (*liṅgābhāsa*), since there is no such experience.
To this, he says: "And it is observed... (*dṛśyate ca*).
"Because it is touched by the instrument (karaṇa).
