Therefore, sublation (*bādha*) and counter-argument (*pratirodha*) are defects of the object of cognition (*prameya-doṣa*), because they consist in the absence of the nature of a valid means of proof (*sādhana-ahetu-rūpa*),
because they directly obstruct inferential cognition (*anumiti-pratibandhakatva*),
and because they manifest even before the statement of the reason (*hetu*) following the thesis (*pratijñā*).

Because the term "perception" (pratyakṣa) is common [to both the subject and the example], and because the capacity of the instrument [of cognition] is not impaired, these are not defects of the reason (hetudoṣa);
rather, they are defects of the proposition (pratijñādoṣa).
As for the view of the commentator:
"When there is no observed deviation, it is clearly known by the witness alone that 'this is the means of proof'; however, that would not occur if the means of knowledge were sublated."

This explanation—that inference is subject to deviation due to the sublation of perception by a subsequent explanatory statement (*anuvyākhyāna*)—refers to the stage of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

At that time, there is no division into the proposition (*pratijñā*) and other members [of a syllogism]. However, at the stage of inference, sublation constitutes a defect of the proposition itself, as it involves the removal of the object of cognition.

Otherwise, a proposition whose object contradicts the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) would constitute a contradiction of the proposition itself, because it would conflict with the definition of the means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, regarding the explanatory commentary (*anuvyākhyāna*):
the sense is that there is no perception of an instrument (*karaṇa*) in the case of a valid cognition of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvapramā*).
Therefore, he explains the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) in five ways according to the previously mentioned method, beginning with "unfitness as a means of proof" (*sādhanānarhatva*), and so forth.
Having raised the objection that this contradicts the nectar-like words of the *Bhaktipādīya*, he refutes it by explaining its intended meaning: "As for [the statement] 'yātu'..."
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is established thus:
"at the time of grasping the pervasion" (*vyāptigrahaṇa*).

The point is that the position—that sublation (bādha) is what arises when there is no pervasion at the time of grasping the pervasion—is indeed accepted, because it will be stated later [in the Yuktipāda] that "it would not exist if there were sublation by a means of valid cognition" (*mānabādhe na tadbhavet*). This is the sense of the statement in the *Sudhā* commentary on the *Yuktipāda*.
Furthermore, he refutes the contradiction with the statement in the *Anuvyākhyāna* on the *Yuktipāda* with the words "As for that which... (*yāpīti*).

In that regard, although it would have been sufficient merely to state "contradiction with the meaning of the proposition" (*pratijñārthavirodha*), [the author] has stated [this] as follows in the *Sudhā* [commentary], which will be explained later:

[From the *Tarkatāṇḍava* with the *Nyāyadīpa*, Third Chapter] (Note: The text provided contains various manuscript variants indicated by the letters ṭa, ga, ka, ṭha, ḍa, etc., which have been omitted from the translation for the sake of clarity.)

“The contradiction [of the reason] is also threefold: being contradictory to the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaviruddhatā*), the absence of the mark (*liṅgarāhitya*), and lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).

This statement that sublation (*bādha*) and counter-argument (*pratirodha*) constitute defects of the reason along with non-establishment (*asiddhi*) and so forth, is intended precisely to show that when a subject is already vitiated by sublation and the like, the reason operating therein possesses the defect known as "functioning outside its proper domain" (*aviṣayavṛttitva*).
But it is not a defect of the object, such as sublation (bādha) and so forth.

The establishment of sublation (*bādha*) and counter-argument (*pratirodha*) as defects of the thesis (*pratijñā-doṣa*). [Commentary: The phrase "of sublation and counter-argument" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) in accordance with the formal division [of the defects]. Thus he intends.
The meaning is that it is because of the cognition [of the object] in the very same way on the earth.

The demonstration that sublation (*bādha*) and contradiction (*pratirodha*) constitute defects of the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*). // 24 // Now, the demonstration that the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) and the deficiency of the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*) constitute defects of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*). // 24 //

Now, is it not the case that an example lacking the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*) is indeed a counter-example (*vipakṣa*), and thus a reason (*hetu*) residing therein—provided it also resides in other similar examples (*sapakṣa*)—is "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) because it resides in all three categories? [This concludes] the demonstration that the defects of an example consist in its being deficient in either the property to be proven or the probans. (25)

Anticipating the objection that it is improper to treat defects such as the "absence of the probandum" (*sādhyavaikalya*) as distinct from the defects of the reason (*hetu-doṣa*), he refutes this with the words beginning "But surely... (*nanu*). [The text continues:

"Because they can be subsumed [within other categories], it is incorrect to regard them as defects of the example (*dṛṣṭānta-doṣa*). [This is the additional portion found in manuscripts Ṭha and Ḍa. (Note: This section addresses the classification of logical fallacies, specifically the status of defects in the example.)
On the objection regarding fallacies of inference (p.

235): "If there is no presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), then because it exists only in the subject (*pakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), it is a contradictory reason (*viruddha*).

Furthermore, if a reason is devoid of the probans (*sādhana*) in an example that possesses the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), it is an unestablished pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*); thus, an 'apparent example' (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) is already included within the 'apparent reasons' (*hetvābhāsa*). If this is argued, we say: No.

For sublation (*bādhā*) and the like appear as residing in the subject (*pakṣa*), just as lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) and the like appear as residing in the reason (*hetu*), and deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) and the like appear as residing in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Since these must be pointed out (*udbhāvya*) in accordance with how they appear, and since that which is to be pointed out is precisely what must be explained (*vyutpādya*).

Furthermore, since inference depends upon its constituent parts, if the inference is already vitiated by a defect in the example (dṛṣṭānta), why wait for the pseudo-reasons (hetvābhāsa) that merely grind what is already ground?

Otherwise, in the case of sublation (bādha), since the subject itself would become the counter-example (vipakṣa), sublation would be included within the category of inconclusiveness (vyabhicāra). Moreover, the contradictory (viruddha) and the inconclusive (savyabhicāra) would both be included within the categories of "lack of pervasion" (vyāptihīna) and "unestablished as the pervaded" (avyāpyatvāsiddha).

Furthermore, since in the case of an uncommon [reason] there is necessarily a deficiency of the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*) regarding the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), that too would be included within "deficiency of the probans. He establishes its status as a defect of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*) according to the method stated in the *Anuvyākhyānasudhā* on the fourth quarter (*bhaktipāda*)—namely, "the deficiency of the probandum and the probans [is a defect] when there is a qualification of the example"—by the words "of sublation, etc. (*bādhādeḥ*).

If it is argued that, "In cases such as the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*), since even fallacies like inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*) can manifest through the force of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it is appropriate to explain them as fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) because they too must be pointed out," [the author] replies: "Furthermore..."—stating that even in that case, due to its status as a prerequisite (*upajīvyatva*), it is indeed a defect of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*).

And because there exist many subverting arguments (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position (*vipakṣa*), it is logical that these are indeed defects of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*); thus he says: "Otherwise... [anyatheti].
Furthermore,

since the absence of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*) is necessarily present in the case of the "non-conclusive" (*anupasaṃhārī*) fallacy, that too would be included within the category of "pseudo-absence of an illustrative example" (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsāntarbhūta*).

Furthermore, although there is no defect in the reason (*hetu*) in the arguments "whatever is a living body is endowed with a self because it possesses breath and so forth, like a pot," and "sound is denotable because it is knowable, like a pot"— where respectively the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) and the positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*) exist—
the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is nevertheless defective even when the lake is cited as an example in the inference from smoke; thus, that defect is indeed distinct [from a defect in the reason].

If it is argued that even in that case, because the pervasion has not been demonstrated, there is indeed the fallacy of the unestablished nature of being pervaded (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*), we say no; for even so, there is no fault regarding the meaning.

Furthermore, since the kitchen (*māhanasa*) was cited as the example, there would be no *vyāpyatvāsiddhi* in that instance, which would lead to the undesirable consequence that this [fallacy] is merely an occasional defect (*anityadoṣa*).
And because, even when the lake is cited as an example, the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—that "wherever there is smoke, there is fire"—is demonstrated by the first part [of the statement].
The meaning is that it is a fallacy of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) merely by virtue of being mixed with other defects of the reason.
And [this applies] to the "non-exclusive" (*anupasaṃhārī*) case as well.
The meaning is that [this applies] in cases such as "everything is impermanent because it is an effect," which are distinct from the varieties of the inconclusive (savyabhicāra) fallacy.

Furthermore, he states that the defect of the example (dṛṣṭāntadoṣa) is separate because it is not conflated with the defects of the reason (hetudoṣa), saying: "Moreover, [in the case of] the living body..."

He states what was said in the *Paddhati*: "Because it is impossible for a probans that exists within a portion of the similar class (*sapakṣa*)—when that similar class has been made the example—to be a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) while existing in the similar class. He says: "smoke," etc.
He raises the suspicion of a confusion of reasons (hetudoṣasaṅkara) with the words: "Even there... (tatrāpi).
"In that very place."
The meaning is: "only in the case of the inference from smoke";
because that [reason] lacks the establishment of its being pervaded (vyāpyatvāsiddhi).
He states that even the suspicion of the unestablished nature of the pervaded (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) does not arise at the stage when the pervasion has been demonstrated—namely, "the heart" (*hṛda*).

Now, even if it be granted that defects such as the absence of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) constitute faults of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*), nevertheless, it is incorrect to say that there are only two kinds of faults of the example, since they are of many types; therefore, he says: "Both... (*ubhaya*).
He states exactly what was well said: "by the deficiency of even one [of these]. [The text notes:

"The term 'ric' (verse) refers to that which has been stated as having deviation (*savyabhicāra*). [This concerns] the removal of the doubt regarding the deficiency of those [factors] in the *sādhana*.
On the Discussion of Fallacies in Inference (Anumānadoṣavāda), page 237:
However, the deficiency of both [reasons] is not a separate fallacy, because the defectiveness is established by the deficiency of even one alone; thus, the deficiency of the other is redundant.

If [the reason] were stated separately merely because of its possibility, then there would also have to be other fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) such as "inconclusiveness" (*anaikāntika*) and "mistimed" (*kālātīta*), as well as "unestablished mistimed" (*asiddhakālātīta*).

Furthermore, the inclusion of fallacious examples (*udāharaṇābhāsa*)—such as those characterized by a lack of a locus (*āśrayahīna*) or a failure to state the pervasion (*avyāpti*)—should be consulted in works such as the *Paddhati*.

As for the statement by the author of the *Ṭīkā* during the explanation of the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely, “The non-occurrence of either the probandum (*sādhya*) or the probans (*sādhana*) [in the example] is a contradiction with the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭāntavirodha*); thus, one should understand it as ‘of both’,” this means that just as in the argument “the mind is impermanent because it is corporeal, like an atom, like an action,” there are respectively the defects of the deficiency of the probandum and the deficiency of the probans, so too is it the case in arguments such as “like space” and so forth.
This is intended precisely to show that there are two faults known as the deficiencies of both [the subject and the predicate];
it is not intended to suggest that the deficiency of both constitutes a distinct fault from the individual ones.
Otherwise, if the example were already defective through the deficiency of either one individually, the conception of their combined deficiency would be redundant, and so forth.

Now, one might ask: even so, what is the status of the faults of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), such as the unestablished nature of the substratum (*āśrayāsiddhi*), the failure to state the pervasion (*vyāptyanabhidhāna*), and the statement of a contrary pervasion (*viparītavyāptyabhidhāna*)? To this, he says: "In the case of the lack of a substratum," and so forth.

for it is perceived that even the deficiency of both [factors] is stated as a fault in the *Lakṣaṇaṭīkā*. Anticipating the objection that this contradicts that [text], he says: "But as for... (*yā tv iti*).

However, the unestablishedness of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) is not a fault. To explain: first of all, the unestablishedness of the locus does not apply to the inference "A jar is impermanent because it is a product. [Here begins] Chapter 26: The Refutation of the Fault of the Unestablished Locus.
Now, it might be argued that the claim—"there are only two defects of a reason, namely non-establishment (*asiddhi*) and non-pervasion (*avyāpti*)"—is incorrect;

for there exist other defects of the reason, such as the unestablishedness of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*), the unestablishedness of the probandum’s locus (*prasiddhasādhyakatva*), and the unestablishedness of being in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhatva*).

Therefore, desiring to demonstrate that the unestablishedness of the locus and so forth are not defects, [the author] proceeds according to the method set forth in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa* and its commentary, which states: "The unestablishedness of the locus, the probandum, and being in a different locus are not defects."
Regarding the point concerning the unestablished nature of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*), he states what has already been said: "But as for the unestablished nature of the locus..."

Now, is this [fault] the unestablishedness of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*), the proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhakatva*), the non-existence of the form under discussion as the subject (*pakṣīkṛtākāreṇāsatva*), having a non-existent locus (*abhāvāśrayatva*), having a non-existent substratum (*asadāśrayatva*), or having a non-existent support (*asadāśrayakatva*)? and "Nor even as consisting of gold... and so forth.

239: It is correct [to claim] that in cases such as "like a jar," there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhakatva*), because, due to the absence of the status of being a subject (*pakṣatva*)—which is inherently imbued with doubt—there is an absence of the locus (*āśraya*) in the form of the subject (*pakṣa*).
This is because it has been stated that the status of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) exists even in the absence of doubt.
For even in my view, that [objection] constitutes a fault because it is included within the category of non-attachment (asaṅgatva).

Nor is it the case that its non-existence in the form of the subject (pakṣa) is due to the absence of a qualification of the subject—as in cases such as "the golden mountain is not fiery"—because even in my view, that constitutes a fallacy by being included within the category of contradiction (bādhā).

Nor is it correct to claim that non-existence (*abhāva*) has absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) as its locus; for since non-existence is insubstantial (*tucchatva*), just as there is no causality in the absence of an obstructing factor, there is likewise no locus-hood in the absence [of a substratum]. Furthermore, absolute non-existence is itself unauthentic because its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is unauthentic. This is because the very counter-correlate of absolute non-existence is insubstantial, whereas non-existence itself is not insubstantial.

Because it has already been stated.

[This is so] because of its being a fault (*doṣatvāt*).

The meaning is that, in the context of discussing the defects of one's own intended inference, it was stated that [the point at issue] is a defect because it is included within the *nigrahasthāna* (point of defeat) known as "inconsistency" (*asaṅgati*) in the case of inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*). [This is stated] by way of the absence of a qualification of the subject (*pakṣaviśeṣaṇābhāva*).

The meaning is that, according to the statement in the *Maṇi*, the "unmixed" fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) is established by the non-establishment of the qualification of the locus (*āśrayaviśeṣaṇāsiddhi*).
"By being included within sublation."

This applies to that [reason] as well.

The refutation of the charge regarding the fallacy of inference (anumānadoṣavāda), page 241:

[The opponent argues that the alleged fallacy is not a defect] because it is either (1) due to the absence of sublation (*bādha*) since [the subject] does not serve as the locus for the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*); or due to the lack of proof (*asiddhi*) because of the absence of the means of proof (*sādhana*); or because, being outside the scope of cognition, it is not the object of any linguistic convention consisting of affirmation or negation; or because, being unestablished by valid means of knowledge (*aprāmāṇika*), it is not a constituent part of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇānaṅga*); or because, in the absence of such a basis, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of calling everything a fallacy]; or because there is an absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*)—defined as the necessary co-occurrence (*niyatasāmānādhikaraṇya*)—between two properties that lack a common substratum (*niradhikaraṇa*).

The first two [alternatives] are not tenable; for if the two properties you have stated—namely, the two probanda consisting in the non-basis of the property to be proven and the property that proves it—are absent, then even for you, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a sublation (*bādha*) and so forth, since the probans consisting in the absence of properties (*nirdharmakatva*) is impossible.

Furthermore, because the properties you have stated are of the nature of absences (*abhāva*), if they were possible therein, then for that very reason, my own stated properties such as "not being a speaker" (*avaktṛtva*) and "not being sentient" (*acetanatva*) would also be possible.
As for properties of the nature of existents (*bhāva*), however, I do not admit them either.
And even if there is an absence of being the locus for the non-existence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and so forth—

[the author] analyzes this in six ways according to the method of *vikalpa* (alternatives) in the *Sudhā* commentary, during the introduction to the *Anuvyākhyāna* on the *Bhaktipāda*, beginning with the words “The fault is indeed contradiction [in the proof of the existence of a man’s horn],” etc., starting with the words “What [is it]? and so on.
The ablative endings in "bādhāt" and so forth are to be construed with the phrase "the status of being a fault."
"Of two phenomena."
The meaning is: "of the two properties consisting of the probandum and the probans. [This refers to] not the first two.
The meaning is that the two conceptual constructions (kalpa) are "there is no probandum" and "there is no means of proof.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi) in the phrase "sublation and so forth," the fallacy of the unestablished (asiddhi) is included.
"Of the dharmas spoken by you."

The meaning is: of the properties consisting in not being the locus of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), not being the locus of the proving property (*sādhanadharma*), and being devoid of properties (*nirdharmakatva*).
"Therein" [refers to that].
The meaning is that [the reason] does not exist in cases such as the son of a barren woman.
By the word "by this," he clarifies what has been stated: [The text continues:

"...either because it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇatva*), or because it is not an auxiliary factor (*anaṅgatva*), or because it lacks a basis in valid cognition (*aprāmāṇikatva*). Since the property of not being the locus of the probandum (*sādhyadharma*) and so forth exists [in your counter-example], you do not face sublation (*bādha*) or other fallacies. If that is the case, then even though the absence of being the locus of "speaker-ness" (*vaktṛtva*) is absent [in your example], since the absence of not being the locus of speaker-ness exists [therein], I too do not face sublation or other fallacies.

By this, the objection that "non-speakerness and so forth do not exist either, precisely because [the subject] is non-existent—just like speakerness and so forth—and thus there is a sublation [of the reason]" is refuted.
This is because the non-existence of the son of a barren woman qualified by speakerness serves as a proof for the non-existence of speakerness [in general], rather than being a sublation of it;
for when both the qualifier and the qualified are absent, the absence of the qualified entity is firmly established.
For from that very same [reason], it would follow that just as there is validity, there is also the absence of invalidity.
If it is argued that "lack of being an authority" and so forth are conducive to non-existence, because in their absence there would follow existence by virtue of being an authority, [we reply:
this is the same in the present case as well, for in the absence of not being a speaker, there would follow existence by virtue of being a speaker.
Furthermore, just as there is the absence of being a speaker, so too would there be the absence of non-sublation (abādha), just as there is sublation (bādha).
[Regarding the term] "barren" (*vandhyā*): since it might be asked how that can be a means of proof (*sādhaka*), he says: "By the qualifier," etc.
The meaning is that there is an absence of both the specific property of being the son of a barren woman and the specific property of being a speaker;
[the phrase] "for that very reason" refers to this.
The meaning is "precisely because of its non-existence.
He clarifies what was stated as "equal" with the words "by not being a speaker," and so forth.
It is like the state of being an unspoken speaker.
The meaning is "just as in the case of not being a speaker.

You stated that in the argument "the son of a barren woman is not a speaker because he is insentient," there is a sublation (*bādha*) due to the absence of the probandum-property consisting of "not being a speaker"; I, however, have stated that in the absence of "not being a speaker," there would be "being a speaker."

If you argue that there is a contradiction because "if speakerhood does not exist, then non-speakerhood cannot exist either," then it follows that since speakerhood—which is the absence of that [non-speakerhood]—also does not exist, there would likewise be no contradiction. This is the meaning.

The meaning is that the object of dispute is characterized as being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent because it is sublatable;

otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (atiprasaṅga), whereby even such statements as "the earth possesses the horns of a hare" would result in being considered valid means of knowledge simply because they are [grammatically] well-formed.
"Composed of that."

The meaning is that when the probandum (sādhya) is unestablished, the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti) defined by it is impossible, and thus the pervasion is destroyed. [This refers to the term] "unknown" (avidita).
The meaning is as follows: in the proposition "the earth is scratched by a rabbit's horn," the referent of the term "rabbit's horn" is not known because it is non-existent (*aprasiddha*).

Consequently, since it is impossible to grasp its denotative power (*śakti*) therein, the recollection of that word-meaning is precluded; thus, there arises the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the proposition would fail to convey the connection with that [meaning]. Following the logic of the *Tārkikas*, he himself proposes another alternative mentioned in the *Sudhā*: "of the cause," etc.

Or else, because it would follow that [the word] is non-expressive due to its being a mere denotation of the word-meaning (*padārtha*); or because of the destruction of pervasion (*vyāpti*). [The reading] "at that time" (*tadānīm*) is an addition found in the Ṭa, Ṭha, and Ḍa manuscripts.

Regarding the phrase "by way of contradiction and so forth": if one says "it is not existent," non-existence would be asserted;
since non-existence consists in the negation of existence, if one then says "it is not non-existent," there is a contradiction with one's own statement.
Thus, by the statement "it is not non-existent," since "two negatives convey the original meaning with an intensification," existence (*sattva*) is obtained.
When it is further stated "it is not existent," there is indeed a contradiction of one's own words.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), sublation by valid cognition (*pramāṇabādha*), lack of pervasion (*vyāptyabhāva*), and so forth are included.

Now, one might object: "Why not simply accept that contradiction (*vyāghāta*) and so forth alone constitute the fault, and in those cases, accept that the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) is the fault? To this, it was said: "by what is already established" (*kḷptena*).

The meaning is: "by that which has been established as a defect in cases such as 'the mother is barren' (*mātā vandhyā*). "Horn" is a mere name;
for there is no such thing as a horn that transcends the senses.

When it is maintained that what is unestablished serves as the means of proving the probandum— by means of such things as horns and so forth— this results in the fallacy of having an unestablished qualifier (*apraddha-viśeṣaṇa-asiddha*).
Regarding the discussion on the defects of inference (anumānadoṣavāda):

since [an inference] is already vitiated by other defects such as *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established), there is no possibility of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the validity of an inference like "the class of living bodies possesses a self because they possess breath and so forth," which is accepted as being free from other defects.
On the contrary, there is the over-extension [of the definition] precisely to the case of what is unestablished (*aprasiddha*),

because in the inference of the connection between a mountain and fire based on its being an effect and so forth, it is precisely the unestablished omniscience of God and the like that is established;

and because even fire that is not connected with a kitchen or similar place is established as "fire" and as "terrestrial fire"— that is, as something new (*apūrva*) in reality— by way of those very modes.

Objection: Is it not the case that the establishment of something unestablished other than what is obtainable through the force of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) does not constitute the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*)? Reply: No. Because even though it is not obtainable through that [force], the oneness of the agent and other such qualities are established in those things inferred from the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*).

This is because [the probans] is redundant (*vaiyarthyāt*).
The sense is that the defect consists precisely in the uselessness of the qualification.

Now, in the case of the general definition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) stated in the *Maṇi*— namely, that "pervasion is the co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of a probans with that which is not delimited by the delimiter of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that resides in the same locus as the probans but does not reside in the same locus as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogi*)"—

it follows that even between two things residing in different loci there is pervasion, just as there is pervasion between smoke from a kitchen and fire located on a mountain. This is the position [of the opponent].
He states another fault with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). [The text continues: ...from the absence of grammatical derivation, [the word] would be devoid of its own nature (*svabhāva*). (Note:
*vyakaraṇāddheḥ* is interpreted as *vyākaraṇād dhetor abhāvāt*, meaning "due to the absence of a cause consisting in grammatical derivation.")
The Refutation of the Charge of Inferential Fallacy, p. 271.
Furthermore, even if pervasion (*vyāpti*) exists, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in treating "residing in different loci" (*vyadhikaraṇatva*) as a logical fallacy;
for it is observed that the rising of the sun is [inferred] by means of the blooming of lotuses, even though they reside in different loci.
As the rising of the moon is inferred from the swelling of the ocean, as clouds are inferred from shadows, and as the sun above is inferred from light reaching the ground;
From the whirling of a wheel, there is the inference of the potter's presence; from the rising of the Kṛttikās, the inference of the approaching Rohiṇīs;
and from a river flood at a lower location, the inference of rain at a higher location.
There is an inference of the fire in the lower part by means of the smoke situated in the upper part.

[Objection: But surely, even here, one may establish co-location by taking time, place, or the like as the subject (*pakṣa*). For example: "This time possesses sunrise, because it is time, like a [previously] agreed-upon instance"; or "This place possesses the proximity of a potter, because it possesses the instruments such as the revolving wheel, like a [previously] agreed-upon instance"; or "This river possesses rain upstream, because it is a river," or "This smoke possesses fire at its base, because it is smoke, like a [previously] agreed-upon instance. Thus, by taking time, place, and so forth as the subject, co-location is to be accomplished.
This would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
The meaning is that there would be the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) consisting in the fallacy of good reasons becoming bad reasons.
To the question "How so?", he says: "For it is seen..."
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is with the word "inference" (*anumiti*).
Considering that the example cited in the *Anuvyākhyāna* is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), he says: "the lotus," and so forth.
Having taken up [the categories of] time (*kāla*) or place (*deśa*), he raises the doubt regarding universal grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words "Now, indeed" (*nanu*).
By the phrase "or place and so forth," the word "river" (*nadī*) is included by the term "and so forth" (*ādi*).

pu – 272. *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam* (Third Chapter) Is this a common worldly cognition, or is such a modification of the formulation merely imagined for the sake of establishing the restriction of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as you intend?

The first [alternative] is not tenable; for even among worldly people who do not know the artificial construction you have described, one observes the inference of sunrise and so forth for their own sake based simply on seeing the blooming of lotuses and the like, and one likewise observes the inference for the sake of others that follows from that. Furthermore, investigators must devise a system that conforms to the methods established in the world; they must not invalidate it with a system of their own invention.
Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the principle].
And it has been stated in the *Nyāyaṭīkā*: "It is proper for investigators merely to follow what is already established."
There is no negation of that which is established by the consensus of the entire world through its defining characteristic.
For indeed, a relationship of indicator and indicated (*gamyagamakabhāva*) is observed between today’s sunrise and tomorrow’s sunrise.

[Objection: Even if this is the case according to worldly convention, why should I—just like you—formulate a technical definition merely out of deference to worldly convention? To this, he replies: "By the investigators... (*parīkṣakaiśca*).
Because it would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
The meaning is that [if your position were correct], there would be no production of an inference of fire from smoke and so forth;

nor would it be possible to postulate that even a cognition is a cause of activity by way of desire; nor could one establish that a staff and other such things are causes of a jar—such over-extensions (atiprasaṅga) would follow.
Alternatively, the meaning is that one would be forced to establish that even for co-located factors, there is no relationship of the signified and the signifier (gamyagamakabhāva).
1. What then [is] the worldly [view]? (ga.ṭa.rā.
— [End of section on the refutation of the definition of inference] — Discussion of the defects of inference, page 273. — [End of section] — *Vyākhyā-naya-dīpikā* (Commentary on the Lamp of Logic).

Not the second [alternative], because it involves mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*). Otherwise, in order to establish the lack of common locus (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) and so forth as I intend, one would have to argue: "The region below the mountain possesses fire, because the region above it possesses smoke," or "The disputed time or place is connected to a fire-bearing mountain, because it is connected to a smoke-bearing mountain."
The transformation [of the world] would also be like that of a consensus (*saṃmata*), and so forth.

Furthermore, since such grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) could be easily established in all cases, the charge of "unestablished due to being in different loci" (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhi*) would have no scope. If you argue that it does have scope when such coreferentiality cannot be established, then that unestablished status would be a defect of the argument itself.
[The author] refutes the aforementioned alternative in order to maintain the rule of coreferentiality as intended by you: "Not the second."
Thus: "mutually."

The meaning is that there is a circular argument (anyonyāśraya): once the rule of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is established, one must assume a modification of the usage to account for it; yet, once the modification of usage is established in the manner described, the rule of coreferentiality is established. Thus, each depends upon the other.
4. "It is without opportunity."

The point is that since it is easy to state a co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) even in cases of the fallacious reason known as "unestablished due to being in a different locus" (vyadhikaraṇāsiddha)— such as "this time possesses eternity because it possesses the blackness of a crow"— no example of a vyadhikaraṇāsiddha could ever be found;
consequently, its inclusion among the fallacies would be unjustified.

The meaning is: "in its non-establishment," that is, in the failure to establish co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) due to [obstacles such as] place, time, and so forth. [Note on the commentary: The phrase "for the sake of establishing my intended [position]" means for the sake of establishing the heterolocation (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) intended by me. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is understood that in all applications [of the argument], one must establish the position by taking either place or time alone as the subject (*pakṣa*).
Thus, there is no defect in the meaning—more on this in [the section marked] ṭha.
— *Nyāyadīpuyutatarkatāṇḍava* (Third Chapter), page 274.
— No defect in the meaning.

Furthermore, there is no fault of "stating what has already been said" (noktidoṣa) either; for even when it is stated that "the rising of Rohiṇī is imminent because Kṛttikā has risen," an inference arises in the minds of the listeners.
The second [alternative] is not tenable;

for we observe that even when there is a lack of co-referentiality (*vyadhikaraṇa*), provided the relationship cannot otherwise be accounted for, it constitutes a valid mark (*liṅga*), whereas even when there is co-referentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), it fails to be a mark if the relationship can be accounted for otherwise. Thus, the requirement of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is not indispensable. Furthermore, one infers the existence at another time and place of a cause appropriate to an effect that is currently existing here and now, even though that cause itself does not exist at that other time and place.
It is not a defect of the object.
And thus, even when the person who employs [the argument] is defeated, the inferential cognition arising therein would still be of the nature of valid knowledge (pramā); this is the sense.

Now, one might object: "In cases where there is a defect in the statement, the meaning itself is also defective because no such inference arises in that situation. To this, he says: "Furthermore" (kiñca).
He refutes the position that [the reason is fallacious] "because of the failure of its presence in the subject" by stating: "Not the second."
"In those cases where [the probans] would otherwise be impossible."
The meaning is: "Let there be pervasion in the form of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*)," referring to the previously mentioned cases such as the blooming of a lotus;
that is, [the objection applies] to those instances where [the reason] is established otherwise.
The meaning is: in cases such as "the mountain possesses fire because it possesses stoniness" or "because it is knowable," and so forth.
"Non-liṅga-hood" means the state of not producing valid cognition.
[This refers to] the status of being a *liṅga* (probans) even in those cases where the terms reside in different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*), provided they are otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapanna*).

It was stated [above] that [this occurs] "from perception"; he now demonstrates this with respect to those things that have entered into the relationship of cause and effect, beginning with the words "here" (iha).
The analysis of the word is "sataḥ" (of that which exists).

The meaning is that by the observation of the present sprout and so forth, one infers the existence of the seed at a prior time through the effect in the form of the blossoming of the lotus, just as one infers the sun has risen over the eastern mountain;
therefore, the meaning is precisely because the relationship of signifier and signified (*liṅgi-liṅga-bhāva*) exists between cause and effect even when they are not co-located and not simultaneous.

For this very reason, even by the Vaiśeṣikas it is stated that "the inferential [cognition] arises from: 'this is the effect of that,' 'the cause of that,' 'the related,' 'the inherent in the same object,' or 'the contradictory'"— thus, while the marks consisting of effect and cause are mentioned separately, in your own view, although there is a difference between the falling and the fallen due to the loss of parts and so forth, [the cognition occurs] through the falling residing in the falling [object].
And because of the inference from weight when [the object] has fallen.
You too [must admit] that cooking occurs without my action, provided that [the agent] exists—as in the case of "this is the effect of this. "This is the effect of this" means:

"This is the cause of this," "this is related to this," "this is inherent in the same object as this," and "this is opposed to this"— in these five ways, inferential knowledge is pervasive; such is the meaning.

He demonstrates that, even according to the consensus of others, there exists a relationship of indicator and indicated (*liṅgi-liṅgin*) between two things residing in different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*), by stating "in your own view": first, rain and so forth from the excellence of clouds and so forth; second, fire and so forth from smoke and so forth; third, color and so forth from taste and so forth due to conjunction; fourth, the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and so forth from destruction and so forth; and fifth, [the example of] the excellence of intelligence and so forth.
Thus, he shows the relationship of indicator and indicated between two things in different substrata.
It falls.
The meaning is "of that which is falling and of that which has fallen";
that is to say, of that which possesses the action of falling in the present and of that which possessed the action of falling in the past.
For although there is no loss of parts during the state of falling, once it has fallen, a loss of parts necessarily occurs due to the impact.

Furthermore, in cases where there is a reduction of constituent parts (*avayava*), the process of baking a *pīlu* fruit is accepted as involving the destruction [of the whole] down to the level of the atoms (*paramāṇu*), followed by the production of a new substance.

Consequently, just like a falling fruit, the fruit in its state of having already fallen is a different entity; for in that case, one observes the inference: "This fallen fruit possesses gravity (2), because it possesses the action of falling (3), like the [previously observed] agreed-upon instance.

Now, since the falling [action] and gravity—which have entered into the relationship of the sign (*liṅga*) and the signified (*liṅgin*)—reside in different loci both spatially and temporally, how [can they be related]?
1. ṣṭhenapa – ka, ga, rā; 2. tam idaṃ phalam – ṭa, ṭha, ḍa; 3. tv-avatvāt – ṭha.

For in the inference "this is the means to achieve what I desire because it is my food, like [food] I am currently eating," the cognition of the probandum (sādhya) residing in the subject (pakṣa)—which is the yet-to-be-prepared dish—is said to arise from a reason (hetu) that is already known as residing in a prepared dish.

Furthermore, in your view, either (1) validity (*prāmāṇya*) itself, or (2) the state of being a determinate cognition (*niṣkarṣajñānatva*) itself, constitutes the property of being knowable (*prameyatva*). Likewise, [in your view] the nature of an effect (*kāryatva*) is nothing other than effort (*kṛtitva*), and the nature of being desired (*iṣṭatva*) or being loathed (*dviṣṭatva*) is nothing other than desire (*icchātva*) or aversion (*dveṣatva*). If this is so, how can there be "property-of-the-subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*) in an inference such as "Sound is denotable because it is knowable"? If you argue that there is an indirect relation (*paramparā-sambandha*) between sound and validity, we say no.
The meaning is that [the reason] is a fallacy because it is unestablished due to having a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhi*).
"O you of perfected cooking!"
The sense is that, because the reason (hetu) is absent when the cooking is unaccomplished, you lack knowledge of its being restricted to that [accomplished state].
And because it has already been stated.
In the theory of positive injunction (*vidhivāda*):

therefore, the point is that the fallacy of "incompatible locus" (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhi*) is not a defect by virtue of its disrupting the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Furthermore, he demonstrates that even in other instances, according to the opponent's own view, there is the capacity for an incompatible locus to be a prover—stating, "Moreover, in your own view... and so forth.

Since validity (*prāmāṇya*) is also not a genus (*ajāti*) because it is conditioned by the existence of the object, [the author] states that "knowledge-ness" (*jñānatva*) enters into that validity which consists in being a cognition having a particular qualifier with respect to that which possesses it—this is what is meant by "without further analysis."

The meaning is: "when there is an investigation into the universal (jāti) as an undivided [entity], through the discernment of the limiting conditions (upādhi) that constitute the body of truthfulness.
To the question, "Let it be so; what follows from that?", he says: "And thus... (tathā ca).
In such passages as these.

The meaning of the phrase "and so forth" includes such [cognitions] as: "This has an agent because it is an effect," "This is to be accepted because it is desired," and "This is to be rejected because it is disliked."
How so?
The meaning is that validity and so forth reside in the knower and do not reside in the word and so forth; thus, it is by way of a causal chain (*paramparā*).

The meaning is that there is a "succession" (paramparā): the relation of identity-in-difference (*svarūpa-sambandha*) between the word and the valid cognition, and the inherence (*samavāya*) of the property of being a valid cognition (*pramātva*) with that valid cognition.

For, by the force of common experience, the status of being a property of something can be postulated through any kind of relation—even through a successive relation—as in the cases of "the black cloth" or "the red crystal. He says "the word" to show that such a [direct] cognition does not indeed arise in this way.
Because its nature is that of valid cognition (*pramā*).

[Note on variants: 1. *vātiniṣkarṣe jñā* – ka, ga; 2. *vātiniṣkarṣajñā* – ṭa; 3. *prameva vā* is added – ka. [Grammatical analysis: Due to the elision of the suffix *ṇa*, there is the substitution of *ṅ*.
The Discussion on the Faults of Inference (Anumādoṣavāda), p. 277:
Because it is never perceived that validity belongs to verbal testimony (*śabda*), and, on the contrary, it is perceived precisely that it lacks validity.
For that [quality of being an object of knowledge] cannot logically belong to it (the word).

Nor should it be argued that "knowability" (*prameyatva*) consists in being the object of a valid cognition of the same class, or being the object of God's valid cognition, and that this exists in the word.
For, in your view, even the relation consisting in the state of being an object is of the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*),
and valid cognition does not reside in the word.

Furthermore, since in your own view it is the negative concomitance (vyatirekavyāpti) that is directly the constituent factor [of inference], then just as there is the status of being the "comprehender" (gamaka) despite the lack of co-location between the pervasion and the property-of-the-subject (pakṣadharmatā), let there likewise be the status of being the "comprehended" (gamya) and the "comprehender" (gamaka) between the probandum and the probans despite their lack of co-location.

In that case, if the relation of counter-positive and locus (pratiyogyanuyogibhāva) is the regulating factor there, then here too, let the vertical arrangement (ūrdhvādhārībhāva) of the two locations—the one where the rain was previously observed and the one where the flood is seen—be the regulating factor.

Moreover, since smoke of a certain class is pervaded by fire of a certain class, smoke on a mountain is likewise pervaded by fire in a kitchen according to your own view; how, then, can there be co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the pervaded and the pervader?
The sense is that otherwise, there would follow the non-existence of knowability (*prameyatva*) in the past and so forth.
Furthermore, by way of a counter-argument (*pratibandī*), he states that lack of co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is not a defect: "Moreover, in the case of negative concomitance... and so on.

In the view that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) mentioned in the *Maṇi* [of Gaṅgeśa] consists in co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), pervasion is admitted even between two things that do not share a common locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Following that [view], he says: "Moreover" (*api ca*).
[From page 278 of the *Tarkatāṇḍava* with the *Nyāyadīpa*, Third Chapter.]

By this, the claim that the certainty of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), etc., is the cause of inference because it obstructs [other] inferences, is refuted;
for we observe inference even when there is certainty regarding the co-occurrence and negative concomitance between rain and the swelling of a river.
Not the third [alternative], because pervasion has been established even in the case of a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (vaiyadhikaraṇya).

The refutation of the objection that [the reason] is defective due to being unestablished in a different locus (vyadhikaraṇāsiddhi). // 27 // He rejects the position that it is a defect because it disrupts the pervasion (vyāpti), stating: "Not the third."
The refutation of the view that the fallacy of "incompatibility with the locus" (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhi*) constitutes a distinct defect.

// 28 // Sublation (*bādha*) and counter-inference (*pratirodha*) are identical insofar as they both constitute a contradiction between the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*) and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). // 28 //

Some, however, maintain that there are five fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*): the inconclusive (*savyabhicāra*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the counter-balanced (*satpratipakṣa*), the unestablished (*asiddha*), and the sublated (*bādhita*).

[In this view], sublation (*bādha*) and counter-resistance (*pratirodha*) are unified under the single category of contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*).

Now, one might object: "Even if *āśrayāsiddhi*, *sādhyāsiddhi*, and *vyadhikaraṇāsiddhi* are not considered defects, since fallacies such as *vyabhicāra* (inconstancy) and others do exist as defects of the reason (*hetu*), it is incorrect to say that there are only two types of defects of the reason—namely, *asiddhi* (unestablishedness) and *avyāpti* (under-extension). This objection is raised with the passage beginning "Some, however...
and ending with "...it is incorrect to say that there are only two types of defects of the reason."
Some logicians,

although following the tradition of the ancients by enumerating seven types of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)— namely, the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), the unspecified (*anadhyavasita*), the mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), the counter-balanced (*prakaraṇasama*), and the refuted by the similar (*satpratipakṣa*) as explained in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa-ṭīkā* and other works— included the "unspecified" within the "inconclusive" and the "counter-balanced" within the "impossible."

For sublation (*bādha*) is of many kinds—distinguished by contradiction with a stronger perception, contradiction with a strong inference, contradiction with a strong scripture, and so forth—as is clear from the *Lakṣaṇaṭīkā*.

Thus, just as there are internal subdivisions such as contradiction with a stronger means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), even in the case of contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa-virodha*), it would have been pointed out through further subdivisions such as contradiction with a stronger visual perception or a stronger tactile perception;
yet this has not been accepted.
The sense is that if it were so, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the collapse of the fivefold division.
[This refers to the phrase] "atyaśakti" (extreme incapacity).

The meaning is that since [the statement] is intended to indicate incapacity by asking, "Did you not recognize even a powerful contradiction, let alone a mere contradiction with the means of valid cognition?"— it is for the purpose of making known [his] inability.
"Only of that which makes known [the object's] incapacity."

Since the defeat of the opponent and one's own victory are possible merely by making [the opponent] aware of his own incapacity, that alone constitutes the objective; therefore, since the awareness of an "excessive" incapacity is not the objective, the claim that it serves a purpose by being for that sake (tādarthya) is incorrect.
The point is that even without specifying intermediate distinctions, that much is established in the manner already described.
To the question, "If the awareness of an excessive incapacity is obtained, why should it be abandoned?", he says: "Because of the knowledge of sublation," etc.
Thinking that "I do not know even one who is more powerful, much less one who is equal; let there be some such excellence," he says in reply: "And what [more]? (kiṃ ca).
It should be construed as "by the speaker" because of his being easy to address.
[Note: *dhājñā* (Rā.
[Note: *bāpraye-prarthapraṇa-vinaikya*]
Since it could equally be said that "this [reason] was employed by the opponent because of his [superior] capacity," why would the opponent's excellence of power not be established?
Furthermore, even in this case, the redundancy of the term "equal strength" (*samabala*) in the context of a counter-argument remains exactly as it was.

Furthermore, even if sublation (*bādha*) occurs, since the status of being "strong" (*prabala*) is already obtained by the word "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) itself, the inclusion of the word "strong" is redundant;
on the contrary, by excluding those of equal strength, it produces the opposite result, namely, a deficiency.

Although the result of *pratirodha* (counter-objection) is merely the obstruction of the opponent's position, whereas the result of *bādha* (sublation) is also the establishment of one's own position, nevertheless, the establishment of one's own position must be treated as a separate task.
"Of the opponent" (*parasya*) means of the proponent (*vādī*) who employs the sublated inference (*bādhita-anumāna*).
"Even so" (*evam api*) [means even under such circumstances].
The meaning is that even though it is purposeful because it serves to indicate the extreme power of a particular means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
[the objection] remains in that very same state.
The meaning is that this is because every previously considered [reason] has been refuted.

Not only is the term "powerful" (prabala) redundant, but it should not be accepted as a non-probative inference because its meaning is contradictory; thus he says: "Furthermore, even in the case of sublation... (kiñca bādhe 'pi).

The meaning is as follows: when it is stated that "this is not a proof because it contradicts valid cognition" (*pramāṇaviruddhatvāt*), since one gains one's own intended [opponent's] position—that it is contradicted by a stronger valid cognition—as a fault, it is possible for this to apply equally to contradiction by a valid cognition of equal strength; therefore, the phrase "only by the word 'strong'" (*balavat*) serves to exclude that [equal-strength case].

Now, one might object: "The sublation (*bādha*) that excludes [a counter-argument] of equal strength does not result in a contrary outcome by way of causing harm, because sublation consists in the dual form of establishing one's own position and refuting the opposing position; since these two are absent when the strengths are equal, it results only in a favorable outcome for the stronger side. Therefore, it is not even useless. Having thus restated this objection, he refutes it with the words beginning "Even though... (*yadyapi*).

He states that even if [the word] were meaningful for the purpose of making known an excessive incapacity, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), saying: "Moreover, in this way for the opponent... etc.
In short, since the bondage itself is the intended object [of the inquiry], only that much should be stated as is necessary for the establishment of the non-contradiction; nothing else.

Furthermore, since [the reason] is sublated because it contradicts stronger means of knowledge— by virtue of its being dependent on plurality, its lack of scope, and so forth— in order to demonstrate the opponent's extreme incapacity, then [if your logic held],
the statement of multiple reasons to demonstrate one's own superior capacity would also be [sublated], which would result in the total abolition of the "additional" (adhika) ground for defeat.

In a formal debate (*vāda*) proceeding according to the rules of debate, as well as in a treatise (*śāstra*), it is appropriate to state many defects in order to demonstrate that [the opponent's position] is utterly contemptible.
But not in the case of verbal debate and the like, without having bound oneself by a formal agreement.
[Objection: But surely, *bādha* (sublation) consists in the subject (*pakṣa*) possessing the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) as established by valid cognition;

and in this case, there is no pointlessness (*vaiyarthyam*) of the qualification. [Response: If you say this, it is not so. [Question: How then is it that in the debate (*vādakathā*) and in the treatises (*śāstra*), multiple defects are demonstrated in the inferences put forward by others? For even in those cases, there would be the occurrence of the occasion for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as "excess" (*adhikya*). To this, he says:
—This refers to *vāda* (debate), but not to *jalpa* (wrangling) and the like.
It has been stated that in *jalpa*, *vitanda*, and *kathā*, there is no restriction on the number of points.

For when a formal agreement (*samayabandha*) is made that "as many as two, three, or more [points] as occur to one shall all be stated," there would be no fault in failing to state them; therefore, he says: "without a formal agreement."
Anticipating the view of the Maṇikṛt, he refutes it with the words "nanu" (but surely).
The meaning is: "having as its subject a locus (pakṣa) which possesses the absence of the probandum (sādhya), where that absence has been determined by a certainty regarding its validity.

This is because it is accepted that there is a "sublation" (bādha) when there is a certainty regarding the validity of a cognition of the absence of the probandum, and also because of the subsequent passage beginning with "two contradictory cognitions," etc.
Alternatively, this is stated according to the view that sublation consists in a valid cognition of the absence of the probandum.

In the view that "sublation" (*bādha*) consists in the ascertainment of the validity of the cognition of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), even you must admit that the result of sublation is the valid cognition of the absence of the probandum; consequently, it is impossible for that [cognition of the absence] itself to be the sublater. Furthermore, if sublation were merely a conditional adjunct (*upādhi*) of the cognition, then since there would be no sublation at the time when the absence of the probandum is not yet cognized, it would follow that sublation is a non-eternal defect (*anityadoṣa*).

Furthermore, when two contradictory cognitions arise together, since the ascertainment of validity in one case can be accounted for even without an ascertainment of the superiority of its instrument, it is more appropriate that the defect consists precisely in the contradiction with a stronger means of valid cognition, which is necessarily present.

Furthermore, since contradiction (*pratirodha*) is already established [as a fault], it is more appropriate that the defectiveness of the conflict between the instruments of knowledge (*karaṇavirodha*) itself constitutes the fault.

Moreover, just as in the case of contradiction, since an obstruction can occur through the necessary factor of "having equal strength" (*ahīnabala*) even in the case of sublation (*bādha*), what is the purpose of the qualification "validity" (*pramātva*)?

It should be noted that this statement—"the two cognitions of contradictory objects," etc.—is intended to state another fault by accepting the meaning [of the definition] as "that which has for its subject a locus (*pakṣa*) possessing the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) which is the object of certainty."
Because it has been stated thus.

And thus, it must be stated that sublation (*bādha*) occurs only when there is a contradiction with a stronger means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for only then is the cognition of the absence of the probandum established as the result. Therefore, the sense is that the qualification [in the definition] is indeed redundant.
Regarding the phrase "two contradictory cognitions":
The meaning is: "two cognitions that are contradictory and have as their objects the probandum and its absence.
[Regarding the term] "instrument" (karaṇa):...
The meaning is "the instrument for the cognition of that.

Even in the case of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*), where there is an opposition, he states—saying "furthermore, as in the case of opposition"—that even here, in this view, futility (*vaiyarthya*) indeed prevails. Regarding the phrase "as in the case of opposition," it was stated thus because, even in opposition, the qualification of "strength" (*balatva*) by means of futility and so forth has already been established through the qualification of the qualification. Thus, it is said "as in the case of opposition."
Regarding "pramātva" (the nature of being a valid means of knowledge): [it is] as follows.
The meaning is that [the sublation] occurs by means of the qualification of "truth" (*prāmāṇya*) in the cognition of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*).

Alternatively, the meaning is that an obstruction (*pratibandha*) is possible either through contradiction with a proof possessing non-deficient strength, or through contradiction with a prover possessing non-deficient strength, or through the subject (*pakṣa*) possessing the absence of the probandum as cognized by a proof possessing non-deficient strength.
1. *...na bādhakatvayo* — ka. 2. *pi vyarthame-* — ṭa.ḍa. 3. *nāhīna* — ṭa.ṭha.

Furthermore, in this way, in the argument "Fire is cold because it is produced," there would be no sublation by valid cognition (*pramā*) such as "Fire is hot," because the sensation of heat consists in the absence of the sensation of cold.
If, by the term "non-existence" (abhāva), one intends merely that which is contradictory, then my intended point—the commingling with the *satpratipakṣa* (counter-balanced) fallacy—is established;
for the valid cognition of the reason in the refuting inference has as its object that which is contradictory to the probandum in the inference to be refuted.

Furthermore, by abandoning the path already established and resorting to a fallacious construction, one could also define "contradiction" (*bādha*) as follows: either "the state of having a subject that lacks a proven probandum," or "the state of having a subject that lacks a proven relation with the probandum," or "the state of having a subject that possesses a mutual absence whose counter-positive is something possessing the proven probandum. If these were accepted, contradiction would become manifold.

And here, is there only one mark for non-establishment, or all [of them]? Furthermore, he states the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the definition of "sublation" (*bādha*) as "the state of having a subject (*pakṣa*) that possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) as established by valid cognition"—namely: "Moreover, in this way..."
The objection regarding the lack of pervasion is raised: "In the case of non-existence... and so forth.
The intended meaning is that the subject possesses a cognition of something that contradicts the proven probandum; this is the point.
Thus it is established.
The meaning is that the confusion of the "counter-balanced" (satpratipakṣa) fallacy, which is my intended position, is established.
To explain how this is so, he clarifies it with the words: "dūṣaka... [and so forth].
The meaning is "stated by the opponent" (prativādyukta) because it serves as an adversary to the probative inference (sthāpanānumāna) stated by the proponent (vādī).

And thus, since the counter-position (pratipakṣa) is likewise exactly so, it follows that sublation (bādha) and the counter-position are subject to the same refutation; the point is that the fivefold division [of fallacies] would thereby be destroyed.
[This concludes the section on] "the struck" (prahata).
The meaning is: by abandoning the path that consists in contradiction with all established means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In the first case, there would be no obstruction to the inferential cognition (*anumiti*) when there is knowledge of something else.
However, the claim that the inference is obstructed by only one [mark] inferred from another is not consistent with experience.
