Or, if it were so reduced, my intended position—that non-pervasion is included within [the category of] non-pervasion—would be established.

Even in the latter case, does the cognition of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the subverting [reason] in its own form act as an obstacle to the cognition of the pervasion in the inference to be subverted? Or is it the state of being an obstacle [to that]? He refutes the first alternative with the words: "Not, first of all... (*na tāvad iti*).
He specifies the second [point] by means of the words "but" (*kintu*) and so forth, preceded by a question.
The division is indicated by the phrase "as shown by the example. Therein, he further analyzes: "and its state of being an obstacle thereto" (*tatpratibandhakatvam ca*).
The word division is *tad-grāhyā* (that which is graspable by that). The meaning is: "graspable by the cognition intended as the object to be obstructed.
[This refers to] "of the defilement" (*dūṣikāyāḥ*).
The meaning is: "by means of one's own knowledge, [it refers to] that which has become an obstacle";
this is because it lacks the nature of being a non-existent entity (abhāva) that pervades [the locus].

The pervasion of the absence of the reason (*hetvabhāva*) by the probandum (*sādhya*) consists in its being the counter-positive of an absolute absence that resides in that which possesses the probandum (*sādhyavat*).

And here, the meaning is that there is no inclusion of either the factor of "co-occurrence with the probandum" (*sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇya*) or the factor of "deviation," which consists in a relation with the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*). Even granting this, he states the fault: "Even if it exists... (*bhāve 'pi*).
1. Or *vaṃ*—Ga.Rā. 2. After "Where there is the probandum (*sādhya*), there is the means of proof (*sādhana*)," the portion of the text beginning with "dūṣyānumānīya" is missing—Ka.Ga.Rā.
3. *piraśeṣayati*—Ḍa. (The portion within parentheses is corrupted).
The discussion on the defects of inference (anumānadoṣavāda), page 319:
[The definition of a fallacy is] the cognition of something as being pervaded by the absence of pervasion (vyāptyabhāva) belonging to what is to be measured (mānīya).
Not the first [alternative].
Because it would lead to an over-extension;
nor is the latter [the case],

since, given the possibility of knowing the absence of pervasion (*vyāptyabhāva*) upon knowing the absence of its being pervaded (*tadvyāpyatva*), it is established that the necessary absence of pervasion alone constitutes the defect.

Furthermore, if a contradictory reason were considered a fallacy simply because it is pervaded by the absence of pervasion—just like an extraneous condition (upādhi)—then it would not inherently be a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa).

Furthermore, having abandoned the knowledge of the connection with the absence of the probandum—which is internal, simpler, and established through experience—one [resorts] to one's own fabricated procedure;
this is because it leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

The meaning is that there would be the consequence of an obstruction [to inference] by either that non-conceptual [perception] or even by a cognition of it (the subject) having "being an object of knowledge" (*prameyatva*) as its qualifier.

With the thought that, on this view, the very existence of the contradictory fallacious reason (*viruddha-hetvābhāsa*) is difficult to establish, and thus how the division into five [types of fallacies] could be maintained, he says: "Furthermore... (*kiṃ ca*).
"Like a limiting adjunct (upādhi)":
that is to say, just as a limiting adjunct,
because it merely brings about the appearance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and lacks intrinsic defectiveness, does not constitute a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), so too [is the case here].

Now, since the limiting condition (*upādhi*) is pervaded by deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it brings about the cognition of the absence of pervasion (*vyāptyabhāva*) through the inference of that [deviation], but not directly.
For deviation itself is not the absence of pervasion;
rather, pervasion consists in an invariable concomitance (*sahacāra*). Thus, the absence of the probandum and the reason is pervaded by the pervasion between the probandum and the reason.

To one who argues that there is no similarity with the *upādhi* because the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is understood directly [in the former case], he replies: "Furthermore, what is internal (*antaraṅga*)? etc.

Since the cognition of the relation to the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva-sambandha-jñāna*) has fewer objects than the cognition whose object is the state of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*) with respect to the absence of the pervasion between the probandum and the reason (*sādhyahetu-vyāptyabhāva*), its status as "internal" (*antaraṅga*)—
that is, its greater simplicity (*laghutara*)— is indeed evident. Thus it is established.
The sense is that the status of being a common (sādhāraṇa) contradictory reason has already been established.

This is stated by setting aside the cognition of a connection with the absence of the probandum, in accordance with the well-known definition that "the contradictory (viruddha) is that which is pervaded by the absence of the probandum."
The term "process" (prakriyā).

The meaning is that there are exactly five fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), categorized as *savyabhicāra* and so forth, in order to complete the systematic framework (*prakriyā*). [End of section] Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava (Third Chapter) [Page 320] (Note: The text provided contains fragments of a commentary on the classification of fallacious reasons in the Nyāya system.)

It is utterly improper to assume that the cognition of a pervasion between the reason and the negation of the probandum acts as an obstacle to the cognition of the pervasion between the probandum and the reason— thereby serving to justify an external, more cumbersome, unestablished, and non-experiential pervasion of the negation of the probandum by the reason— because here,

unlike in cases such as "being a killer" (*hiṃsātva*) or "being the son of Mitrā," the connection with the absence of the probandum is not manifest; for if it were, then, as in those cases, one could infer [the pervasion] through a limiting condition (*upādhi*) as you have suggested, namely, through "contradiction" (*viruddhatva*).

Furthermore, what kind of knowledge is this? Is it opposed to the perceptual knowledge of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that is the object of the inference to be refuted, or to the inferential [knowledge] itself?
It cannot be the first.

For even when there is the apprehension of "conch-ness" as being pervaded by the absence of yellowness in a conch, the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of yellowness is still observed. Regarding the latter [case], [it may be argued]: "But in this way, even in cases such as 'He is dark-complexioned because he is the son of Mitrā,' the defect would simply be the connection with the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*)."

And that very knowledge [of the pervasion] is the obstacle, and that alone should be pointed out, rather than the adventitious property (*upādhi*) of "being produced from the cooking of *śāka* vegetables"; therefore, he says: "For not... (*na hi*).

Alternatively, just as the statement of a secondary condition (*upādhi*) is made in cases such as "being the son of Mitrā" to indicate the connection with the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), so too here let there be "contradiction in the stated form" for the very purpose of stating that [condition]; to this he says: "For not... (*na hi*).

To the opponent who argues that even when there is no knowledge of the connection with the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), this too must be stated as a distinct fallacy because it is observed to obstruct the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) when— by the force of some causal complex or by the word of a reliable person— a cognition of the aforementioned form occasionally arises, the author replies: "Furthermore,
what is this cognition?"

The meaning is that the knowledge of pervasion consists in the absence of the pervasion between the probandum and the reason being concomitant with the absence of the pervasion between the reason and the probandum. This refers to the "last" [case].
(End of section on internal non-pervasion.)
On the Faults of Inference (Anumādoṣavāda), page 321:

If [the opponent's] cognition were inferential, then regarding the reason (*hetu*) in that inference which is to be refuted, there would be an inclusion within the category of "counter-balanced" (*satpratipakṣa*), because—according to your own stated method—the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the probandum and the pervasion of the absence of pervasion would both be known.
For a counter-balanced argument does not become a contradictory (*viruddha*) one merely by a difference in the example (*udāharaṇa*).

Furthermore, the meaning is this: in order to avoid the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*), if one defines "contradiction" (*viruddhatva*) as being the counter-positive of the absence of a pervader of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakābhāvapratiyogitva*), then—given that for a reason possessing occurrence (*vṛttimataḥ*) there is either non-occurrence in the locus of the probandum or the property of not being co-locative with the probandum—as in the contradictory reason "Sound is eternal because it is produced," the inferential cognition of the pervasion defined by the probandum is itself the sublater of the cognition of the aforementioned state of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*). This is the position.

In this view, it must be stated that the knowledge of pervasion (vyāpti) between the contradictory reason (viruddhahetu) and the probandum (sādhya) is itself inferential; otherwise, the necessary connection (pratibandha) would be impossible. With this intention, he says "dūṣya" and so forth. Furthermore, in the case of a contradictory reason such as "being produced" (kṛtakatva), the inferential cognition must be understood as the knowledge of some pervaded property (vyāpya) with respect to the pervasion defined by the probandum, such as "eternality" (nityatva). With this intention, he says: "of the pervasion of the reason in the inference to be refuted" (dūṣyānumānīyahetau vyāptivyāpyasya).
"According to the method stated by you."

The meaning is: [the fallacy consists] of that which has the nature of pervasion between the probandum and the absence of the reason, and of that which is the pervaded with respect to the absence of the pervasion between the reason and the probandum.

Now, one might object that examples of a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*) are precisely such cases as "sound is non-eternal because it is produced" and "sound is eternal because it is audible," and not of this [present] kind; to this he says: "For not... (*na hi*).

The meaning is as follows: the probans "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), which establishes impermanence, is pervaded by the probandum because it co-occurs with the probandum in the subject (*pakṣa*); yet, the probans "being produced" is not pervaded by the probandum under discussion, because it is the counter-positive of the absence that pervades the probandum. This is stated merely to distinguish between types of examples.
To one who thinks that "counter-position" (*pratipakṣa*) occurs only in cases other than those involving the inference of pervasion or its absence, he says: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) of the phrase "it being so stated" is that there would not be a contradiction [with the claim] that [the cause] is manifold.
To the question "How so?", he states exactly what was said in the *Maṇi*: "of that which possesses a function" (*vṛttimataḥ*).

Alternatively, since it could also be easily stated that "contradiction" (*viruddhatva*) consists in having a property distinct from that which exists in the locus of the probandum (*sādhyavat*), contradiction would become manifold. In that case,

as per the method explained in the section on sublation (*bādha*), one would have to assert that each of these is a separate fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), resulting in an excess of fallacious reasons.

As for what someone has said—that there is no redundancy because [the other factors] are subsumed under the status of being the object of a cognition that contradicts the knowledge of concomitance (sahacāra), which is the cause of the knowledge of pervasion (vyāpti)—[that is incorrect].
That is not so;
for even when there is no knowledge of the object as you have described it, inference is obstructed simply by the knowledge of the connection with the absence of the probandum.

Furthermore, the phrase "that which possesses occurrence" (*vṛttimataḥ*) is stated in order to exclude over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "the mountain possesses fire because it possesses the sky," where the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) serves as the instrument.
Nor should it be argued that this [example] is already included within the category of the intended objects of the definition.

The point is that even if the contradiction consisting in the absence from the locus of the probandum (*sādhyavadavṛttitva*) is known in that case, there is no obstruction to the apprehension of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*), and thus there is no impairment to the arising of inference (*anumiti*) by means of that [contradiction]. To the question, "Let it be so; what is the fault? he says: "And in that case... (*tatra ca*).
It afflicts.

In the discussion concerning the identity of sublation (*bādha*) and counter-argument (*pratirodha*) as both being contradictions with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārtha*), it must be asked: is there only one probative mark (*sādhakatāliṅga*) for all of them, or are they all distinct?
In the first case, there would be no obstruction to inference by means of a different cognition;
however, the claim that the obstruction of an inference occurs through only one [mark] while another [mark] does not obstruct the inference is not consistent with experience.
In the second [alternative], the probans (liṅga) is either conjoined or individual.
In the first case, since [the conclusion] is established by one alone, the remainder is redundant.
In the latter case, there is an excess of fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa), according to the method already stated; such is the meaning.
That by the knowledge of which there occurs an obstruction to inference must indeed be defined as the "comprehender" (*saṃgrāhaka*);
however, this [your definition] is not so.
And thus, with the intention that what is stated would be superfluous to the five [reasons] and unavoidable, he says: "tvadukta" (as stated by you).

Even in the view that the intended meaning of what you have stated is to be unified [with our own], the knowledge of the connection between the reason (*hetu*) and the absence of the probandum (*sādhya-abhāva*) is indispensable.
Thinking, "In that case, this [other argument] is superfluous since that alone suffices," he says: "Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti-jñāna*)," and so forth.

Since the knowledge of a contradictory adjunct (*viruddhopādhi*)— which consists in being the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakābhāvapratiyogitva*), namely "wherever there is the probandum, there is the absence of the reason"— does not directly contradict the knowledge of concomitance (*sahacārajñāna*) regarding the probandum (i.e., "wherever there is the probandum, there is the reason"), it must be defined as contradiction insofar as it involves the conceptualization of the absence of the probandum occurring in every locus of the reason. Thus, contradiction is established as nothing other than being pervaded by the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavyāpyatva*).
And in that case, it has been stated that the restrictive element (niyamāṃśa) would be purposeless.

Furthermore, since by the term "concomitance" (sahacāra) one must intend precisely that concomitance which enters into the body of pervasion (vyāpti), it is established—by virtue of parsimony—that [the fallacy of] "non-pervasion" (avyāpti) is included within the very object of a cognition that contradicts the cognition of pervasion.

By this, since contradiction (*virodha*) depends upon the absence of pervasion (*vyāptyabhāva*), contradiction itself is the defect; for even when the absence of pervasion is not known, [the defect remains].

Now, against the proponent who claims that there is an obstruction to inference even when the relationship with the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is not known, but the knowledge of the aforementioned nature of the object (*viṣayatva*) exists, he says: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
Regarding the "body of pervasion" (vyāptiśarīra):

The sense is that such a [definition] is necessary because something else cannot serve as the cause for the cognition of the pervasion under discussion, and because there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since the state of being the object of a cognition of coexistence and a cognition of contradiction exists— even through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*)— in the case of the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of smoke and fire. Having restated the separate status of the contradictory (*viruddha*) as a distinct fallacy according to another method following the direction of the *Maṇi*, he refutes it with the words "by this" (*etena*).

The meaning is that [the reason] is "refuted" (*prahata*) because it is well-known (*prasiddha*) that what is pervaded by the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavyāpta*) is "contradictory" (*viruddha*), as this is accepted by everyone.

The view that even a cognition [of such a nature] is a defect is also refuted. Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava (Third Chapter) — Page 324. ...is also refuted. [End of section.]

The nature of contradiction (*viruddhatva*), which consists in being pervaded by the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavyāpyatva*) and so forth, is indeed dependent upon the very absence of pervasion (*vyāptyabhāva*), because it is that upon which the latter relies.
For it is not possible to know the state of being pervaded by that [absence] without first knowing the relationship of the reason with the absence of the probandum.

Regarding the contradiction (*viruddhatva*) conceived by you—characterized as being the counter-positive of the absence of the pervader of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakābhāvapratiyogitva*) and so forth—even with respect to that contradiction, the very absence of pervasion (*vyāptyabhāva*) is what must be relied upon.

As it has been said: "Although the cognition of the nature of the contradiction conceived by you does not depend on the cognition of the absence of pervasion, nevertheless, it is not an obstacle to inference."

As for the cognition that constitutes an obstacle, since it consists in the knowledge of the absence of pervasion (*vyāptyabhāva*), it is itself dependent upon that very knowledge of the absence of pervasion; how then can the absence of pervasion not be something upon which [the obstacle] depends?
By this very [argument], the claim that "even when there is a confusion of the things to be superimposed (upadheya), there is no confusion of the superimposing property (upādhi)" is also refuted;

for it has been stated that even in the case of a contradictory [reason], the presence of the reason in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa)—just as in the case of a common [inconclusive] reason—is what constitutes the superimposing property.
Therefore, in order to avoid the confusion of commonality, [the author] refutes what you have postulated with the words: "For it is not so," etc.
Now, one might object that in the definition of "contradiction" as stated by Maṇi, there is no dependence upon the absence of pervasion (vyāptyabhāva); therefore, he says: "tvad... [and so forth].
The meaning is "conceived by a jewel-maker" (or "fashioned by a jeweler").
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of [the fallacy] where the locus of the reason does not occur in that which possesses the property to be proven (*sādhyavat*), and so forth.
[This is] dependent upon the knowledge of the absence of pervasion (*vyāptyabhāva*).
The sense is that, when that [counter-positive] is known, it is difficult to ascertain its pervasion as determined by that [counter-positive].
He refutes the distinctness of the contradictory (*viruddha*) from another perspective, as stated by Maṇi, with the words "by this" (*etena*).
"From what has been stated."

The meaning is: "because it has been established by us. [End of section] "That which is imagined by you. [End of section] (Note: The numbers 1, 2, and 3 refer to variant readings found in the manuscripts ga, ṭa, rā, ṭa, and ḍa.)
[The section on] the discussion of the defects of inference, page 325:

That which constitutes "contradiction" (viruddhatva) is merely an indicator of non-pervasion (avyāpti), because it does not consist in the absence of pervasion and so forth, just like a counter-argument against a limiting condition (upādhi-pratikūla-tarka) and the like.
But it is not itself a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

As for the form of "contradiction" (*viruddhatva*) consisting in the occurrence solely in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), since it is conflated with a common incidental condition (*sādhāraṇopādhi*), it is indeed included within the category of "non-pervasion" (*avyāpti*).

By this, the following distinction is refuted: that the absence of the qualifying portion (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*), namely non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), which enters into the definition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) as "non-deviant co-location" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), constitutes the "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) fallacy; the absence of the qualified portion (*viśeṣyāṃśa*), namely co-location itself, constitutes the "contradictory" (*viruddha*); and the absence of the whole [the compound] constitutes the "unestablished-pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*).

This refers to the specific type of "unestablished" (*asiddhi*) which is a particular form of fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), namely "unestablishedness due to lack of pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*), when one takes its internal subdivisions into account within the general classification of fallacious reasons.

Furthermore, regarding the fallacious reason of sublation (*bādha*), in cases such as "the lake possesses fire while possessing smoke," there would result the undesirable consequence of a general classification of fallacious reasons by including distinctions such as the absence of the qualifier, which is included within the absence of the qualified probandum.

In this context, because they are well-established and pervasive, the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) consisting of qualified absences—namely *savyabhicāra* (inconclusive) and so forth—are [already accounted for]; thus, *asiddhi* (unestablished) is also a specific type of *hetvābhāsa*.

Indeed, the non-establishment of pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) consists of two sub-varieties: the non-establishment of the qualifier of pervasion (*vyāptiviśeṣaṇāsiddhi*) and the non-establishment of the subject of pervasion (*vyāptiviśeṣyāsiddhi*). There would be the consequence of a classification of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*);

The meaning is that, because these two apprehend the absence of the object of cognition (*grāhya*), they directly constitute an obstacle to inference.
This is precisely what [the author] intends by "this very thing."
The meaning is: "having intended precisely that object of cognition which has been stated in its extracted form."
The general refutation of the restrictive rule regarding fallacious reasons stated by others. // 40 //
I bow to that Hari, by whose grace I have composed this commentary—
the jewel born from the womb of Anasūyā, the illuminator of Ānvīkṣikī.
May the Supreme Person be pleased by that which I have spoken, as impelled by Śrī Prāṇapati, who is filled with the virtues of faultless exposition.

Because people are generally of dull intellect, we have spoken this merely as a preliminary discussion for the sake of wishing to grasp that [truth]; let the wise forgive us for not providing a full textual exposition.
Thus ends the third chapter of the *Nyāyadīpa*, a commentary on the *Tarkatāṇḍava*, composed by the ascetic Rāghavendra, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Sudhīndratīrtha;
herein concludes the *Tarkatāṇḍava* together with its commentary.
May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Written by Pt. Hegalatarāma for Kyārthamā on July 20, 2001.
